- - "AN OLD MAN'S DARLING." Polly is my little wife, Bo she loves to hear me call her, On her voyages through life May misfortune ne'er befall her. I am growing old and gray, She is—guess how old to-day. Shall I tell you? Never mind, It to you can scarcely matter; How I fear to leave bei.,lnd Such a wealth of youth and chatter Who, I wonder, when I'm dead, Will she learn to love instead? Polly sits upon my knee, When the day its lattice closes. And her heart reveals to me All its laughter and its roses, While her merry, trustful words Fill my train with singing birds. Folly Is my little wife, Polly is my only darling; When embittered with the strife, Folly's kisses stay my gnarling, And her arms about my neck Every sorrow seeres to check. Polly only has one care, That is, how she most can please me, Yet she sometimes pulls my hair, Does her little best to tease me; , Has of saucy ways a score, Which but mike me love her more. - I am sixty, she is six There was social one I remember Who had Polly's smile and tricks, In a long-ago Decemb-r : For my child was her mamma, I am Folly's grandpapa. F-11cocIN Comic A,2n•tal. HOBICE LARD.

A uzeinel hint i 3 wrapm d up in the folawing thin shoes, January, IS—." "Tne only way to look at a lady's faults," exclaimed a gall "is to shut your eyee." Compositors are the most eentlemanly-and self-constrained Of men. They never want a linger in the pie. A little boy being asked what the chief_ end of an editor was, replied, "The end what's got the head on." An old lady, who has several grown-up daughters, feeds them on fish diet, because it is rich in phosphorus, and phosphorus is the essential thing in making matches. Being unable to attend his silver wedding, a man whose home is in Gelyeston, Texas, sent from his mining camp in Nee' Mexico a silver trick as his present to the bride. The weight of the gift was seven pounds. A convict in State-prisonhaamade complaint that.though he was sent there for heing diehonest, he is now compelled 20 cut out pieces of pasteboard to be out in the soles of shoes sold as leather ! He wante to know how he can be expected to reform. THE UNACCUSTOMED PEN.—Art illiterate soldier contrived to spell the word "usage" without using a letter properly belorming to it. He wrote it " yowzitch," and when told that the spelling was incorrect declared that nobody could spell with a quill pen from a strange goose. An Irishman saw the sign of the "Rising Sun" near the jleeen Mel?, and underneath was written A. Moon, the man's name who kept it being Aaron Moon. The Irishman, think- ing he had discovered a just cVSSe for triumph, roars out to hia companion, " Only see, Phelim, see here they talk of . She Irish bulls; only do but see row! here's a fellow puts eis the Rising Son and calls it A Moon." Queen Elizabeth being much enraged against Dr. Hayward, eanteor of the "Life of Henry 1V.," had ordered her law officers to proceed against him; and, amongst others in- quired of Bacon, "it there was not treason in the boa ?" • The whey lawyer readily answered, "No, madam, I cannot answer for there being treason in it but I am certain it con- tains mach felony." "How." eagerly exclaimed her Majesty. - "Bow, and wherein ?" "In many passages," replied hr, "which he has stolen from Tacitns." Joss Bauxos's PHILOSOTRY.—Linv ov notoriety allwus inaVs a pheol ov a man, and often, at last, a knave. I never have seen enny boddy yet that syaz perfekt, but I hay seen sum so perfekt that they wazn't agreeable. What the world wants must just now in more honesty and less genius. Things hay got so krooked that yu kan't hardly find a cow even that kin give milk that ain't watered. I kno what tree will make shingles bi looking at It; this i call instinkt, and It haz been worth more to me than college laming. I rather think the man who lies and don't kno it is a cheaper man in the market than the man who lies and duzkno it; but I may be mistaken about this. KITE•FLYING EXTRAORDINARY.—Brockron, in this state, has recently been the scene of ex*raordinary kite-flying. A doctor was boasting of what he could do in that line, when two lawyers offered to furnish him with the string if he Would repeat what he claimed to have done. Their offer was accepted, and he required them to procure 5,000 feet of rope three-eights of an inch in diameter. He made his kito frame of timber two inches wide and half an inch thick, and covered it with Manila paper. Its area was nearly 250 square feet. The monster rose lightly till all the rope had been paid out, and floated at the height of over half a mile, until it was hauled down by running the rope under a pulley-wheel and hitching a horse to it. If the doctor had made a bole through the centre of a barn door, strung the door on the kite string after the manner of the toy known as a " messenger," and himself gone up and taken a seat in the band of his kite, he would have produced a genuine sense- eatlon.—A meriCan. A LEGRND or WENSLEYDALF..—On oar right lay Addle- borngb, and another hill cilled Bishondale Gavel ; facing us was Bishopdele, running towards Waldendale. Some of these old names call up the memory of the Danes. Our hind guide told us that Swenythwaite and ;Thoresby lay behind Temple; he told no, too, that beyond Addleberough was Raydsle, in which lies the far-famed lake called ilemer- water. The legend has been often told, but still it seems too essential a feature of Wensleydale to omit narrating it here. There is a legend very like it in Brittany. Centuries ago— before the birth of our Saviour, and soon after the Romans %et feet in Britain—there was a large and thriving town on the fete of Sernerwater, beside what was then a little wind- iest stream. The inhabitants of this town were wealthy but hard-hearted, and when one day a poor, ragged old man came into it and asked at their doors for food, he was sent Inca one house to another, and at last, spite of his white hair and miserable starved looks, he was told to depart. Sorrowfully he left the town behind him; but at a little cottage just beyond it he was asked to come in, arid there was hospitably entertained. Next morning he rose early, toek lo eve of his kind hosts, and then began to climb one of the green hills that new surround the lake. When he resesed the top he pointed to the city, and cried out— " Semerwater rise, Semerwater eink, And swallow all the town - Save you hie house, Where they gave me meat and drink :"

Then came the shock ot an earthquake, the eround opened, I the water rose higher and higher, and spread over the land till it covered more than a hundred acres; but the proud city was never seen again' its only vestige was the little wsyside cottage where the hungry beggar had been fed and I sheltered. Sometimes in the gloom of evening a tishertnan on the lake has had a sudden vision of the spires and raofs et the submerged city ; but the vision is rare. The river Baia flaws on from Semerwater te join the Yore, and near Its mouth is Bainbridge. This Bainbringe' or Bainbrigg, meet have been in the heart of the forest, for here it was tests) nary to blow the Forest Horn every night at ten o'clock I • from the end of September till Shrovetide, to guide wander- ; be travellers. Mr. Hardcastle says there was still, in 1564, a village hornblowsr at Bainbridge. THE PRESENT AND Ferrous or Russets—Russia doe not deserve so much contempt. Introduced the Lest of any nation into civilised Europe, the progress that Russia has Attie in two or three hundred years is considerable. It . is still a virgin nation which has never felt its heart beat quickly, and which has borne no fruit. Its genius Is still stammering, and is only just beginning to arrange its thoughts clearly. Let us wait until this people come of age before we pronounce about its future. Until now we have had but the germ of the earliest developments of the Slav nation. This race has not been cultivated and made fertile by Idea. It is a motionlem mass which has as yet received no impulse. So, in the life of this people, everything, up I till our days, has been incoherent, irregular, and rough like forces in course of formation in nature. If there be bar- barity, it is a vigorous barbarity which will contribute one day to the development of the human race, as did formerly the Germanic barbarity which was neighbour to the brilliant civilisation of the Romans and Gauls. Besides this bar- , barity it less in the manners of the country than in the ' proceedings of the Government. Russians do not live in a Savage state like Hottentots. There is nothing more gentle, nose humane, than the Russian peasant, and murders are much less frequent in the Muscovite country districts than in the streets of Berlin and Paris. If we look at Russia from our European point of view, we see it in an absolutely false light. This people has no sentiments in common with us, and that is why perhaps some day It will regenerate many things in this world; forms of State and of private , life. It knows nothing of our modern institutions and our political conquests. In 1825, on the occasion of the insur- :section in becember, the soldiers who cried," Long live the Constitution!" believed that it meant the wife of the Grand "eke Constantine. We are too apt to forget that there are t WO Russlas. At St. Petersbbrg there is the official, feudal, aristocratic, and bureaucratic Russia, half German, half European ; in the immense plains of the rest of the empire there is a Russia clothed in sheepskins, motionless and thcughtful as its ancestor Asia, silent and unchangeable in Its apathetic fatalism and its stiff orthodoxy, faithful to its traditions, thoroughly Russian, and accepting with the re- signation of an animal the yoke with which those to whom he! .ng all the riches, the privileges, the powers, and the rights, weigh it down. Betereee these two Antipodes the world of the revolution is at work. This latter is a miser- able minority, outcome of the higher ranks, isolated and sa.shout support in the nation, and consequently obliged to h'ite itself in darkness, to strike with mines, bombs, and desegers, and then to run away.— Victor Tissot. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c. The Sussex Advertiser reports the capture of a fine gyr falcon, now an exceedingly rare bird, at Batsdean, in Sussex. An Ohio dairyman, who claims to have weighed the skimmed milk fed to swine and the gain in flesh thereof, says 100 pounds of ekimmed milk will produce three pounds of pork. On the arrival of the mail train about five o'clock at Card- roe, the village letter-bags are taken from the station to the post-offica by a very handsome collie. Tne dog punctually reachea the station about five minutes before the train arrives, and when the begs are thrown from the van, takes them in his mouth and sets off without delay to deliver them. INFLUENCE OF 'THE WEIGHT OF SEED ON THE YIELD OF THE CROP.—In studying this subject:: Messrs. Birner and Troschke divided various samples of oat-seed into three qualities, which they distinguish as iheavy, medium, and light, and in every case it WAS found that the beet crop was obtained from the sample in which the individual seeds were heaviest. Similar experiments with beans gave correspond- ing results. This investigation is one which deserves to be widely confirmed, and, as it is Of an extremely simple char- acter, it commends itself at once to the attention of all culti- vators. VEGETABLE CREESB.—It is well known thatlthe Chinese cultivate certain varieties of peas for the purpose of extract• ing from them legumine (vegetable casine), of which to make cheese. The legamine is soluble in water, and is pre- cipitated by diluted acids. It is found:in large quantity in leguminous grain, such as peas, lentils, and kidney beans, in which it takes the place of gluten (vegetable "fibrine) of Icereals. Tne European farmer no more suspects of presence ' 6f cheese in ripe peas than he recognises the "rennet" in leguminous gran in germination. In fact, there is de- veloped in the peas and beans, at that time, an acid fer- mentation which absolutely disselves the Altman ,in the same manner as the gastric juice in the stoma* of 'rumba- ants. . Au EXTRAORDINARY DUCK I—A. :I:cerreepondent writes that he possesses a clack which ha-s performed the extraor- dinary feat of laying a large double yolked-egg daily for the past fortnight. She is a young clack of tine common kind, and commPnced laying on the 3rd September, when she was only 22 weelts old. Strange to say her eggs at first were small, more so even than is usual with a young beginner, till she began favouring us with these giant pro- ductions. It need hardly be stated that her appetite is wonderfully good, the food she consumes being almost twice 1 as much an a duck generally eats, her favourite dish being barley-meal and ground maize mixed.—The Farmer. THS SHOREHAM WEATHER STONE—DO the Shoreham people know that they have in their church one of the best barometers in existence? We did not know it till the other day the custodian of the building called our attention to it. It was fins and bright at the time as we passed through the churchyard, where we met him hard at work trimming some of the graves. We spoke about the weather; and he shook his heed, and in oracular style said it was going to rain. We asked his reason for thinking so, and he led us into the church, where he pointed out a particular slab almost under the tower, and called our attention to a dark mark on it about the size and shape of a man's sock. In fine weather, he said that mark was hardly to be distinguished, but when it showed up it was a sure sign of rain. And true enough ..t. efore traly hours the rain came down. There is little 4oubt but that come kind of stones are very susceptible to atmospheric influences. CANON BAGOT.—The following lively description, from the letter of an Irish lady, of an Irish canon who was the hero of the dairy show held last week in Dublin, affords a pleesent picture of a clerical type unfortunately somewhat rare on tither side of the Channel. She writes;—" Canon Begot, to whom all honour is due,lectured pleasantly and instructively while the churning was going on. The Canon is a short, broad, good-humoured man, with a brown rosy face and fine brown eves, and looks as if he had been always nourished on the milk of human kindness, together with some of his own A 1 Irish butter. He is rector of Pouts- down, county Kildare, and his father, grandfather, and great- grandfather were all his predecessors in the rectorship. His church and school are kept in the nicest order, but not hav- ing enough parish work to engage all his energies, he de- votes himself to the improvement of what is one of the stable manufactures of his country. He farms about eighty acres of land, has a fine dairy of his own, and besides butter, sends fresh liquid cream to London. Not satisfied with the usefulness of his dairy labours, he keeps a number of the best agricultural implements and machines. and lends them to neighbours who may wish to borrow them. Canon Begot is a favourite with all who know him. PLANTING Rosr.s.—The time has arrived when this be- comes an important consideration, because if planted at once, even before the leaves have been shed, the earth will still retain an amount of warmth which induces -a very free emission-of roots at once thus placing the plants in a very superior position to late-planted ones. In these, as in many other cases, the great element of success consists in a tho- rough preparation of the soil. Drainage, of course, is first to be attended to; and as the border should be trenched 3 feet deep, the depth of the drain should be at least 4 feet, and over the pipes should be put a foot of rubble. This may seem an unnecessary precaution, but no roses can be ex- pected to flourish long in a satisfactory manner whose roots are in a cold wet medium charged with stagnant moisture. With these precautions the nature of the soil is not of that, great importance ',which some consider indispensable, pro- vided it is well broken up, and a good amount of well- decomposed manure incorporated with it during the opera- tion; for choice, however, a soil which is strong and what is called holding, and in texture stiff, approaching clay, is preferable to a very light soil. A CREAM-PRODUCING MACHINE.—The opportunity was afforded me while recently in Berlin of contemplating a ' novel and curious invention, the introduction of which int? London can be only a matter of time. This consists in the cream-extrtcting machines of Lefeldt and Lentech, at pre- I sent at work in the establishment of Herr Bolle, a not in- appropriate name for one dealing in milk. The principle of these machines rests on the application of centrifugal force. Milk, as it comes from the cow, is put into a species of drum, which is kept rapidly revolving; the milk, as the heavier portion, flies to the outer circumference and is col, lected by a species of lip; the cream, which is lighter, falls to the inner circumference. The establishment of Herr Bolls is not unlike an English sugar refinery. The milk, lifted into tanks on; the top floor, falls by gravity into the creaming machine. Two or three qualities of cream are extracted. The thickest quality goes to the confectioners, and the second quality to hotels. Butter ,and cheese are made on the premises, and the skim milk is sold at twopence a quart. What is not required for human consumption is converted into a:species of condensed whey, which is useful for feeding horses. One hundred and twenty of these ma- chines are now, I am told, in use in Germany. About 35,000 litres:of milk are, when the eight machines in em- ployment in Berlin are in fall work, dealt with per diem.— Gentlerean's Magazine.

Teat DALMATIAN.--This breed of dogs is sometimes erroneously called the lesser Dane, and at times vul- garly, but graphically, termed the plum-pudding dog, !Manse Of its being spotted all over upon a white ground with round even spots. It is evidently a variety of the p Acter, the occasional appearance of liver spots in- stead of black ones pointing to this origination. The chief points of the breed are a graceful body, between that of the pointer and ball-terrier, and the body, heed, and ears free from any pitch, but profusely spotted all over with round spots, from the size of a shilling to a halfpenny; the closer these spots, without being run or joining, the better, and they should be the same distance apart all over the body ; the black-spotted is to ;be preferred to the liver. spotted, but if a dog of the latter colour is really well spotted it would be better to breed from it than a badly marked black dog. The liver-spotted are generally free from patches, but the black are often more closely spotted. \lt is deemed a great fault to have white hairs growing on the spots and for this and other reasons the Dalmatian is a I very dificult dog to breed up to a high standard, but so are 1 all other high-class kinds of dog, and there is no credit to (1 any one who succeeds in obtaining easily-bred dogs, and II therefore this may not be deemed a drawback. The !Jaimetian is far before many other races in respect to beauty, but has lover become really fashionable, though it will probably have its turn some of these days. It is regarded as a car- riage dog, and is generally seen following the horses, where 1 it certainly looks very well if a well-marked specimen. BEDDING FOR DOGS.—There is nothing to equal straw as bedding for dogs to lie upon, and, where there is an abun- dance, it is warmer and softer than anything else. If there is no difficulty in obtaining it, we would prefer the oaten in winter and the wheaten in summer. Shavings may form a •tolerably good:bed, but we do not think the dogs care for them. Dogs have been known to be injured by them, espe- cially where some had got mixed with the food. If they are used a little turpentine may be sprinkled over them from a fine syringe. Hay is not to be recommended for bedding, as with some dogs it produces an irritable condition Of' the nasal passages. Whether this is produced by the diig snit/lug in minute dust like sporulee, or from the smell of the hay, we do not pretend to say. The soiled portion of the straw should be taken away every morning, and the bed well shaken up, the straw to be changed once in about four days, and the old taken away and put in a manure heap to rot. Amateur gardeners will find manure from a kennel, if perfectly metered, as good as any other to be obtained, and splendid for growing either flowers or vegf.tible, but of coarse care must be taken as to how it is used. THE CLEANLINESS OF CATS.—Of all our domestic animals the cat is certainly the most particular as to her personal appearance, and is very careful in the attention she pays to cleanliness. Nature has adorned her with a nirst beautiful coat of the softest, silkiest fur, and loveliest of colours, and she spares no pales to keep it clean. Thera c..n be little question but that the eat is very proud of her appearance, and likes to look her best, so that she is ever claaning and washing herself. A well-bred parlour cat which has been properly trained will never allow a speck of dirt to stilly her fur, aud you can always tell whether pussy is neglected or properly cared for by the appearance of her coat. If she 1 has no place she can call home or if left to herself, badly fed land badly kept, she loses that self-respect which is her great Characteristic, and becomes a dirty Ishmaelite. When a Cat's coat begins to appear rough and stare, it is the first 1 sign of approaching illness, but upon thli point we shall have something to say later on. PEnnexs, &C., IN PIGEON LOFT.—Last week we described how to fit up the nest boxes, but in addition to what was then stated, a nest-pan must be put in each box. These pans are of saucer shape, and the most nesfal ones are made lef ware and glazed. They can be bought at a reasonable

price at almost any pottery' or Ware shop. What is to be put in them we will deal with at the proper season of the year. The next thing is to fit up perches on the walls and ledges, and of these there is an endless variety. We may first mention what must be done, no matter the kind of perch adopted, and that is to so arrange them that the drop. pings of the birds in one row will not fall upon those in the row below, for it will be necessary to have more than one row. And, in addition, the perches must be from twelve to eighteen inches apart, so as to prevent the birds being crowded or pecking at each other. The commonest plan is to have projecting perches made of broom handle!, cut about six inches long, and fastened into the walls, or rounded pieces of wood about the same length and thickness. These can be placed so that there will be no bird immediately below, but this wed° not think sufficient, and wherever this form of perch is adopted, there should be a slanting board placed underneath upon which the droppings can fall and be directed on the floor without touching the birds. These I beards can easily be cleaned, and if a little sand is thrown over them every day, wiU be found very effective; but the distance between the bottom of the board and the perches below must be sufficient to prevent the birds hurting themselves. Another form of perch, and one which is used by some of the beat fanciers is in the shape of the letter At:with the top portion taken off, making it of this shape ' The perch board should be about two inches wide, and the widest part between the side boards six inches wide. No slanting board is needed when this plan is adopted, and they are equally as good perches as any other. Whatever the kind used round off all corners, so that the birds may not injure themeelves by striking against them, the young ones bend their bones by perching upon them, or the feet of young and old cut by sharp edges. This is an important point, and when it is attended to the loft will be complete. FITTINGS FOR- BIRD Ce.azs.—There are one or two little etceteras in connection with cages which need to be attended to, and will conduce to the comfort of the inmates or of the owner. In some cages a drawboard or false bottom is fitted, but we prefer those made without it. having a turn-rail. Nearly every cage sold nowadays is fitted with this handy contrivance. It consists of a portion of the front, the fall width of the cage, turning on a stout wire, and the sand or other contents can be raked out, with a scraper made for the purpose, without disturbing the inmates. Soma outlet for this is necessary, or the contents of the cage battom must be lifted through the door' a plan Which has nothing to recom- mend it, considering the simplicity of the tarn-rail arrange- ment. This rail should be about an inch and a half wide, which will leave ample room for all purposes. Perches come next, and should not be made too small. About three.eightbs of an inch is the right size, giving the bird something to rest on as well as grasp. The perches should be cut an inch or two longer than the cage, and if the ends are notched they can be put in and taken out without opening the door. The best wire for a cage is No. 16, galvanised, and the distance between the wires half an inch. A door will be needed, about three inches square, and on one aide, a wire or two from the end, should be the water-hole wire, and on the other side two wire holes for seed. With a small sliding drawer for special food the cage will be complete. but before it is occupied it should be first varnished or sized inside, and than this covered over with whiting mixed with size, of which two coats should be given, the second after the first is dry. TROUGHS, &C., FOR FEEDING RABBlTS.—Ribbiti should always be given their food in a proper trough, one that can- not easily be overturned, for there is nothing more disgust- ing than to see food scattered about the ground, mixed with manure and dirt, and giving forth an odour more strnng than pleasant. There are various kinds of troughe.sold, the best of which is made from glazed ware with a wider bottom than top, so that the animal cannot very easily get the food out of the dish. Others are made of iron and others also of wood, but if there are several rabbits it is best to get a large one made of zinc with wire stretched across the top, and thus give to each rabbit a place to itself. In addition to this there should be a rack for hay, which is best made in the same way as are racks in stables. The first cost, which need not be large, will be far more than compensated by the saving of material. Nothing can be more wasteful than feeding rabeits in the ordinary pie dishes and throwing the hay on the ground, but, unfortunately, both these are very
practices

Tiu RIOTS AT SALEII.—SOMe months ago very serious riots occurred at Salem, an, important town in the Madras Presidency. A number of the principal Hindoo inhabitants organised an attalk on the Mahometaas, destroyed their mosque, and killed several women and children in circum- stances which recalled the horrors of Cawnpore. It is satis- factory to know that the Commission instituted by the Government has dealt with the criminals in an exemplary manner. The first accused, a merchant, has been sentenced to penal servitude for life; the second, a pleader, to five years' rigorous imprisonment and 2,000 rupees fine; the third, an overseer, and the fourth, a surgeon, to seven years' rigorous imprisonment; the fifth and sixth, subordinate judicial officers, to five years' rigorous imprisonment; the eighth and ninth, Government clerks, to seven years' penal servitude; the 10th, a merchant, to one day's imprisonment and 10,000 rupees'fine ; the 12th, a moroliont, to five years' imprisonment and 2,000 rupees fine; the 13th, a merchant, to five years' imprisonment and 1,000 rupees fine; and the 14th, a shopkeeper, to three years' imprisonment. Five thousand rupees of the fines will be given to the Mahometan c,mmunity for the purpose of building their mosque in a different locality. SOCIALISM IN FRANCE.

Arabi's trial and the progress of the false 'prophet divide public attention at Cairo. At a Council of Ministers bald under the presidency of the Khedive, the progress of the Mandi was discussed, and it was decided to despatch a mes- sage to the Governor if Khartoum, urging him to hold eut against the attacks of the prophet until assistance arrived. There is now considerable apprehension as to the situation in the Soudan, the whole of which. except Khartoum, is in the hands of the Mandi, and it has been decided to enlist as many black troops as possible to fight against him. The latest telegrams from the Soudan do not represent the situation there to be so gloomy as was pictured by the de- spatches of a few days ago. Khartoum is declared to be safe, and the false prophet still at some distance from the fortress. Baker Pasha expects to be able to despatch 10,000 troops against Mandi in the course of the next three weeks. THE JOINT CONTROL. The inter- rogatory was addressed to the Cheri( Pasha, and related to the claim of M. Bredif, the French Comptroller, to attend the Egyptian Council meetings. Cherif replied that as the English Comptroller-General had been instructed not to at- tend the sittings of the Council, it had been decided not to invite M. Bredif. No exception could be taken to this:ex- planation of the situation, and thus the matter stands.

div.head: GENERAL ROBERTS ON THE STATE
div.p: GENERAL ROBERTS ON THE STATE

OF THE ARMY. General Sir Fredetick Roberts has an article in the Nin,e- teenth Century for November explanatory of his speech at the Mansion House in February, 1881. He shows that the system at present in force differs widely from that which a two years' experience in the field enabled him to criticise with some confidence; and that because he had misgivings regarding the organisation of the army as it then existed, it by no means follows that he is equally dissatisfied with the present state of affairs. He always advocated reforms likely to benefit the army. It never occurred to him that the old system of long cervice could be reverted to, but no trial could be sstisfactory unless due consideration were ' given to the results of practical experience in the field. His criticisms of the short service system were not made with- out sufficient reason, and had been fully justified by the altered conditions of enlistment. What had been done to improve the position and prospects of non-commissioned officers woald help more than anything to render the army efficient. The non-commissioned rank is the backbone of a regiment, especially under short service, where a number of young soldiers pass rapidly through the ranks. Still he should like to see a slight leaven of old plivates in the ranks. The wholesale discharge of needy men is an inevitable shortcoming of the present organisation• which would have to be faced. He hopes the connection between the militia and volunteers and the regular army may become so intimate as practically to remove difficul- ties about the reserve. England should not rest satisfied until she possesses a large, thoroughly trained reserve, and is able in one week to embark a well-organised corps of 25,000 —every unit physically fit for service, suitably dressed and equipped—with the necessary arrangement previously made for sufficient transport at the base of operations.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

About 700 weavers at Messrs. M. Oldroyd and Sons factory, Dewsbury, are on strike against a reduction of -?Id. per string on fancy woollens, and id. on other goods. If the dispute is not shortly settled 3,000 persons will be out of employment. Sir Joseph Pease, M.P., has agreed to act as arbitrator in the North of England iron trade wages dispute, provided' that the evidence upon which he will have to base his award can be taken in London, his Parliamentary duties not per- mitting the honourable gentleman to leave London. 13tras or SALE AND FAILURES. - In the week ending October 28, 1882, there were 937 bills of sale in England - and Wales, a decrease of 130 over those of tho correspond- ing period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 202, a decrease of 13. The totals for portion of year to October 21, 12, are—bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 33,843, a decrease of 2,970; the failures gazetted number 8,767, a decrease of 785.—Stubb's .3lercantile Goradge.

FARMING AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Express says:—" A week of very heavy and almost con- tinuous rainfall has delayed wheat sowing everywhere, and there are now elerdents in the situation _which, so far as they go, are distinctly adverse to the wheat crop, of 1883. Amother week of adverse weather would materially contract the probabilities of next year's wheat harvest. The weather has been such as to render thrashing an impossibility, ex- cepting from barns, and has further reduced the very im- perfect condition of farmers' deliveries. There has not been much quotable alteration in prices, but all damp and inferior samples are increasingly difficult to sell, and in some markets rather cheaper to buy. Country flour, too, has been rather cheaper to buy, and trade for breadstuffs in London closed on Friday with a decidedly weaker tendency. There has been no change in values of other descriptions of home- grown produce. The trade for wheat off stands in London has been exceedingly slow throughout the week, and on Fri- day red winters were 61 cheaper to buy. In Liverpool on Friday values for wheat were generally id. per cental lower all round. American flour was occasionally 6J. cheaper in London on Friday. Maize was dearer. Linseed I 3d. dearer.

THE Lexcestinn InoN TRADE.—The market on Tuesday was well attended, but the new orders offering either for pig or manufacturediron were few, and as a rule only for small quantities. Consumers, who are mostly hell bought, are running off their contracts before buying further; whilst makers, not having much iron to offer, are generally firm, although not holding out for the full extent of the recent advance. In Lancashire pig iron a few odd lots are sold on the basis of 493. for forge and 50s. for foundry, less 21 de- livered, equal to Manchester, and district brands average 49a. 6d. to ses. for forge and 51s. to 525. for foundry, less 2. In the finished-iron trade now business seems to be quietening down somewhat, and prices are a trifle easier upon the full quarter-day quotations, local bars delivered into the Manchester district being obtainable at from X 6 Ns. per ton' with other descriptions of finished iron in propor- tion,although one or two makers hold for more money. For shipment there is still a fairly good demand, although this branch of trade is not so brisk as it was. Tan LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE—The advance in the price of coal and in the rate of wages paid to the men, of which an indication has already been given, commenced on Wednesday. In the Manchester district the pit and delivery rates upon all descriptions of house fire .coal are advanced 10d per ton, and furnace coal, burgy, and slack 5d per ton. In the Wast Lancashire districts the advance represents is per ton upon last month's prices for all classes of round coal, with advances ranging from 3d to 6d per ton upon engine fuel. The advacce in wages to the men throughout Lanca- shire, except where the sliding scale is in operation, aver- ages 10 per cent. The market has yet to be tested as to whether this upward movement can be permanently main- tained. The rates now quoted for coal delive.red- into the Manchester district are as under :—Best, 13s 4d to 14s 7d; seconds 12s 6d ; common house coals and best riddled nuts, us to us 8d; furnace coal, 9s to 9s 7d; burgy, 7s 7d; and slack, 9s 9d per ton. The average pit prices for Lancashire are about us for best coals, such as the Wigan Arley, 8s 61 to 9s for seconds, 70 6d to 8s for common.house coal, 6s 9d to 7s 6d for furnace coal, 4,s 9d to 5s Od for burgy, and 3$ 9d to 4s 3d for good slack. - _

div.head: RETURN OF SIR G. WOLSELEY FROM EGYPT.
div.p: RETURN OF SIR G. WOLSELEY FROM EGYPT.

Sir Garnet Woleeley met with a splendid reception on his return home on Saturday. He landed at Dover at half-past three in the afternoon. Notwithstanding the boisteroue state of the weather, thousands of persons flocked to the Admiralty Pier and heartily cheered Sir Garnet, the first to welcome him being Lady Wolseley and her daughters. On proceed- ing to the Lord Warden Hotel the gallant officer was pre- sented with an address of welcome by the Corporation, to which he briefly replied, saying that it was most encouraging to know that his services were appreciated. He thanked them for a compliment in which the gallant officers and men who served under him were to share. He left for London by special train, which arrived at Charing Cross about 5,50. A distinguished company was present on the platform, includ- ing Mr. Gladstone, the Duke of Cambridge, Earl Granville, Mr. Childers, Earl Morley, the Duke and Duchess of Teck, Baroness Burdett-Coutts, Mr. A. B. Burdett-Coutts, Sir John Adye, General Willis, and General Sir Lintorn Simmons. As the train drew, up the Duke of Cambridge stepped to the carriage door and was the first to greet Sir Garnet, Mr. Gladstone following immedi- ately afterwards. The distinguished General drove out of the station amid the enthusiastic cheers of several thousands of persons. Sir Garnet, who had been commanded by Her Majesty the Queen to visit her at Balmoral, reached Perth on Monday morning on his journey north. He travelled by the east coast route, and breakfasted ht Perth, where he was loudly cheered by a crowd of spectators assembled on the platform. He arrived at Aberdeen about twelve o'clock, and was received at the station by the Earl of Aberdeen and Lord Provost Esslernont. Sir Garnet and the Lord Provost drove in an open carriage through several ef the streets of Aber- deen, and the General, on being recognised, was loudly cheered. He left Aberdeen for Balmoral at 20 minutes past twelve, and was accompanied on his journey by the Earl of Aberdeen. A large crowd assembled at Ballater station, and ' hearty cheers were raised as Sir Garnet drove off to Balmoral, which was reached about four o'clock. Sir Garnet Wolseley left Balmoral on Tuesday afternoon, and travelled by the Queen's messenger train from Ballater, at which place he received a most enthusiastic greeting. At Aberdeen station there was assembled a crowd of several thousands of spectators, who gave the gallant general a very 'warm reception. In the same train was a saloon carriage conveying the Duchess of Connaugnt on her southward journey to meet the Duke of Connaught, who is expected to arrive from the East at the end of the present week. The Duchess was also loudly cheered at .Aberdren.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

It is stated that Sir Stafford Nortlacote will vlsit Belfast in December to open the new Conservative Club, but will not be accompanied by the Marquis of Salisbury. A meeting of about three hundred labourers was held in Naas on Wednesday night, at which resolutions were adopted calling on the farmers net to injure the labouring classes by stopping hunting and thus preventing the circulation of money through the country. Reports received in Dublin on Saturday state that terrible distress is threatened in the West. On Tory Island, nine miles from the nearest land, over 300 people are without food and the means of getting any. Other portions of the western population are described as in a state of impending starvation.

Mr. Mooney, the president of the Land Leagne in America, has informed Mr. Egan, by telegraph, of his unalterable devotion. No amount of "British slanders," says Mr. Mooney, shall destroy his trust in the treasurer of tke League. It is to be observed that the statements whish are here described as "slanders" have been published mostly in Ireland and by Irishmen. It had • been expected that the trial of the ten persons charged with being concerned in the massacre of the Joyce family in county Galway would have taken place at the Commission Ceert in Dublin this week. On Tuesday, how- ever, one of, the counsel for the ollfence asked for an ad- journment on account of the disappointments his instruct- ing solicitor had met with in the effort to retain senior counsel; and Mr. Justice Barry postponed the trial to Wed- nesday next. Friday night's Dublin Gazette contains 37 notices by the Lord Lieutenant of his intention to appoint persons to in- vestigate claims for compensation tnder the Crime Act for murders and personal injuries. The particulars. as briefly and technically stated in the notices, recall the history of crime and outrage in Ireland during the past two years. The list includes no fewer than 17 murders.

The rewatd of £l,OOO offered by the Crovernment for the conviction of the murder of Constable Kavanagh, at Letter- fuck, has been paid. This large sum has been divided be- tween a few of the civilian witnesses. Of course the mem- bers of the constabulary force did not receive any portion of the reward, and some of the cililian witnesses would not ac- cept anything more than their travelling expenses, so that those amongst whom the reward was divided have received very considerable sums. A crowded meeting of members of the National Land and I Labour League of Great Britain was held at Burton Hall, London, on Sunday night, when the future policy of the Irish Parliamentary party was discussed. Mr. F. H. O'Don- nell, M.P., denied that there was any disunion amongst therm on the main points of the Irish national question, and said the Land Act was a standing obstacle to a reform of that vexed question of Irish discontent. Mr. Parnell intended shortly asking the Government to appoint a day for the further discussion of the land laws, and the hands of the Irish representatives must be strengthened in view of the Government refusing. Mr. Michael Davitt addressed a crowded and somewhat turbulent meeting at Aberdeen en Saturday night. Mr. Davitt, after dealing with various objections against the scheme of nationalisation, explained in detail the different features of the land for the people movement; and referring to the effect of the scheme on land tenure in Scotland, advis:A the farmers of Scotland to demand a reduction in rent by claiming the right of an independent tribunal to arbitrate between them and the landlords—a right that Mr. Gladstone had conceded to Ireland, and which it might be I possible to get him to concede to Scotland. A resolution in favour of a land nationalisation scheme was put to the meet- ing, and carried. •

A PULLMAN CAR ON FIRE. A PASSENGER BURNT TO DEATH. A disaster, the like of which has never before occurred on an English railway,happenea to a Midland express train early on Sunday morning, as it reached Leeds on its way from Lon- don to Scotland. Shortly after tickets had been examined at Normanton, it was found that a Pullman car, in which four gentlemen and an attendant were travelling, was on fire. The attendant at once raised an alarm, and endeavoured to communicate with the guard, but the cord seems to have failed to work, and the train travelled on at a high rate of speed until the engine driver saw the fire. Then he stopped the:train, and the attendant and three gentlemen in their nightdresses made their escape. Every effort was at once made to extinguish the fire, but for a time the fourth pas- senger was never thought of. At last the attendant made known the terrible fact that a passenger was still in the burning car. Redoubled efforts were immediately made to subdue the flames, but it was about half an hour after the fire began before this was accomplished, and then the charred remains of the nnfortuna.te gentleman were dis- covered in his berth. The deceased gentleman is Dr. Arthur, who was returning home after ten years' absence in Ceylon. His brother when he received the terrible news was waiting to meet him at Aberdeen. div.head: IMPERIAL
div.p: IMPERIAL

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. TEE BURNING OF ALEX ANDRIA.—Sir CHARLES DILKI Said the composition of the Commission which is to adjudi- • tate on claims arising out of the burning of Alexandria was at2resent the subject of negosiation between the Powers. r PALMER EXPEDITION.—Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMA.N, ;Plying to Mr. Ritchie, explained the purposes of Professor ahner's expedition, and gave all the information possessed by the Government as to its fate. He said that the evidence regarding the death of Professor Palmer could not be said to absolutely,conclusive, and that until Colonel Warren's rePort was received the Government could not say precisely _llO were the guilty parties, and it was therefore impossible State yet what steps would be taken for their punishment. THE OtrBAN INSUERECTION.—Mr. EVELYN ASHLEY in- Mr. O'Kelly that the surrender of leaders of the ,Cuban insurrection to the Spanish authorities by the Chief constable of Gibraltar ought not to have been, made except '4 conformity with the provisions of the Extradition Treaty, alld the Secretary for the Colonies had sent a despatch to Qibraltar in which he expressed his strong disapprobation 'c,c4 the transaction, and called for a full- inquiry. The . 'Vanish Government had also been informed that the sur-
lender was made in mistake. Lie TRANSPORT AND COMMISSARIAT SERVICES IN CIIILDERS said be should in a few days have

a full report from Sir G. Wolseley on the Transport and 'Commissariat Sarvic,3s in Egypt; meanwhile he was bound to say that nothing had occurred which could be called a ! breakdown of those services. TAR TROUBLE'S IN SOUDAN.—Mr. CrLADSTONR said the Government was at present in possession of only very im- I , Perfect information with regard to what had occurred in ,Boudan. The Egyptian Government had. applied to the talglish authorities for the counsel and aid of certain officers, aad that matter was now under consideration. . Tint PROCEDURE Rur.xs.—The House resumed considera- tion of the rules of procedure. Mr. BRYCE moved an ainendment to the first resolution, to the effect that the - aPeaker should not put the closure to the House except ,11Pon the request of a Minister of the Crown, or of the mem- Der in charge of a bill or of an original motion then under discussion, and that the Speaker should then give leave to the member to move the closure.—Mr. GLADSTONE opposed the amendment, which, after a long discussion, was negatived by- 152 votes to 100.—Mr. GransoN moved an amendment requiring the Speaker or the Chairman not to enforce the Pule until after such notice as he might consider to be just. The amendment was defeated by 149 votes to 88.—Cap- ta1n AYLMER then proposed that after the closure had been declared, the vote upon the subject closed should not be taken at once, but that the Speaker should name an hour 01 the next sitting but one of the House for the division.—The proposal was rejected by a majority of 58. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. SKr AND WOUNDED IN THE EGYPTIAN CAMPLION.—III taioly to a further enquiry as to the allegations of the want ..,01 proper treatment of the sick and wounded in the 4gytian campaign, Mr. CHILDERS, without prejudging the questions to be investigated by the Committee appointed, laid that beyond dispute no military expedition ever left this eountry with anything like the proportionate strength of Medical officers and attendants. _ ._.

--- THE SURRENDER Or POLITICAL PRISONERS.—The 811f- ftuder of certain political prisoners to Spain by the acting Police magistrate of Gibraltar was again referred to, and save rise to a warm discussion. Mr. EVELYN ASHLEY

Stated that the Secretary at the Colonial Office at Gibraltar, ill reply to a request from the Spanish' authorities, gave orders that the men should be arrested, but he naturally allprehended that inquiry would be made to see that their cases were such as to warrant compliance with the request. --Mr. CoWEN wished to know if the men were not purely Political exiles, and he elicited from Mr. Ashley the remark tlaat if one friendly Government catne forward to ask for the arrest of offenders it was the act of another friendly Government to comply with the request, a statement which Was met with loud cries of "No, no." Mr. Cowen desired to know if the remark applied to political exiles in this country, and was told that the Government received no statement whatever that these persona were political offenders, but it was said they were convicts who .had escaped from gabl. THE PROCEDURE Buts.—The debate on the procedure resolutions was resumed by Mr. WARTON, who moved the in- IMinion of three or four words in the cleiture resolution pro- Posed by the Government for the purpose of preventing klisunderstanding, and the PRIME Mnetsren at once agreed to accept them as placing the matter beyond all doubt.— Air. Gilmore then moved his " two-thirds " amendment. The right hon. gentleman, in supporting his amendment, urged th, e arguments made familiar by reiteration during ths oebate on the first reading of the resolution, and which have been frequently recurred to in the debates of last week. , Referring to the letter Mr. Gladstone had written to Sir : Stafford Northcote in April last, proposing to accept this sta. endment if the Conservative party gave their assistance i ill advancing public business, Mr. Gibson insisted upon l % knowing why that letter was written. Was it, he asked, ' from weakness on the part of the Government, or from a sense of public convenience? The Prime Minister was in this position, that he had to show why he was then ready tO propose to make the first rule, as amended by Mr. Gibson's Proposition, a standing order, and why now he thought it necessary to resist the proposition.—Mr. 01. am-rotes I followed, and to this part of Mr. Gibson's address he gave an answer for which the House could not ave been unprepared. The Premier explained that at the i Voe the letter referred to was written the House stood on i the threshold of May. There war a disposition on the part Of the Conservatives to extend the debate; and, although the Government had not altered their opinion as to the two- thirds majority, they made the proposal of a compromise in the hope that if the rules were got through they might oave about six weeks of useful legislation. He admitted that this was a very high price to pay for the boon, and it Was extremely doubtful whether they were right or not in offering it. Dealing with the objections to the proposal of the Government, the Premier showed that the gagging of a larZe minority is impossible. , There never had been a case in the House when a large minority wanted protection. Against the amendment he quoted the opinion of Sir .Stafford Northcote set forth in public speech in ,4877 and again in 1880, in which the right aenourable baronet strongly opposed a two-thirds Majority. Mr. Gladstone on his own part stated two objec- tions to the amendment—first, its injustice to small minori- ties, and secondly, its injustice to majorities in the House, who, being held responsible by the country for the business transacted in the House, had a right to corn- Plain of of a curtailment of their rights. The simple demand Of the amendment was that the pewer of the majority to Push forward the business of the House should be arbitrarily arrested by the veto of the minority. Rather than accept, the two-thirds majority, Mr. Gladstone declared amid loud Cheers, he would have no closure at all. It would be an ex- seas of power on the part of the Ministry to say that they Would resign if the amendment were carried. If it related to a matter of legislation there would be no alternative from that course. But it was essentially a matter for the House to decide, and Mr. Gladstone besought members not to give their sanction to the new principle advocated from the other Side. His personal interest in the matter was very small. 11 My life," he said, "is in the past." But he carried his thoughts forward to the work that might be done by other and abler men, and on their behalf he besought the House not to sacrifice the rights o! the majority to the demands of the minority. The right hon. gentleman, who spoke for an 11. Our and a quarter, sat down amid repeated bursts of cheer- mg from the crowded Liberal benches. The House imme- diately emptied, and with slight variations remained in that condition for the greater part of the night, during which it Was addressed by Mr. Ecroyd, Mr. Baxter, and Mr. Gregory (,:who gave expression to the diffidence'with which he addressed the House after the powerful speech of the Premier), Mr. 4.m01d Morley (who modestly presented himself in these salfavourable circumstances to make his maiden speech, .......Which was ranch applauded by those who heard it), Mr. Whitley, Mr. Buchanan, Col. Alexander, Mr. Alderman Powler, Mr. Heneage, Mr. Davey, Mr. Grantham' Sir John L, Übbook, who supported the amend.nont, and Mr. Whit- ,Dread, who cordially supported the original resolution. iSing just before midnight, Sir Richard Cross supported .•„oe amendment, speaking in a House of 60 members, who Lunstrated the two-thirds majority to the extent that that Proportion was on the Liberal benches. The debate Was 4d.lourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNICSDAY. , THE BURNING OF A PULLMAN CAR.—Mr. Alderman ,44wianasms gave notice that on Monday he would ask the fresident of the Board of Trade whether his attention had l'eell directed to the inquest upon the body of Dr. Arthur, Who was burned to death in the Pullman car near Leeds, and especially to the evidence of the engine driver, who stated , that he felt a pull at the cord, but did not immediately stop L, the train, because, on looking back, he could not discover ItlaYthing amiss with it. ' THE CLOTURE.—The debate on the rules of procedure was !eslimed by Mr. O'Doresextx, who urged that tLere were many I,.°lllortant measures upon which it was of extreme importance 'oat the minority should be allowed the fullest discussion. 1 ---,Mr. A. ARNOLD strongly objected to the amendment, and contended that the proposal of the Government was in har- IttlY with the ancient and time-honoured practice of the u ftse.—Mr. E. CLARKE objected to the Government resolu- because he believed it was simply intended to enable 'AI party at present in power to force on certain measures Ivhich they could not pass unless they were able to gag their :DPonents.—Mr. STANSFELD argued that the daunt with- an effective check entirely outside the question of ts4:ljorities whether bare or proportionate would ab a power tending in the long run to be d• used- Lord J. Marsrents denied that the con- of the House of Commons was such as to PtifY the drastic innovation now proposed.—Lord E. tifrZMAURICE thought it would be proved by experience ~, at the fears which had been expressed as to the effect of We Proposed changes upon our Parliamentary institutions lo „rte exaggerated, and asserted that the order which existed of the House was most distasteful and abhorrent to the mind looevery moderate Liberal.—Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL upon proportional majorities as a much greater inn°. s. li°ll on their ideas and customs than the oloture itself. - ge was a firm believer in the general infallibility of the laajority, and he was surprised that the Tory or Constitu- Liona t, 1 party should put forward with eagerness and avidity ',S innovation of a two-thirds majority. One certain con- 7nence of the adoption of the amendment would be that it ort!ld be mainly used to stifle the expression of Irish ba_!•lronal feeling in the House, and such a result would be te.) a fatal to the unity of the Empire than famine, pesti- iinthce.., and foreign conquest. Let them oppose the cloture to h°7 would, defeat it if they could, but he asked them not v"° Woad into falling into foreign fancies, and not to
I

div.head: PARLIAMENT.
div.p: PARLIAMENT.

abandon or damage the great trust which the past, present, and future of a great party commanded them diligently to secure.—Mr. GOSCIIHN thought the proposed rule would not stifle, but promote, discussion of the most important subjects, and the result would be an improvement in dehate.—On the motion of Mr. A. Rusous, the debate was adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THIIRSDAY.

USE OF REVOLVERS ITT BURGLARS.—Sir WM. HARCOURT, in reply to Mr. W. James, said that, in view of the re- cent extensive use of revolvers by burglars, he was in communication with the Commissioners of Police with the view of ascertaining what steps could be taken to limit the indiscriminate distribution of such arms which at present prevailed. BAYER PASHA.—In reply to Mr. O'Kelly, Sir CHARLES DILEE stated that, according to the latest information, Baker Pasha had not yet been appointed generalissimo of the Egyptian army. The Government had no concern in the views with which Turkey might regard any ap- pointment in connection with the Egyptian army. SUB-COMMISSIONERS.—Mr. HEALY raised a discussion in connection with the action of Sub-Commissioners and the appointment of valuers under the Irish Land Act, and moved the adjournment of the lions:. Mr. PARNELL warned the Government that unless they undertook dis- tinctly to afford an opportunity for the discussion of the latter question before the prorogation it would be continually bubbling up at awkward and inconvenient times.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in answer to an appeal from Mr. C. Russell, said it was impossible at the present moment to arrange to give a day for the discussion of any of the important ques- tions which were awaiting consideration. When further progress had been made with the business resolutions, the Government would be prepared to consider what other ques- tions might be advantageously introduced.—Mr. Healy withdrew the motion for adjournment. THE PALMER EXPEDITION.—MT. CAMPBELL-BANNER- MAN, in answer to Sir H. Tyler, read a letter from Captain Gill intimating his intention of accompanying Professor Palmer's expedition personally in order to cut the telegraph wire, and admitting that the journey would be attended with considerable risk. The route was selected by Captain Gill, in consultation with Professor Palmer. The Government had no particulars of the precise route followed. , THE EGYPTIAN HEROES.—MT. GLADSTONE, in reply to Sir Stafford Northcote, stated that he could not say whether the annuities to Sir Garnet Wolseley and Sir Beauchamp Seymour would be moved for during the present session, but, whether that were so or not, it would make no differ- ence to the two gallant gentlemen, as their annuities would date from the date of their peerages. There would be no necessity for the Committee of Supply upon the grants, as they would be charged upon the Consolidated Fund. The expenses attending the occupation of Egypt by her Majesty's forces were being defrayed under the authority already given to the Government by Parliament. Some demands would probaLly be made upon Egypt for a contri- bution towards the expenses of the expeditionary force. It would be necessary for the Government to ask for a further vote before the subject was wound up, tut the expenses over the vote of credit already granted would not, he hoped, be very large. He thought it would be hater not to pro- duce the Budget till the Government were in a position to to lay the whole matter completely before the House. THE CLOSURES DEBATE: GOVERNMENT VICTORY.— The debate on Mr. Gibson's amendment to the first of the Government resolutions en procedure was resumed by Mr. A. BALFOUR, who defended the "two-thirds" principle against that of a bare majority. The discussion was continued by Mr. LABOUCHERE, who stated "the views of the democracy" on the question, Colonel STANLEY, who thought the necessity for the cloture might be avoided by better arrangements for ensuring the progress of business Mr. Jesse Collings, Mr. Newdegate, Mr. Stuart Wortley, Mr. H. H. Fowler, and Mr. Chaplin.— Mr. PARNELL adnounced his intention to vote against the amendment.—Sir STAFFORD NORTIMOTR charged the Irish party with baying been influenced by "secret negotia- tions" with the Government.— The Marquis of HART- INGTON replied, and the House divided, when Mr. Gibson's amendment was rejected by 322 to 238; the result giving the Government a majority of 84.

MISCELLLNEOUS.—The following persons were charged with drunkenness and fined ;—James Heath (19th appearance), lOs ; James Mason, Is; John Clark, ss; Dennis Burns, Is; and Ann Ramsbottom, Is—A boy named James &riven was ordered to pay 7s 6cl for letting off fireworks in Church-street. WOMEN'S QUAERELS.—Sarah Booth summoned Bridget Weir on a charge of assaulting her, on the 22nd September. The complainant alleged that the defendant, who had threatened to take her life several times, followed her down the street and kicked her without provocation. Defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined Is and costs.—Mary Rooney was charged with asseultitig Elizabeth Rooney. In a quarrel which took place between the women the defendant, it was alleged, picked up an axe and threatened to take the life of the complainant. Another witness stated defendant attacked the complainant with a '4 porter bottle," and beat her with her own umbrella. The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for three months.

THE MEW OF A HEN.—Sarah Ann Grayson was charged on remand with stealing a hen, of the value of 2s 6J, the pro- perty of George Billington, on the 15th October.—The evidence for the prosecution has been previously reported in The Examiner.—Mr. Peters, solicitor, appeared for the defence, and called seve-al witnesses, who stated that they had driven the hen off their premises about the day in question, and it was contended that the hen had found its way into the prisoner's cote without her conuivance.—The Chairman said the Bench was of opinion that the hen had rambled about and the prisoner had locked it up, though without any intention of stealing it. The prisoner bad acted imprudently, but the charge against her would be dismissed,
