div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.
MISCELLANEOUS.

Sir Beauchamp Seymour is not expected home till the new year. His command of the Mediterranean Jeet expires about Christmas. One man was killed and others were injured by the burst- ing of a water tank at a chemical works at Calder Vale, Wakefield, on Saturday. Subject to arrangements to be made for a debate on affairs in Egypt, it is the Prime Minister's intention to bring forward the vote of money for Sir Garnet Wolseley before the prorogation. A gallery gave way at a Radical meeting at King's-cross, London, on Saturday night. A panic ensued, and the suffer- ers were with difficulty rescued. Twenty persons Were injured, some of them seriously. The Cobden Club essay prise at Owens College, Man- chester, has been awarded to Mr. Foster Watson, M.A., of the college. The subject of the essay is "Peasant proprie- torship." The amount of the prise is £6C. Lieutenant John Weyland, of the Ist Life Guards, has died at the-hospital at Malta, of fever contracted at Cyprus, where, soon after tip war commenced, he was sent out with drafts for the squadron of his regiment in the field. The Assembly Rooms in Cecil Square, Margate, together, with the Vicarage and an hotel, forming together one side of Cecil Square, were destroyed by fire on Saturday morn- ing. The loss is said to amount to £40,000, but that is pro- le-ably an exaggeration. The Royal Commission on City of London Guilds will resume its sittings in the course of the next fortnight. Fur- ther evidence has been tendered by one or two city compa- nies, after hearing which the Commission will be in a posi- tion to shape their report. The members of the Curates' Alliance are annoyed by the appointment of Mr. Percival, president of Trinity, Oxford, to the additional post of a canonry of Bristol. At their meeting on Saturday the curates passed a resolution con- demning the "system of pluralities " in the Church. A committee is being formed to purchase a set of John Leech's drawings for presentation to the Manchester Permanent Art Gallery. Mr. Ruskin has given his name as a member, and has written a letter en the collection of drawings from which it is proposed to make the collection. A telegram has been received at Carlisle from Chief Con- stable Mackay, who has gone to Berlin, identifying a man in custody there for diamond robberies as James Grey, who fled while under remand at Carlisle nearly four years ago, on a charge of stealing £3OO in banknotes from a Preston cattle dealer.

Colonel Ewart, who commanded the Household Cavalry in Egypt, has arrived at Balmoral, where he was presented to the Queen, and afterwards dined with Her Majesty. It is stated that both Colonel Ewart and Lieutenant-Colonel Milne Home are to be recommended to receive Companion- ships of the ilath. The labours of the Royal Commission on Accidents in Mines have been further prolonged, at a time when they seemed to be about to close, by the necessity for fresh experiments with lamps. A meeting of the commissioners has jest been held, but there is noOmmediate prospect of the report being issued. The Watch Committee of the Leioester Corporation have decided to recommend an advance of 104. per man to the police. They have also decided to retain the good conduct badges and good conduct pay, and the chief constable has introduced a scheme which will give the men entire relief from Sunday duty in rotation. Different forms of violence caused 46 deaths in London last week; 40 were the result of negligence or accident, among which were 18 from fractures and contusions, 2 from burns and scalds, 13 from drowning, 8 from poison (includ- ing one nitric acid taken in mistake for gin), and 6 of in- fants under one year of age from suffocation. The oldest naval officer on the official record, Staff-Com- mander James Charles Atkinson, died at Southampton a few days since, in the 100th year of his age. He was born in Middlesex on the let of May, 1783, and commenced his sea- faring career by entering the merchant service in 1798, in which he remained until 1803, when he joined Her Majesty's Navy as a volunteer. I LITERARY TORIBB.—Lord Carnarvon having recently publicly attributed three-fourths of •the literary power of the country to the Conservatives, Mr. Gladstone was ques- tioned as to the veracity of the calculation. His private secretary writes in reply :—" Mr. Gladstone desires me to acknowledge receipt of your letter, and to say that he is not aware of any ground for the assertion of Lord Carnaryon to which you allude. A Sheffield correspondent says all fear of a colliers' strike is now past. On Tuesday the colliery owners of South Yorkshire resolved to increase their offer of 5 per cent. ad- vance to 16 per cent., though still adhering to their pre- viously expressed opinion that the present price of coal did not warrant the advance asked by the men. The offer was accepted by the union officials. The advance commenced on Thursday. John Bailey, the man charged with shooting an engine driver and fireman en the Midland Railway, was on Saturday committed for trial by the Nottingham magistrates. The curious defence was set up that the driver, while his train was running at the rate of fifteen miles an hour, held up his cap and invited the prisoner and two other men to fire at it.

The improvised railway corps sent to Egypt, even with the crippled engines and wrecked permanent way with which at the beginning of the campaign it had to work the traffic, having proved hew essential such an organisation is to a modern army, Mr. Childers proposes to establish it on a permanent bai, and, in co-operation with the existing railway administration of the country, to afford it constant practice_ in railway traffic and maintenance.

Two MEW BURIED ALIT.—Two labouring men were at work at a large sewer at Chester-road, near Birmingham, the other evening, when, owing, it is believed, to the recent floods, the ground gave way, and the men were precipitated into a hugs excavation and buried alive. Several persons ivitnessed the occurrence, and great excitement prevailed, but when the two unfortunate men were dug out both were found to be dead.

The Bishop of Manchester has caused to be served upon the churchwardens of St. John's. Miles Platting, formal notice of a sequestration of the revenues of that benefice— "as customary on the occasion of a vacancy." It is •an- flounced that Lord Penzance, Dean of Arches, will hold a Court to-day (Saturday) to hear an application on the part of the Bishop of Manchester for the release of the Rev. S. F. Greta.

Mr. Gladstone will not, the Observer understands, be able to bold out to the Irish members any definite hope of a day for discussing the questions of the administration of the Land Act and the Coercion Bill. Apart front the considera- tion that one day would not be sufficient for the purpoee, such an arrangement would be a violation of the under- standing that the autumn session was to be exclusively devoted to debate on the Procedure Rules.

The Thames rose to an unusual height on Saturday, and considerable damage was done along its course from Windsor , to the Nore. No loss of life is reported. The large steam- boat pier at Westminster was lifted from its bed and carried down the river for some distance. At Goole thd tide was very high, and the quays and roads near the river were flooded. A very heavy storm broke over Northampton on Saturday, and in Leicestershire the floods have not abated. Henry Starbuck, the fellow who committed an inhuman assault on a child 10 months old, of which he was thelather, was 'again brought before the Nottingham magistrates on Saturday. Had the charge gone for trial there would no doubt have been considerable difficulty in establishing a case against the prisoner, but as the scoundrel whiningly "threw himself on the mercy of the court," the magistrates were enabled to deal with him summarily, and they committed him to prison for six months with hard labour. MEMORIALS TO TWO PREMINRS.—The busts of Mr. Glad- stone and the late Lord Beaconsfield, which have been placed in tke Guildhall, London, were on Tuesday unveiled by the Lord Mayor, in the presence of a number of aldermanic and civic dignitaries. Mr. Sidney Day, ex-chairman of the city of London committee, made the presentation, and the Lord Mayor, in a subsequent speech, referred briefly to the ser- vices which the two great statesmen had rendered to the country, and concluded by complimenting the sculptors, Messrs. Woolner and Belt, on their works.

Mr. Monck, M.P., President of the Associated Chambers of Commerce, has forwarded to Earl Spencer and the Home Secretary, memorials on the proposed amendments of the Factory and Education Acts, with the object of securing uniformity in their application to children in employment. Mr. Monck has also sent to the President of the Board of Trade a memorial suggesting that a bill should be intro- duced next session to confer a local standing—before parlia- mentary committees and before railway commissionere— upon Chambers of Commerce and Agriculture.

TRIPLE MURDER A.ND SUICIDE.—On Saturday morning the bodies of the wife and two children, the latter aged five and two years respectively, of a fishmonger named Hiram Meakin, living in Kentish Town, London, were found dead in bed with their throats cut. Meakin had disappeared, and despite vigilant search, could not be traced. In the evening, however, the body of a man was left by the receding tide on one of the buttresses of London Bridge, and it was subse- quently identified as that of Meakin. It appears that he has lately been pressed for money, and owing to losses was in fear of distraint for rent. TRAGEDY IN LONDON.—A shocking case of attempted murder, followed by suicide, has occurred in Pentonville- road, London. A woman named Elizabeth Brown had been living for some time with a man named James Farev, and on Friday night, after visiting a music hall in his company, went with him to a house in Pentonville-road, where he cut her throat and attempted to murder her. Farev left in the morning, after paying the landlady, who afterwards found the woman Brown upstairs with her throat cut. The injured woman is now lying in the hospital in a serious condition. Farey was a butcher by trade, and had a wife and family living at Boweston-street, Caledonian-road, where he pro- ceeded on Saturday, after having been absent several days. I While there he went into a closet at the back and corn-
- ---- -- - -- mitted suicide by cutting his throat. THE NEW LAW ON BILLS OF SALE. —On Tuesday the new Act on bills of sale, which extends to the whole of _ _ _ ___ _ _

England and Wales, came into operation. It amends the former Act of 1878, and effects several important alterations, one of which is the provision protecting the removal or sale until "five clear days" after the seizure of personal chattels. All bills of sale under £3O are to be void, and not to protect personal property from poor or parochial rates. A form is given in the schedule, and a schedule is to be made of the article, and not to affect after acquired property. A bill of sale is to be attested and registered, and the clause by a solicitor of attestation is repealed. Bills of sale can be in- spected and particulars taken on "a shilling stamp." Ques- tions are likely to arise on the two Acts, but the non-removal sr sale of goods within five days is an important improve- ment in the law.

The results of Wednesday's municipal elections through- out the country are in favour of the Conservatives. At Liverpool, on Monday, Patrick Meehan was committed to the assizes on the charge of shooting at Patrick Bevan, with intent to murder him, in the public street. _ On the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, on Tuesday, the guard's van and a second-class carriage of a Manchester train were thrown off the line near Ramsbottom Station. The passengers escaped without injury. A Strndard Rome telegram says: Those nearest the per- son of the Pope assert that he has sent by Mr. Errtngton an autograph letter to the Queen thanking her for her good disposition towards the Catholics, and trusting that it would bear fruit in renewed diplomatic relations. About one hundred and fifty members of the Conservative party in the House of Commons assembled on Tuesday at the Carlton to take counsel together on the Closure. Sir Stafford Northcote presided. It is understood that the meeting resolved to persevere in opposing the proposed rules.

A general order from the Horse Guards has been promul- gated at Chatham announcing that Her Majesty has no further use for the services of the first-class Army Leserve, recently called out, and they will therefore at once be dis- missed. They will, however, be allowed to be retained on active service with their battalions under certain con- ditions.

A man named Bartlett, manager of a mine in Cornwall, was convicted at Exeter Assizes the other day, of the de- liberate murder of his illegitim;te child, an infant only a few days old. It was proved that he had received the infant from its nurse, strangled it, and thrown the body into an old shaft. Sentence of death was passed. The Rev. James Benham, late vicar of Marden, Kent, has made an abatement of 15 per cent. on his tithei for this year in consequence of the failure of the hop crop. The Rev. J. G. Brine, vicar of Lower Hardres, also in the county of Kent, has foregone all claims where no hops have been picked. Joseph Bell, miner, aged twenty-seven, was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude at Cumberland Assizes, on Tuesday, for attempting to murder his brother and sister- in-law at Dalston, near Carlisle. Prisoner threw an explosive into a bedroom where he believed his brother was asleep, but the room was that of a neighbour. The Home Secretary (Sir William Harcourt) will, it is , expected, perform the opening ceremony at the new Reform I Club at Heywood; and it is hoped that during his visit to Lancashire—for which the date is not yet fixed—he will also address a meeting in Manchester. Sir Thomas Boyd, Lord Provost of Edinburgh, has received the appointment of chairann of the new Scottish, Fishery Board, the salary attached to which is about £BOOl per annum. Sir James Maitland and sevtral of the sheriffs of Scoth counties have been appointed commissioners. The new railway station buildings at Southport of the West Lancashire Railway Company, fell in on Wednesday with a great crash. They were almost near completion, and the structure would have been a most handsome one. The I contractors had soon several gangs of men at work clearing iaway the debris, but it will be some time before the station will be completed. The military authorities at Aldershot have put the Royal Exchange public-house out of bounds. The meaning of this order is that the military police are ordered to make I prisoners of all soldiers found in his house because the pro- prietor, Walter Clarke, took a soldier's medal as pledge for payment for lig*. The action of the authorities has 'nulled considerable sensation in the town. EDINBURGI UNIVERSITY DEOREIS.-011 the occasion of the rectorial address by Lord Rosebery to the students of Edinburgh University, to be given on Saturday, the degree of LL.D. will be conferred on the following noblemen and gentlemen, besides the rector :—The Marquis of Bute, the Marquis of Lothian, Earl Crawford, Lord Reav, the Lord Advocate, Mr. Trevelyan, M.P., and Mr. William Fraser, Edinburgh Register House. The arbitrator in the suit brought by Countess Ossalin- sky, the proprietor of land at Thirlmere, against the Cor- poration of Manchester, delivered his award on Monday. In stating the claim, a year ago, counsel for the Countess said that the sum involved was " more than £60,000, and perhaps something less than £100,000." The arbitrator finds the Countess entitled to £64,445, and a sum of either £B,OOO or £4,000 additional, contingent on the view that may be taken of a special point in the case. HOME RULM—II is stated that two bills will be introduced into the House of Commons next session for facilitating Irish private bill legislation. One bill, promoted by Mr. J. Leeman, M.P. proposes that, the initial formularies of gas, water, and railway bills should be taken in Dublin, before the County Court judge. The second bill, by Mr. P. J. Smyth, M.P., proposes that Irish private bill legislation should be dealt with in Dublin by a Parliamentary Com- mittee.

_ The Hon. E. L. Stanley, M.P., in a letter strongly son- demns Lord Randolph Churchill's motion to adjourn the House on the cloture. He says the nominal leaders of the Tory party, who never dreamt of Lord R. Churchill's con- stitutional mare's nest in the summer, now follow him into the lobby, so that impudence and audacity take the lead in fory counsels, and Sir S. Northcote and Sir R. Cross have not the courage to disregard the vapeurings of their inde- pendent ally. A robbery was committed daring the service of the Salva- tion Army, at Wrexham, on Sunday night. The hall, as usual, was packed, especially the gallery. It appears that a young lady sat in the gallery during the service, and, on ooming out during a great crush at the close of the service, she missed her watch, only the chain being left, and the swivel being broken. Information was given to the police, but no clue has been ottained.

ARITISIL MISSIONARY CONTRIBURIONS.—The annual sum- mary of British contributions to 77 societies, for foreign mission work, during the financial year of 1881, has just been completed by Canon Scot Robertson, of Sittingbourne. The total is £15,381 less :than that of the previous year. The chief items are as follows :—Church of England Mis- sions, £460,395; Joint Societies of Churchmeß and Noncon- formists, £153,320; English Nonconformists Societies, £313,177; Scolch and Irish Presbyterian Secieties, £155,767; Roman Catholic Societies, £10,910. Total British con- tributions in 1881, £1,093,569. STAG SLAUGHTER. The annual catching of a stag in Powis Castle park, preparatory to the stag hulit which is al- ways held on Lord Powis's birthday, ended on Tuesday in a very extraordinary manner. A large number of persons, including Lord Powis, were present at the proceedings, and open house was kept at the castle. The stag was started, and, after being pursued for some time, was caught, when it immediately dropped down dead. A second stag was started, and, strange to say, when canght, also dropped down dead. So great was the surprise at this untoward re- sult, that all further attempt to secure a stag was aban- doned.

DESPERATE Exoomensu WIT!! A BtraGLAR.—At the Dur- ham Aassizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justic Hawkins, John Knight a notorious burglar, pleaded guilty to breaking into the dwelling house of Mr., Joseph Townend Eltringham, a borough magistrate for South Shields, and stealing a quantity of silver. Mr. Eltringham caught the prisoner in the house, and a desperate struggle took place. Mr. Eltringham was bitten and his head battered against the wall. He was also thrown downstairs, injuring his leg. He only left loose of the prisoner on 'becoming unconscious. The prisoner was sentenced to 14 years' penal servitude. A SAD END.—The inquest was resumed at St. George's Hospital, London, on Monday evening, on the body of the young woman who was found in a dying state outside Hyde Park gates, Knights-bridge, last Tuesday. The body was identified by Mrs. Message, of Eastbourne, as that of her daughter, Mary Ann Message, aged 24, of whom she had beard nothing for the past two years. Evidence was now given that, on the night of the accident, deceased was seen at Knights-bridge the worse for drink, that she staggered off the pavement into the road, and was knocked down by a passing waggon and run over. A verdict of "Accidental Ideath " was returned.

NRWSPAPER LinaL.—The utility of the Newspaper Libel and Registration Act passed last year was illustrated at the Liverpool Police Court, on Monday, when Mr. Raffles refused to grant a summons against the proprietor of a Liverpool weekly paper for alleged malicious libel on the ground that the permission of the director of public prose- cutions in England had net been obtained by the aggrieved person. Had it not been for the very reasonable protection afforded to journalists by the Act of 1881, Mr. Raffles would have had no alternative but to have granted the summons, though the matter at issue might be altogether unworthy of _ _

legal investigation. ST. domes, MILES PLarrugo.—We learn that the Bishop of Manchester has appointed the Rev. Walter Ruthven Pym, 8.A., of Magdalen College, Cambridge, curate of St. Cuth- bert's, Lytham, to the curacy-in-charge of St. John's the Evangelist's, Miles Platting. pending the nomination of a successor to the Rev. S. F. Green. Mr. Pym was ordained by the Bishop of Manchester, deacon in 1880 and priest in 1881, his only curacy having been at Lytham. It is under- stood that the ritual of the church will be reduced during the charge of the new curate to the Cathedral stdndard, as enjoined by the Bishop in his admonition delivered at a Synod of the clergy on November 25, 1881. Mr. Pym will enter upon his duties at Miles Platting on Sunday next.

_ FEARFUL GAS EXPLOSION IN A. THEATRE.-At soon on Monday a serious gas explosion occurred in the Royal Princess Theatre Main-street, Glasgow, by which four per- sons were severely injured. A shade had fallen from the roof, and in descending broke the pipe connected with a gas bracket, from which there was a great .escape. The acci- dent being unknown to the employes, who were in the habit of entering the theatre every forenoon, four of them as usual proceeded to resume their work at noon yesterday, taking with them a lighted candle. They had not pro- ceeded far, however, before the gas ignited, and a fearful explosion followed. The four persons were much burnt about the body. Mrs. Connel, wife of the secretary of the theatre, is so severely injured that she is not expected to re- cover. The theatre is under the management of Mr. T. R. Cecil Beryl, and is a favourite house in Glasgow. ImAtrartiNTs TO THE 'UNITED STATES.7-During the las

quarter the number of immigrants into the United States show a considerable falling off, the total being about 14,000 fewer than in the corresponding period of last year. This, however, is scarcely matter for surprise. In the earlier portions of this year the arrivals were greatly in excess of last year, and the present year's figures still show more than 20,000 above last year's. The conclusion of the harvest in

lue States, and the utter failure of the gnat strike in the iron districts, consequent in no small degree upon the exces- sive supply of labour, warned European workmen their pres- ence in the:States was not urgently needed. Many, therefore, who otherwise might have emigrated stayed at home, And as the harvest generally throughout Europe has been good, I the piobability is that they will have no reason to regret that they did not leave borne.

The writ for Ennis will be moved for on Monday, and the nomination will be fixed for Friday or Saturday. In the event of a contest, the polling will be about Monday week. Princess Dolgorouki' the late Czar's morganatic wife, is shortly, according to the Havas Agency, to start for Russia, her younger daughter remaining at Pau for the sake of her health.

An Ennis telegram states that the official valuer attached to the Land Commission Court there has ceased to be con- nected with it. This is regarded as another triumph of the agitation against these officials. Twelve additional bodies have been recovered at the Dinas Colliery, which exploaion occurred some years since. There are thirty-four more bodies in the pit. A small fishing cobble belonging to Beadwell, North- umberland, was lost off Berwick, on Thursday. Three brothers, John Fawcus, Robert Fawcus, and Andrew Fawcus, fishermen, two of them married, were drowned. _ _ . _

It is stated that the convict Amelia Jordan will be libera- ted on a ticket-of-leave, on the 13th inst. Efforts are being made to raise a sum of money to enable her to make a fresh start in life on her release.

The Lord Chancellor received on Thursday the Lord Mayor elect of London, and, on behalf of the Queen, acknowledged the citizens' choice. Lord Selborne after- wards received the jadges, and proceeded with them to Westminster to open the law courts for the coming term. St. Mary's Church, Monmouth, was reopened by the Bishop of Llandaff, on Thursday, after its restoration at a cast of over £7,000 from designs by the late Mr. Street, R.A. The church was founded in the year 1069. The Select Committee appointed to inquire into the ques- tion of Mr. Gray's imprisonment, met for the second time on Wednesday. A motion was made to admit the press, but it was opposed by Mr. Gladstone and the Chairman (the Attorney-General), and on a division it was negatived by a large majority. The Town Council of Flint will again appoint Alder- man Muspratt Mayor of the borough on the 9th instant. Alderman Muspratt may apparently, if he chooses, regard it as a life appointment, for this will be the fifteenth succes- sive occasion on which he has been unanimously appointed to fill the civic chair at Flint.

-At Birmingham, on Thursday, Elizabeth Winwood was committed for trial for the manslaughter of her husband, Richard Henry Winwood, a fruiterer, of Broomsgrove-street, Birmingham, by throwing a heavy weight at his head during a quarrel. The coroner's jury at the inquest also re- turned a verdict of manslaughter against the woman. A Bombay paper publishes a description of 14 couvicts who have succeeded by some means in making their escape from the penal settlement at Port Blair, in the Andaman Islands. Thirteen of the 14 were life convicts, the offences being chiefly murder and dacoity. The fourteenth, a Bur- man, convicted of murder, was sentenced to eleven years' transportation in June, 1875, so that he had only four years longer to serve. The whole 14 appear to have got off together. No tidings of the fugitives have been obtained. The Paris Boulevards, on Wednesday afternoon, were infested with individuals carrying parcels of small prints with a black border /and shouting, "Demandez les dernikes depeches de Londres ; Death of the Empress Eugenie; her Agony and her Last Worde." The streets at the time were crowded with holiday-makers, it being the Festival of All Saints, so that the vendord of this unblushing and malicious piece of false news probably drove a roaring trade. r, A public meeting was held on Thursday afternoon, at the Mansion House, London in aid of the National Anthem for India Fund, the object of which is to popularise the anthem amongst the natives of India by translating it into the native languages. Lord Stanhope presided, and Canon Harford read a statement showing that the project had the lapproval of the Viceroy of India, and was being carried on with the sanction of the Secretary of State for India. It 1 I was resolved that the nation should be invited to co-operate in the work.

THE DERWENTWATER ESTATES.—Mr. Driver, acting under Instructions of the Lords of the Admiralty, offered for sale the well-known Derwentwater estate, situated near Haydon Bridge, Northumberland, comprising 8,385 acres, and producing an annual income of £9,300. The property was sold in lots, and Mr. W. D. Cruddas, of Newcastle, was the principal purchaser. These are the estates which were forfeited in the insurrection of 1715, when they came into the possession of the trustees of Greenwich Hospital. GRAND Commtrntss.—The question of providing accom- modation for the proposed Grand Committees is already engaging the attention of the Government. Any of the existing committee-rooms would be insufficient for a meeting of 60 or SO members, and even if two rooms were knocked into one as has been suggested, the enlarged room would hardly be sufficient to accommodate a Grand Committee, the officials, aril the Press. A scheme is now under the con- sideration of the Board of Works for obtaining the necessary accommodation in the old Law Courts, which will be vacated in the course of a few weeks.

Axonnert LONDOW TRAGEDY.—A shocking tragedy occurred at Sankey's Wharf, High-street, Canningtown, Essex, on Thursday afternoon. A clerk named Henry Wells had a dispute with another clerk, named Hanry Callaghan. Wells was seen to draw a revolver from his pocket and fire at Callaghan, and afterwards to place the pistol in his own mouth and pull the trigger. Death was instantaneous in Well's case, while Callaghan was picked up insensible, and now lies at the London Hospital in a critical condition. Jealousy is supposed to have been the motive for the crime.

THE NATAL SCANDLL.—Chief gunner Fitzgerald, of Her Majesty's ship Clyde, who has been under arrest for several days in connection with the alleged irregularities in the dis- posal of the ship's stores, WAS removed to Queensferry on Thursday, under the charge of an officer of the Lord War- den and two members of the Royal Marine Artillery. It is expected that the court-martial will be held on board the Lord Warden. A quantity of silver plate, presented to the commander recently on the occasion of his marriage, has been taken charge of on behalf of the Admiralty, as it is a violation of the rule of the service for the officers to accept presents from men under their command. OVERWORK IN THE SIGNAL Box.—ln reporting the result of his inquiry into the cause of a collision last July at Sum- merhill Station, Cork, on the Great Southern and Western Railway of Ireland, Major-General Hutchinson says—" This inquiry has brought to light the objectionable practice of keeping signalmen on duty for periods, in Tomkinson's case (at a level crossing) of 22 hours, and in Tyrrell's case (at Grattan-hill Jurction) of 20 hours at a stretch. It is true that these long hours occur only occasionally to exchange the night and day duties, but they ought not to be allowed to occur under any circumstances." Lo OF OF A STEAMER AND TWELVE LIVES. —P. J. M'Carthy, a fireman belonging to the screw steamer Secret, which left the Tyne for Plymouth, has arrived at South Shields with particulars of the foundering of that vessel and the loss of twelve lives. The steamer was commanded by Captain Cheers. She experienced a heavy gale with a high sea, and drove ashore on Newcombe Sands. All the boats were stove except one, into which M'Carthy and six others got. This boat was capsized, and all were thrown into the sea. M'Carthy seized hold of an oar, and reached the shore. His companions were all drowned, together with those aboard the Secret, which foundered, twelve lives in all being lost.

_ At Oldham, on Thursday, James W. Wood, landlord of the Dog and Gun beerhouse, was charged with allowing betting on his premises. The police made a raid, on the 24th ult., on a number of suspected houses, and found bett- ing going on on the premises of the defendant. In one house was found a hatful of money which nobody would claim. The defendant was fined £3O, and his licence ordered to be endorsed. Thomas Henry Whitehead, beerhouse- keeper, was fined £6O and his licence endorsed.—The Chief Constable said a number of boys went to these houses. James Whitaker, beerhouse-keeper, was also fined £6O and costs for a similar offence, aud John Smith, a bookmaker, was fined £lO and costs for aiding and abetting. LOCKING UP A BRIDEGROOM.—An amusing incident took place at St. George's Church, Shrewsbury, on Sunday. A bridal party had been waiting at the church for some time for the bridegroom, who did not turn up. The clergyman took compassion on the bride, and volunteered to go and look after the bridegroom. He went to his mother's house and asked where her son was. She replied, "He is safe enough. I have him safe under lock and key upstairs, and I shall not loose him. He is under age, and has no right to marry." She further added, "She was sure if he broke out of his room he would not come to church, as she had locked up all his clothes." The clergyman went back to the church land sent home the heart-broken bride. On Monday morning, however, the wedding canie off, the mother having with- drawn her opposition. A CLERGYMAN'S CLAIM AGAINST A CLERGYMAN.—At the Liverpool County Court, on Thursday, a summons was re- turnable against the Rev. E. A. Fitzßoy, the vicar of St. Jude's Church, Hardwick-street, the plaintiff being the Rev. J. J. Swann, of Manchester, who sued for the recovery of a fee for taking Sunday duty at St. Jude's. Mr. Grace (of the firm of Messrs. Whitley, Maddock, and Co.) ap- peared for the plaintiff, and said that the plaintiff (Mr. Swann) was the curate of the Albert Memorial Church, Manchester, and he sought to recover 1.2 2s. from Mr. Fitaltoy for taking a full Sunday's duty in June, and also 4s. 6d. travelling expenses from Manchester. Mr. Grace also mentioned that the defendant had not taken notice of the plaintiff's applications for the money.—The learned registrar (Mr. Cooper) made an order for immediate payment of the plaintiff's claim and costs, amounting in all to £4.. TiaE COLLIERS' AGITATION.—At a conference of miners' delegates, held on Saturday at the Old Town Hall, Manches- ter, Mr. E.. Cowey, South Yorkshire Miners' Association, presiding—the question of restriction of output was dealt with. The following resolutions were adopted :—" That we, the representatives of this conference pledge ourselves to support any district both morally and financially which may fight for the advance of wages, but whatever levy i may be laid in each district, the same to be collected n the way which will secure and realise the most money ;" "That a committee be appointed by this conference to deal with the wages question, and that their power shall be to ascer- tain the numbers on strike, the levy to be laid, the amount to be paid to the striker, and to call a conference wherever the same may be considered necessary;" " That the follow- ing gentlemen form the committee, viz., Thomas Ashtor, L. Pickard, Enoch Edward, James Haslam, Joseph Hopkins, Jonathan Griffiths, and James Aspinall, and that the com- mittee be empowered to do any business considered neces- sary in the interest of the aims of this conference ;" " That Mr. Pickard be the secretary of the above committee, and have power to call the committee together when necessary to arrange a conference."—A conference of Yorkshire miners was held at Rotherha.n on Monday, at which it was decided to refuse the South Yorkshire owners' offer of 5 per cent. advance, and to authorise the acceptance of the proferred 10 per cent. advance in West Yorkshire, and endeavour to obtain risimilar increase in the sowitiern division. A strike committee was appointed.
THE ALLEGED PERJIfitY AT WIDNES.

PRISONER COMMITTED FOR TRILL. At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. John Brock, a labourer named Wm. Oilier was brought up on remand charged with having, on the 18th October, committed wilful and corrupt perjury in a case heard at the Widnes Petty Sessions on that day, ix which an affiliation claim was ma& against the prisoner by Alice Wild, a single woman, living in Viaduct-street.--Mr. Husband defended the prisoner.—The first witness called was Alice Wild, who stated that she made the acquaintance of the prisoner at her father's house in September 1831, when the prisoner went to help her father to remove his furniture. She began to keep company with the prisoner. She knew a woman named Mrs. Griffiths. Mrs. Griffiths had frequently seen her (witness) and the prisoner together. She did so at Runcorn wakes on the 7th November. At that time witnees conversed with her some time whilst standing opposite the Runcorn :Parish Church. The pri- soner could see her. A man named Henry Bott also saw her and the prisoner together at Runcorn on the same night. When the prisoner took her to Runcorn wakes he promised her father he would bring her back by nine o'clock. She was in court on the 18th October, and heard the pri- soner swear that he had never been in Runcorn in his life; but she swore then as she swore now that she and the pri- soner were at Runcorn wakes together last year. She was still prepared to swear that the prisoner had been guilty of immoral conduct with her.—Mr. Charles Henry Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, said he was acting in his capacity of deputy magistrates' clerk at the Whines Police Court, on the 18th October, on the hearing of a complaint made by the witness Alice Wild for an order to be made against the defendant, Wm. Oilier. After the evidence of the complain- ant had been heard, the defendant, Wm. Oilier, offered him- self as a witness in his own defence. He (witness) duly administared the oath. Amongst the evidence given by the prisoner in the witness box, he swore that he never was guilty of immoral conduct with Alice Wild; that he did not court her; that he had been out of work six weeks; that he did not go to Runcorn Wakes with her; that he had never been to Runcorn wakes; that he had never seen Mrs. Griffiths and Alice Wild in Runcorn; that he had not been at Runcorn wi h her between seven and ten o'clock at night; that he was not at Runcorn with her on the 7th November, but was at Manchester at the time. While the prisoner was givil g his evidence he (Mr. Lewin) was so struck by the mann, r in which he gave it that he took the precaution to call attention to the fact that he was upon oath, and had better be careful what he said. The magistrates, after hearing the evidence for the defence, dismissed the complainant.—By Mr. Husband: Front the complainant's statement he was under the impression that something wrong had taken place at Runcorn. There was no doubt that Mrs. Griffiths, in cross-examination, said she was at Runcorn on the 6th November, and that she met the prisoner and the complain- ant there on that date.—Superintendent Barker: Was the complainant asked if anything improper had taken place at Runcorn ?—Mr. Lewin : I don't remember that she was.— Superintendent Barker: In taking down Mrs. Griffith's evidence is it not possible that you Made a mistake by put- ting the 6th inst. instead of the 7th November ?—Mr. Lewin: It is possible for everyone to make a mistake, but I don't think I took it down incerrectly.—Mr. John Brock, one of the magistrates on the Bench on the 18th October, gave evidence confirming Mr. Lewin's statement, and said he thought the prisoner was giving his evidence in an un- satisfactory manner, and cautioned him to tell the truth. An order was not granted to the girl, and the case was dis- missed. The evidence given by the prisoner affected that given by the girl, especially in that portion in which he said he was away at Manchester from the 3rd to the 9th November. As one of the sitting magistrates, he considered that the defendant not being in Runcorn between the 2nd and Oth November material to the case. Speaking for him- self, he thought the case fell through for want of corrobo- rative evidence.—Mrs. Griffiths, wife of James Griffiths, deposed that she saw the prisoner and Wild near Runcorn Parish Church on the 7th Nov., and hada conversation with the latter. She asked Wild to return, but she refused, as she was going to the wakes. She told Wild that "she would repent her visit there in time to come." It was about half- past seven in the evening, and the prisoner, who she had known two or three months, was standing on the parapet.— William Wild, 23, Viaduct-street, stated the prisoner went to his house and asked for permission to take his daughter to Runcorn. He consented on the condition that the prisoner brought her back by nine o'clock. The returned at ten, and explained their long absence by saying that they had been enjoying themselves, and did not imagine that the time had gone so quickly.—John I:Lindley, platelayer, 12, Parsonage- road, Widnes, said on the night of the Runcorn wakes Fe met the prisoner and, Alice Wild coming out of the latter's father's house. The prisoner said he was going to Runcorn. —Henry Bott, 5, North-street, Widnes, and Emily Roberts, 12, Parsonage-road. Widnes, deposed to seeing the prisoner and Wild together at Runcorn wakes.—lnspector Barnett said he apprehended prisoner at his lodgings on the 27th October. He remembered hearing the prisoner say at the court on the 18th ult., that he never was at Runcorn with the prisoner in his . life.—Mr. Husband contended, for the defence, that whether or not the defendant was at Runcorn on a certain day was inmaterial to the issue, and the case, he submitted, fell through on that ground. Mr. Brook, too, said distinctly in his evidence that they decided to dismiss the case because there was not sufficient evidence. He remarked on the fact that the complainant on the 18th ult. fixed the date of her visit to Runcorn as the 6th November, and now altered it to the 7th, a circumstanee which tended to lessen the effect of her evidence. The defendant being put hurriedly into the box when examined, might not have remembered exactly whether or not ha was at Runcorn on a particular day in November last.—The Bench were of opinion there was a prima facie case against the prisoner, who was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. Mr. Husband applied for bail on the prisoner's behalf, but the Bench refused the application.

div.head: RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB'S CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB'S CONCERT.

Now that such strenuous efforts are being made to estab- lish a Royal College of Music, the public performances of. what may be termed our local colleges—the choral, orchewi tral and madrigal societies of our towns and villages— which undoubtedly do much to raise the musical tastes of society, are watched with _much keener interest than for- merly, and the manner in which those performances a e received by the public is, however erroneously, to some extent accepted as an indication of the reception which would be accorded to the Royal College. It is too true that in many towns the public exhibitions of musical ability by these societies, which are often aided by artistes of recog- nised talent, are received with an apathy which leads to pecuniary difficulty and disheartens the performers, but it would be unwise to say the Royal College, if established, would meet with no better fate. A short time ago the mem- bers of Widnes Choral Society seriously discussed the pro- priety of terminating their labours, but, we are Way to say, determined eventually to continue providing music for the public. On Monday evening, on the occasion of the first concert of the season by the Runcorn Madrigal Club, the audience which assembled in the Public Hall was not of such proportions as to encourage the performers. The reserved seats were well filled, many of the elite of the town being present, but the remaining seats were very sparsely occupied, a fact which is to be the more regretted, as the musical entertainment which was given, was on the whole of a highly enjoyable nature. The concert opened with the overture " L'ltaliani in Algeri "which was followed by the part song " Echoes " (J. Catkin) by the chorus, who, as throughout the evening, acquitted themselvessin a manner which redounded to their own credit, and that of Mr. W. J. Argent, the conductor. Madame Edith Wynne, who possesses a soprano voice of considerable intensity and power of expression, next gave the classical piece "Far greater in His lowly state" (Gounod). We cannot compliment her upon the manner in which the rendered the piece, althongh she imparted to it considerable dramatic force; nor did she awaken in the audience any appreciable response. For her ren- dering of Pinsuti s song, "Heaven and earth," she received an encore, to which she responded by singing a portion of "The three old maids of Lee." Her most auccessful effort was during the second part of the concert, When she sang "The ash grove" and "The bells of Aber- dovey." The sentiment of the former song was inter- preted with true feeling, whilst the latter, which she sang in her own "mountain tongue," was given with a vivacity which "brought down the house," and in response to the encore she favoured the audience with " The three old men of Wear." Miss Kate Wynne at once established herself a favourite. Her mellow contralto voice was well suited to the songs she bad chosen, which were sung with much taste. Her first effort, "Cleansing fires," was rapturously encored, and she repeated the last verse. Molloy's beautiful song, "Darby and Joan," received from her a feeling inter- pretation, and she responded to an irresistible encore. An encore also rewarded Madame Kate Wynne for the song "Down the golden woods," and in response the audience were favoured with Brindley Richards' duet "Oh, the wandering star," which was sung by the two sisters with good effect. The other principal vocalist was Mr. H. Latham. Mr. Latham has a tenor voice of much sweetness, but greatly lacking in pewer, a defect which becomes more apparent through his, what we may term, "stiff style." The sweet song " Madoline," by S. Nelson, he sang, however, with con- siderable effect, and he was loudly encored. He then sang "The shades of evening." The performances of the band, and, as we have said before, of the chorus, were excellent. ' Mendelssohn's "Wedding march," and a Gavotte from the Opera Mignon, were perhaps the most enjoyable pieces by the band; and the part song " Autumn ' (Mendelssohn) was a splendid piece splendidly sung by the choir. During the evening Mr. F. Coaier gave a solo contra-basso of his own composition. His skilful manipulation of his some- what unwieldly instrument was great, and he received a hearty encore. It is to be hoped that the club's next concert will be more successful as regards the attendance of the public.

On Thursday, the decision of the Inspector-General of the Irish Constabulary was made known as to the result of an inquiry into charges brought against Sub-Inspector Stritch and Head-Constable Reid. The former was accused of not attending any place of worship for seven months, and that he was invariably in bed till midday, and not avail- able for official duty. Tim latter was charged with absent- ing himself without leave, and making a false statement. Sub-Inspector Stritch is reduced ten degrees and removed to another district. The Head-Cmstable is band guilty, and removed from county Kildare.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.

PARLIAMENT has been engaged for the most part of this week with the reform of its rules of procedure, the legitimate work for which our legislators are now in attendance at St. Stephen's, and the progress which has been made—during the past few days more especially—has on the whole been better than was at one time anticipated. Last week there were evidences in Tory circles that every form of the House was about to be used for the purpose of obstructing the Government, for of course it is well known that there could be no reasonable hope of defeating the Ministry; but this week a very different and more conciliatory attitude has been taken up, with the result that the main question has been discussed, and in reality, disposed of. We are at a loss to explain why this sudden change of front on the part of the Opposi- tion, or rather of the gentlemen who have been dubbed the Conservative "light horse ; " but perhaps the secret is to be found in the fact that the obstructive tactics were commenced in expectation that the over- tures of the Conservatives to the Irish party to join them would be successful. These having failed, our Tory friends were thrown upon their own resources, and they wisely decided to be a little more manageable.2on Tuesday evening, Mr. Gibson, who wag the Attorney-General for Ireland under the late Administration, moved his amendment to the now celebrated first resolution, substituting for the maxi- mum closure4by 200 members, as provided by that resolution, " two-thirds majority of those present." The amendment was submitted in a speech of great ability, and it is one which must enhance 31t. Gib son's reputation with his party; but what, strikes us most in [perusing it is that Mr. Gibson did not so much urge the advantages to be derived by the acceptance of his own proposal as find fault with the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.

resolution of the Government. Throughout his whole speech, eloquent as it no doubt was, he appeared to labour under a deep consciousness that he had no case, and consequently he could only speak from the standpoint of a special pleader. He completely cut the ground from under him by his as ;ertion that he was opposed to all closure, notwithstanding Parlia- ment has decided a closing power shall be vested in the Speaker. It is clear that. Mr. Gibson, too, much as he professes to be jealous of the rights of [minorities, has no sympathy with any minority but that which he himself represents. His amendment would protect the C( neer tive minority, who would always be able to 311110 '?.r a considerable force against the application of the closure ;:but to a 'minority 'such as the Irish party it;would give no protection whatever. Indeed, it would almost seem as if it were the policy of the Conservatives to crush the Irish partf,entirely. Sir Richard Cross, in the course of the debate thisi,week, stated that we, should never have heard of the resolutions if it had not been for the action of the Irish party, and then be proceeded to argue that the obstruction of: that party should be put down. This is just what the Govern- ment proposes to do, but they' are not so blind as to be unable to discern that tobstruction comes from others besides the Irish members; and, that being so, it would be manifestly:mafair to direct their resolutions against the Irish party only. Mr. Gibson a chnittel that there was a necessity for reform,' and as he is a gentleman who seems open to' conviction we may reasonably hope experience will teach him that his proposal is fraught with injustice to small minorities, while that submitted by. the Government protects all minorities alike—great'and small. The hon. mem- ber made a point of the offer made some time ago by Mr. Gladstone to accept the "two-thirds amend- ment," and was pardonablyr.inquisitive as to why it was not aecepted now. It by no means followed that although such an offer was made, that the Government' approved of it. So far from that, the GcNernment entirely disapproved of it, as did the majority of their supporters; but it was thought that by a compromise with the Opposition at that particu- lar time, and adopting the two-thirds majority as an experiment, the remainder of the resolutions would have been carried without much opposition, and this would have enabled some useful legislative measures to be placed upon the statute book. We all know that the hopes then entertained were rudely blasted by the awful tragedy in Phcenix Park, Dublin ; but, apart from that, the *Opposition never signified their willingness to ,accept Mr. Gladstone's offer—a very good reason, certainly, why the compromise was never brought about. The speech of the Premier, in reply to Mr. Gibson, was, to our thinking, unanswerable. He put the whole thing in a nut-shell when he objected to the amendment ;because of its apparent injustice to. small minorities, and its injustice to majorities as well. It is only natural that a majority should rule; but pass the amendment of Mr. Gibson and the power the majority now possesses would practically be handed;over.to the minority, or to the regular Opposition, who, of course, are in the minority. The majority decides;thelfate of Ministries and of measures ; and we fail to :see why it should not also be invested with the power to close a debate. 1 But as we have said, Parliament has already decided that it shall have the power, and to us it seems need- less to be cavilling how that power shall be applied. In common fairness a simple majority ought to be sufficient, and with the safeguards which the Govern- ment introduces there need not be the slightest fear of any abuse. But even if there were an abuse of the power by the majority it would, as Mr. Gladstone pointed out, only be an abuse of a power which naturally belonged to it ; whilst if the minority abused its power, the power is one which it would get under a factitious arrangement. The best answer which can perhaps be given to Mr. Gibson and those who are of his mind, is supplied by their leader, Sir Stafford Northcote, who, on the 27th July, 1877, is reported to have said :—" I would lay special stress upon the importance of avoiding the introduction of a distinction between tbe absolute majority and a majority of two-thirds or three-fourths. I cannot help thinking there would be great danger in intro- ducing such a distinction, because it might begin a system to which I should very much object, of giving to a majority of two-thirds or three-fourths the power to do that which we should not like to do with an absolute majority." This was in reality repeated by Sir Stafford Northcote on the 26th February, 1880, when he spoke as follows: —" The hon. member for Plymouth proposes another thing that I do not agree with. He said that when a motion is made it should not be carried except by a majority of two-thirds. I think that a very awkward rule to lay down. It would be an entirely new practice in this House. We know of no such thing as a majority of two-thirds, and I should be exceedingly sorry to see the introduction of such a principle as that in our proceedings." This is the sort of evidence which Ur. Gladstone was able to quote on Thursday in support of his unanswerable argument. Sir Staf- ford, it will be noted, was then an occupant of the Ministerial benches, with a mechanical majority at his back; now he sits on the front Opposition bench with a demoralised minority behind him. Then he condemned the very two-thirds majority which he now advocates. Sir Stafford may be left to wriggle out of his dilemma as best he can ; we feel sure that after the atspose his influence,will not be worth much. A two-thirds majority is unknown in Parliamentary warfare ; its adoption would lead to endless complications altogether apart from its injustice, and we are glad to find it has been rejected by a sweeping and decisive majority. A majority of 84 for tha Government is more than their most san- guine supporters anticipated, and it ought to disarm further opposition.

SEEING that the London School Board, which has now completed the twelfth year of its existence, has jurisdiction over an area containing a population larger than that of Scotland, and that it, as a rule, takes the initiative in all educational matters, Mr. Sydney C. Buxton's "Notes on School Board Questions," in the current number of the Nineteenth Century, will be of interest to all friends of universal education. Mr. S. C. Buxton, who with Mr. Ingram contested Boston in the Liberal interest at the general election, is a well-known writer on political, educa- tional, and social questions. Although but a young man, the desirability of his becoming a candidate for the vacancy at Edinburgh, consequent upon the retirement of Mr. Cowan through ill-health, was seriously discussed in Liberal circles in the Northern capital ; while in London he is looked upon as a future prominent member of the Liberal Parliament- ary party. On elementary educational questions Mr. Buxton is entitled to speak with considerable authority. Elected at the head of the poll as one of the representatives of Westminster on the third School Board for London, he has for the last six years devoted himself most thoroughly to the cause of education, and for some time has been chairman of one of the important committees of the Board. His contribution to the Nineteenth Century is specially of importance at the present juncture, when the triennial election Of the Board is engaging the attention of the metro- politan ratepayers and of educationalists in all parts of the country. The article deals mainly with the two questions—free schools and higher grade elementary schools. It is on the former question that we wish to remark. At some length, and with considerable success, Mr. Buxton clears the ground of the stereo- typed arguments which are constantly brought forward by the opponents of free schools. To the worn-out contention that free schools would have to be supple- mented by free food and clothing, the writer contents himself with replying that food and clothing are I essential to life and health, and that the parcnt who

neglects to supply them is morally or actually guilty of manslaughter. They, therefore, stand on an absolutely different footing to education. Coming next to the argument that the value of education is only brought home to the parent when he is made to pay for it, Mr. Buxton shows that the "caring less if paying less, caring nothing if pay- ing nothing," sort of reasoning has not the slightest foundation in fact. The abolition of fees, he holds, would not lower the appreciation of those who value education; while the careless or poverty-stricken parent would have one serious stumbling block and excuse for non-attendance removed from his path. Adverting to the financial aspect of the question, Mr. Buxton says that in London £90,000 would be the loss from a general remission of fees. Against thi s however, there must be recioned • the appreciable saving which would be effected in office expenses, and in the time of the teachers and officers, while there would be a considerable indirect gain from the in- creased attendance, the diminution of truancy and javenilelcrime. Mr. Buxton, however, admits that there still remains a sufficient argument against free schools in the enormous loss to education that would elsue from the disappearance of the voluntary system, which at present provides accommodation for 263,000 children as compared with 350,000 provided for by the London School Board. This, in his opinion, out- weighs the arguments which can be adduced in favour of free schools. It cannot he de i A that during the last ten years voluntary schools have evinced con- siderable vitality, but in face of the compulscry calls which are made upon friends and subscribers to volun• t ry schools for the expenses of the School Board it is not surprising that the free school question should be discussed, and it must be admitted that we are within measureable distance of the time when that question must engage the more general attention of the public.

CLEVER SHOOTING BY A RUNCORN RESERVE SOLDIER. —Those interested in the use of the rifle will be gratified to hear of the success on the range of Mr. John Williams, L Company, 63rd Regiment, let Manchester, now at Ash- ton-under-Lyne. In the regimental practice the other day Private Williams scored a remarkable figure, and received the congratulations of the Musketry Instructor. At 200 yards (standing) Mr. Williams got ten bulls eyes, and at 300 yards, nine bulls and an outer. This was a total score of 78 out of a possible 80.

How Tuu ;Pon Livz.—Mr. Church, inspector of lodging-houses in the borough, occasionally brings before the Warrington magistrates cases which reveal a shocking over- crowding in houses inhabited by the poor. One of these catne under the notice of the Mayor and ex-Mayor, at the Borough Court, on Monday, when John Hardy, Filling's Court, Dial-street, was summoned for keeping lodgers with- out having his house registered. The inspector visited the house, and found there eight persons—defendant, a grown- up son, foUr young children, and a man and woman. The two latter Mr. Church termed lodgers, although the woman was the daughter, and the man the son-in-law, of defend- ant. There was only one sleeping room, which was without beds, the people sleeping on the floor. The house was described as being unfit for pigs to live in, so filthy was it, and it was oply adapted for six persons. The Bench looked upon the case as a bad one, but they adjourned it for a week to give defendant an opportunity of finding a larger house or reducing the number of inmates at his present abode.— Peter Carey, summoned for keeping an unregistered lodging house, was fined ss. and costs. THREATENING TO MURDER AN UNCLE AT WIDNES.— Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sen., and Mr. H. S. Hall, at Widne9 Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Michael Boyle, jun. was charged with using threats to Michael Boyle, sen., on the 21st inst. There was a cross-summons against Boyle, Ben., for whom Mr. Yearsley appeared.—From the evidence it appeared that the plaintiff and defendant were uncle and nephew, and for some time the latter had resided with the former at his house in Catherine-street, Widnes. Recently, however, the nephew bad removed to a house of his own in Grenfell-street, and although previously he and his uncle had been on the best of terms, an estrangement had since taken place, and the elder Boyle alleged that the younger circulated reports of a nature likely to injure his character. On the afternoon of the 21st October, happening to meet one another in the street, the elder asked the younger why he had circulated injurious reports concerning him, and a quarrel thereupon ensued, during which Michael Boyle, jun., said in a threatening tone, that if his uncle were not out of the town in six months he would make his wife a widow. This, Mr. Yearsley pointed out, amounted to a threat to murder the complainant.—The defendant denied that he had used the language complained of, but the Bench thought the case proved. At the suggestion of Mr. Gasket!, who considered the case a family quarrel, defendant agreed tf pay the costs, 13s, in settlement of the charge.—The cross-summons was dismissed.

FELONY BY A RuNoonx FLATMAN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Alfred Thomas and Mr. John Brundrit, George Fryer was charged, in custody, that he on the 27th October, at Rnncorn, being the bailee of £3 for Edward Marwood, appropriated the same to his own use, and did thereby steal the same —Edward Marwood said he was a coal and salt merchant, and the prisoner had been working for him as master of the flit " Lilac." The last trip the flat was engaged in was from Birkenhead to St. Helens, with a cargo of ore. The flat arrived at Widnes on Wednesday night, and either on that night or the night following, the prisoner told witness that he had not sufficient money to take her to St. Helens. He should require £3 to take a horse, pay the hand, and discharge the cargo. Wit- ness gave him £3, on the understanding that it was for the purpose mentioned. The next thing witness heard of the prisoner was that he was in Runcorn drank on Friday, and finding the flat was lying at Widnes he issued a warrant for his apprehension.—P.S. Whalley deposed to apprehending the prisoner at his house in Regent-street, Runcorn, on Mon- day afternoon, When the warrant was read to him prisoner replied, "Yes, I have had £3. I gave my mate 12s. 6d., my wife a sovereign, and I got on the spree with the rest." —The Bench, after a little consideration, reduced the amount with which the prisoner was charged with stealing to £2 7s. 6d.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and stated that through Mr. Marwood stopping his freight at Widnes he was stopped there, and another boat getting precedence he would have had to wait four days at St. Helens before he could discharge his boat had he then started. He therefore decided to start from Widnes on Monday morning, and got on the spree at Widnes.—Mr. Thomas said there was no doubt the prisoner had misappropriated this money, and had made himself liable to six months' imprisonment. The Bench did not wish to he bard upon him, and sentenced him to 14 days' imprisonment.—The prisoner asked if he could not be allowed to repay the money, as he had a wife and four children dependent upon him.—Mr. Thomas said that was out of the power of the Bench.

WOMEN THIEVES AT RuNconN.—Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. A. Thomas, Elizabeth Minshull was charged with stealing and receiving two pairs of boots, value 6s. Bd., the property of Thomas Roscoe, at Ron. corn, on the let Inst.; also with stealing and receiving one pair of boots of the value of 75., the property of Samuel Spruce, on or about the 20th Oct.—Mary Skelding was also brought up in custody to answer a similar charge.—Mr. Roscoe is a boot and shoe dealer at 25 Lowlands-road, Runcorn. On the Ist inst. the prisoner Minshull went to his shop accompanied by a little girl, for whom she said she wanted a pair of boots. Mr. Roscoe was fitting the little girl with a pair of boots when he saw the prisoner handling a string to which was attached a quantity of boots, amongst them being the small pair produced. She then opened the shop door and said to some person outside, "I'll be with you directly." Returning to the shop she asked the price of the ' boots supplied to the girl, and saying she was 3s. short of the price, went outside to borrow that amount from her aunt. Mr. Roscoe then missed the boots from the string, and detained the girl for some time, but the prisoner did not return.— Edward Imison, pawnbroker, Church-street, Runcorn, deposed to the prisoner Skelding pledging , one of the pairs of boots at his shop for 23. 3d. P.C. Kelly afterwards apprehended tke prisoner Skelding, and P.C. Bossoms the pri- soner Minshull. Skalding, in answer to the charge, declared her innecence, but Minshull pulled a purse con- taining two pawn tickets, and said "Yes; here's the tickets. The other woman dropped them in a public-house, and I picked them up."—Evidence was then offered with regard to the pair stolen from the shop of Mr. Spruce, Lowland-road, Runcorn, which had been pawned with Henry Dodd, pawnbroker, Pimlico-street, Runcorn, by the prisoner Skelding.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said Skelding had served five years in a reformatory school, and lately had suffered incarceration for nine months for steal-

ling an apron from a shop in High-street. Minshull came from Wolverhampton, where she had been several times convicted. In 1875 or 1876 she was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude.—The prisoners were committed to take their trial at linutsford sessions.

ACCIDENTS AT RIINCORN.—WhiIst some large loge of timber were being shifted at the dockyard of the Bridge- water Navigation Co., Old Quay, Runcorn, on Wednesday, one of them slipped from its place, and seriously injured the leg of a man named Henry Roberts. A WESTON WOIIIN CONVICTED OF TIIEFT. A married woman named Margaret Darlington, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of having stolen 1121bs. of coal, of the value of Si., the pro- perty of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, Limited.— John Wesley Kirkham said he was the manager of the works, and about nine o'clock on Wednesday evening he was going his rounds when he saw the prisoner walking away from the works in the direction of Rock Savage. She was carrying something very bulkly. He shouted to her that she was heavy laden, and inquired what she had got there. The daughter of the prisoner was also carrying a basket, which witness discovered contained coal. The prisoner then said she had got a little coal, and placed on the ground a bag containing a quantity. Prisoner, he believed, bad been tak- ing her husband, who was employed at the works, his supper. —The woman pleaded guilty to stealing a little coal, but not the quantity named. She had seven children; who were all out of work. Her youngest child was seven years. Three of them had been "sacked "from the works.—Mr. Kirkham said the wa:es of the three last week was £3 is. 91—Mr. Chadwick said the Bench did not wish to be too hard upon her, and they would fine her £1 and £l. 3s. 61. costs.

PoictriNG AT Surrox.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. S. B. Chadwick and Mr. Alfred Thomas, Joseph Rowlands, a young fellow, was charged with having, on the 20th March, at Sutton, unlawfully used certain nets for the purpose of searching for game on land in the occupation of Geerge Gorst. He was also charged with, on the same date, committing a trespass, together with five other persons, on the land in the occupation of Mr. George Gorst ; and further with having, on the 31st March, at Halton, assaulted P.C. Cooper. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the first charge, and not guilty to tLe others.— George Hargreaves, game-keeper, Preston Brook, proved the first charges, and P.C. Cooper state 4 that on the 31st March he was in Sutton-lane, near to Hallwood, when he noticed five men coining along the road. When they got opposite to him, he pl3ced his hand upon the shoulder of the prisoner, saying "Hello, Joe, what are you doing here this time of the morning?" The prisoner shouted "High ho," and jumped over the rails into the field. He then deliberately threw a stone at witness, which struck him on the right shoulder. The other men also jumped over the rails and threw stones too.—P.S. Loundes gave corroborative evidence.—Prisoner denied assaulting the officer, and said at the time he was in Liverpool with his flat —The Bench retired for a short time, and on returning Mi. Thomas said the prisoner had been before the court 12 times for trespassing after game. For using the nets' the prisoner was fined £4 and costs 18s., or one month's hard labour; for trespassing, £4 and costs 195., or in default a month's hard labour; and for assaulting the constable £5 and costs £l, or in default tws months' hard labour. ALLEGED PERstraY AT DADESEURT.—Ann Worrall was charged at the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. Edward Greenall (chairman), J. Marson, and Robert Pierpoint, with committing wilful and corrupt per- jury. Mr. Fleming, of Manchester, defended. Superinten- dent Williamson, in stating the case, said that:on the 29th of August last one William Worrall was charged at that court with an offence against the Licensing Act. He was at that time a licensed beer seller at Whitley Superior. The facts of the case were that the then defendant had been privy to the consumption of beer upon his premises by a man named Buckley and others. The question at issue was: Did Worrall supply the men with the bottle and cup that con- tained the beer? Ann Worrall, the present defendant, swore that they were supplied by Buckley, and on this evidence the case was ultimately dismissed. He might say, on behalf of the police, that the present proceedings had been taken owing to certain statements haying reached their ears. They had no feeling in the matter further than a desire to have it cleared up; and if the case broke down the police would be satisfied.—After hearing one or two witnesses, the charge was withdrawn.—Mr. Fleming said the statement that the police had no feeling in the matter, further than a desire to have the affair settled, was quite true, and as the case had avowedly broken down he would say no more about it.

INQUEST ON THE BODY OF A LABOURER.-At the Main- top Inn, Mersey-road, Widnes, on Wednesday, Mr. Barker, deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the cause of death of Michael Kennion, a labourer, 24 years of age, who was found dead in a shed in the chemical works of Messrs. Golding, Davis and Co., on Monday morning.—Mr. Kirk (Messrs. Goffey, North and Co., Liverpool) appeared on behalf of the firm.—Julia Kennion said the deceased was her son. He took a drop of drink, but she did not "see any harm from it." Deceased was a healthy man. About eight weeks ego he complained to her about the gas at the works, and was ill at home for a few days.— James Jones, labluser, at lessrs. Golding, Davis and Co.'s works, said he believed the deceased had worked for the firm 12 months. Deceased was a man of somewhat intemperate habits. On Sunday night he and deceased were work- ing together. At six o'clock when he came in deceased was apparently quite well, and at seven o'clock he went away, saying he was going for his supper. He re- tuned at 11 o'clock, when be appeared to be " the worse for drink." Although he appeared capable of working, he did not do anything, but again went away, and about half-past one witness found him asleep in a cabin on the premises. Between that time and about half-past three witness awakened the deceased three times. On the last occasion the deceased went into the place known as the "cinder hole," and sat down there. About four o'clock witness noticed the deceased still sitting in the cinder hole. A change seemed to have come over him. His mind seemed to wander, and when requested to come out he could give no coherent reply. When witness left him deceased appeared to be asleep. He viaited the cinder hole again at seven o'clock, and found the deceased was dead. By Corcner : He did not think deceased could have been affected by the gas, because there was none where he was. Dr. MacDougall, when he examined deceased, did net think death had been caused by gas.—Edward Burgess Bates, labourer at the works, gave corroborative testimony, and said in his opinion the deceased was sleeping in consequence of the liquor he had drunk.—The evidence of Mary Lawson, of 5, Bridge-street, Widnes, with whom deceeased lodged, having been heard, the Coroner summed up. It almost appeared, he said, as if the deceased had taken too much drink, and had died of apoplexy, which would account for some of the symptoms which bad been described. However, if the jury thought there was any serious doubt in the mat- ter, he would adjourn the inquest and have a post-mortem examination made. If they did not think this course neces- sary, they would have to return a verdict of death from natural causes, and if they could, to name the cause.—The jury recorded a verdict of "Death from natural causes." THE REV. J. AGAR BEET'S COMMENTARY ON TIIE EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. A recent number of Public Opinion contains the following review of the Rev. J. Agar Beet's "Commentary on St. Paul's epistle to the Corinthians" :—lt is probable that more interest is felt by many Christians in Paul than in any Other apostle, chiefly perhaps because he was a Roman citizen; was born a Jew, and as such received a thorough religious and philosophic education; and was actually executing a commission from the Sanhedrim (a circumstance which may be accepted as evidence that he was of good social position) when he had the vision which led him to become a Christian. These facts, moreover, account for the comparatively judicial control over his apostolic colleagues, and the other members of the Christian society which he seems to have enjoyed. He was the chief scribe of the infant Church, and hence it has been easy to find iv his, for the time, voluminous writ- ings individual passages which are not readily reconcilable with other statements which he made, the result being that commentaries on the Pauline epistles have been very numer- ous, and indeed necessary; and it would be difficult to find one superior to or conveying more real information with re- gard to the Epistles to the Corinthians than that of Mr. Beet. Not only does he display great scholar- ship and extensive research throughout the volume, but there is an entire absence of sectarian bias, and a show of careful and independent thought which are most refreshing and will commend them- selves to all classes of readers, and cause the work to be frequently consulted as a book of reference. The essential feature in Mr. Beet's Commentary is its direct reference to the evidences of Christianity. He demonstrates that the the Epistles are genuine, that our copies and versions are substantially correct, and that the Epistles really reflect the teachings of Jesus Himself. Avoiding the thankless task of attempting to prove that the Bible is all true, iaaffirming which a writer runs the risk of creating doubt amongst the uneducated by the disproof of perhaps but one of his historical statements, leading them to question the whole, Mr. Beet does much to give confidence in the authenticity at least of the Epistles embraced in the Commentary, by making his readers feel that every opinion which he ex- presses has been eluly weighed and is supported upon good authority. Mr. Beet states that he has. "endeavoured by careful grammatical study of St. Paul's words to trace the line of thought they were designed to convey, wed to look through his actual thoughts while writing into his abiding conception of the Gospel and of Christ," and he recognises the fact that in every case the investigation. must accord with the universal laws of human credibility. To attempt to withdraw the matters of fact stated in the Bible from this supreme court of appeal is, as Mr. Beet 'remarks, as absurd as for a man to claim that because lan is a Christian his conduct must not be tried by the laws of human morality. The author has acted upon these opinions throughout, and as a consequence has produce' e a volume which may be advantageously consulted lay all who really seek the truth.
