CREMONA MUSICAL UNION.—From our advertising columns it will be seen that the Cremona Musical Union will visit Warrington during the coming week, and give entertainments in the Public Hall on Wednesday and four following nights. The entertainments will consist of vocal and instrumental music and comic sketches, and we have no doubt the talented artistes who are announced to appear will render the interesting items set down to their names in such a manner as to enable all who visit them to spend an enjoy- able evening. We may mention that the Cremona band ' have six times had the honour of appearing before H.R.H. the Prince of Wales.

A WARRINGTON LICENSING APPEAL CASII.—At the Liver- pool Quarter Sessions, on Thursday, the appeal of Mr. Elijah Lawton, the Grove, Bewsey-road, Warrington, against the recent decision of the Warrington magistrates refusing to grant a renewal of his beer license came on for hearing.—The appellant was represented by- Mr. Segar (instructed by Mr. Percy Davies), and Mr. McConnell ap- peared on behalf of the justices.—The facts of the case are still fresh in the minds of our readers. In the end the appeal proved successful, and the magistrates' decision was over- ruled, the Chairman (Lord Derby) stating that it had been the custom of the court for several years to grant all licenses respecting which there had been no conviction or ;complaint. riet ,„. THE DIRTTCAND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—r or week ending 28th October.—The mean temperature was 41 Fahrenheit, therefore 38 degrees cblder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 54 F. was recorded on the 25th inst., and the minimum temperature 25 F. on the 26th inst. The rainfall measured -85 inches. The general direction of the wind was south-east. During the week, which was the 43rd of the current year, 38 births and 20 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 24.8 per 1,000, against 25.4 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 211 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from croup, 2 from pulmonary consumption, 2 from brain disease, 1 from heart disease, and 5 from lung disease. —4 cases of scarlet fever were reported under the require- ments of the Act of Parliament.—JortN H. GORNALL, medical officer of health.

LANCISUIRE AND CIIEs3IIRE ENTOMOLOGICAL SOCIETY". The usual monthly meeting was held on Monday evening in the Free Library, Liverpool, the president (Mr. S. .1. Capper) in the chair. Mr. A. Short was elected a member of the society. Mr. C. H. H. Walker read a paper, entitled "The Entomology of the Antediluvian World," which he illustrated by coloured diagrams of its fauna and flora. He referred to the necessity of the study of palrontological entomology for a proper idea of the classification of recent insects ; and with reference to discussions which have taken place at recent meetings of the society on the subject of con- necting links between different orders of insects, he in- stanced the presence of insect remains (forming a group known as the Paheedictyoptera) in the carboniferous and permian series of strata, which are generally considered to be intermediate in structure between the Ortheptera and Neuroptera. To illustrate the paper Mr. J. T. Moore sent specimens of fossil insects from the Ravenhead (St. Helens) collection in the museum, and Mr. Walker exhibited a slab of lithographic slate containing fossil dragon-flies. ASSAULTS EY A RECRUIT: COMPLAINT AGAINST MILI- TARY SERGEANTs.—John Mahon, militia recruit, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and the ex-Mayor (Councillor Tairclough) with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge and Bank streets, with assaulting P.C.'s Clynes and Street, and with wilfully damaging the window of Thomas Havey, landlord of the Bird in Hand beerhoume, to the amount of 48. The evidence showed that about 15 or 20 minutes past 10 o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner and another sol- dier went to the Bird in Hand and asked to be supplied with beer. The landlord said it was time. they were in the barracks, and turned them out. The men then palled off their belts and smashed a window. P.C.. Street came up, and the landlotd asked him to get the names of the men. Soon after P.C. Clynes was at Market Gate, when he saw a large crowd at the end of Dolman's-lane. On going there he saw P.C. Street hold of the prisoner by the arm. He rushed through..the crowd, and ascertained what was the matter. Street said he must have the name of the prisoner, when the latter "up with his foot" and kicked him. P.C. Clynes told the prisoner he mast atop that work, but he then kicked him. The constables got hold. of him and opposite Mr. Carter's shop he gave Clynes " the shoulder," and knocked him and two others to the ground. The officer was soon up again, and at Market Gate they saw two mili- tary sergeants, who, although asked, never offered to assist the police. Near the Fox the prisoner "set, himself out," and fought with all his might to liberate himself. He knocked P.C. Street down and kicked him. The Officers Saw two respectable men, named Harry and Alfred Dowd, and called upon them to assist, and they did so. One of the. military sergeants, James Neild, gave Clynes a the back of the neck and knocked him down with chuck " at. the prisoner, and also struck Mr. Harry Dowd. They got the prisonere up, and with great difficulty took him, towards the police. station. There was a great crowd, and opposite, the Cross, Keys, Sergeant Neild, followed them up, held, up his stink, twice told him he would "make it warm for him, and. asked them to let go the prisoner. He told the sergeant to- go away, and the prisoner slipped his hand in front of him, and unfastened his belt and jachet, but he was ultimately got tp the police station and locked up. The, I3eneh regretted to hear of Sergeant Nield'aconatict, which, the Mayor said, might have led to a riot The prisoner was fined ss. and costs, or in default, 7 days' imprisonment, fox being drunk and disorderly, aud was committed fur a month's hard labour for asaaulting the police. The I>ench pnblicly thanked the brothers Dowd for the 'manner in which they assisted the police.—On Tuesday, Sergeant Neild attended before the Mayor, and explained that what he did was to protect the police trona the crowd, lie did not remember the constable asking him to render assistance, or he would have done so. He pushed Mr. H. Dewd away ac he thought he was interfering with the police, but he was sorry for having done se. Mr. Hunt (chief constable) did not press the case, as he had no desire to mar the good feeling between the police and military authorities, =el P.C. Clynes and Mr. Dowd haying expressed themselves satisfied with the apology which was tendered, the matter dropped, the Mayor re..nayke Lug that aye police had acted very courteously'.

AUTUMN FIRESIDE RAMBLES. Sir,—l have accompanied in spirit and with pleasure your correspondent in his rambles round Newton, and have bad for companion and guide Mr. Hardwick's "Ancient Battlefields in Lancashire." The work, in addition to deal- ing with its main subject, gives some curious information on such out-of-the-way suijeets as the battles in and about Winwick, the first Sir Henry de Le, the Gerards of Bryn, Garswood, the search-opening of Castle Hill Tumulus in 1843, and its lady ghost, Robin Hood's Cave (alas! now submerged in the Newton brook improvements), Mote Hill, cremation in Lancashire in ancient times, the gigantic skeletons of the "Newt( n hundred," Winwick's part in the introduction of Christianity into the north of England, also of its demon pig and wild boars, the dragon of Lymm, St. Anthony's pig, the Dun Bull, the marriage of the Dene and the Sankey, &a. The fact of the existence of such a book may be interesting to Newtosians who are fond of "fireside rambles," and that is the only excuse that can be offered for troubling you with these lines by ONE WHO HAS SEEN THE GHOST. London, October 28th.

A TORY TRICK. Sts,—l have no doubt you heard of a meeting being-held by the Conservatives of St. Helens to consider the advis- ability of petitioning Parliament against the Cloture. As the results of the meeting certain individuals received large sheets of paper for the signature of those persons who are against the Cloture. All this is right so far as it goes, but when the canvassers come with lies and deceive you, in order to get your signature, I think I am doing my duty in making the public aware of it. One of these persons referred to came to me the other day, and asked me for my signature, but he produced the sheet and not the petition. (I suppose the petition will be attached to the sheet.) I asked him what it was for. He informed me that it was a petition praying Parliament to grant Sunday closing. Taking the man to be honest, I at 013C0 signed my name. Shortly afterwards I found I had been deceived. Now, sir, I think—nay, I am sure—that when men have to resort to lies to gain their end, their Cann must be a bad one. After all one cannot be surprised at this "Trick," as tricking seems to be the chief character- istic of the party referred to.—Yours truly, St. Helens, Nov., 1882. TRUTH. PLATEWAY AND CANAL SCHEMES. Sir,—ln your valuable paper of the 28th inst. I see a prospectus of the Manchester Plateway Company, "Limited," scheme from Liverpool to Manchester, which is now supported by 100 of the leading men of eminence, millionaires, shipowners, and others. In another column I find a notice of a proposed Manchester Ship Canal supported by about an equal number, but rather minus the shipowners and others whose patronage means success. Seeing, there- fore, that prospects favour, as to actual completion, the plateway, do you not think, Mr. Editor and readers, that a kind of compromise or amalgamation would meet with less opposition both from Parliament, the railways, capitalists, the general public, and difficulties in the canal scheme between Bank Quay and Manchester, to say nothing of a future and continual expense of £l,OOO a week in dredging, 4fm. ? That, in practice, would prove so different to a plain and theoretical specification view, as compared to the one really feasible, viz., canal from Liverpool to docks in War- rington, and from Warrington to Manchester, Oldham, drc., by plateway. As this will probably be introduced and pro- posed at the public meeting on the 6th inst., would you kindly publish this for previous consideration? There is plenty of land for manufactories, mills, shipyards, Sm., between Garston and Warrington.—Yours very truly, C.E.

BAPTIST BAZAAR AT WARRINGTON. A goodly number of persons attended the opening cere- mony of the bazaar commenced in Warrington Public Hall, On Wednesday, with the object of raising funds for the renovation and decoration of G'olborne-street Baptist Chapel. Although not of a very pretentious character, the bazaar compared favourably with some of its predecessors for the tasteful decoration of the stalls and the superior description and artistic finish of the goods exhibited thereon. The decorations were of a simple but most effective character. The gallery rails were hidden from view by crimson cloth, and above the stalls rose canopies of ecru lace, flags being disposed here and there by way of variety, while a collection of flowers and plants on either side of a large mirror in front of the platform contributed much to the general effect. In all there were six stalls, all of which were loaded with goods that had been attractively displayed. The one near the door was under the charge of Mrs. Crowder, assisted by Miss Baxter and Miss Johnson; and conspicuous upon it were a splendid splash mat illustrative of the age of innocence, crewel brackets, a collection of lamps, scents, and ornaments, together with a large variety of ladies' and chil- dren's wearing apparel,both fancy and serviceable,the greater portion of the latter being the result of the ladies' sewing; meetings. Mrs. Lee and Miss Lilly presided over a beauti- ful assortment of articles of Japanese manufacture—such as brackets, jewel cases, and trays ;the stall also containing several handsome plaques and bronzes, a splendid walnut stationary cabinet, and a variety of ladies' companions, work boxes and writing desks, which were very pretty.. Near this stall there were also some admirable specimens of taxidermy. Under The centre gallery stood a large stall on which were exposed for sale various articles of crewel work of artistic designs. They embraced brackets, foot- stools, cushions, tea cosies, ladies' aprons, and an- timacassars, and were judiciously displayed amongst a large and varied collection of useful goods. The stall was superintended by Mrs. Moore, Mrs. Yonge, and Miss Ederton. Prominent amongst the goods on the next stall were a magnificent pair of real buffalo horns, a hand sewing machine, several beautiful crewel-worked cushions, an assortment of antimacassars, a quantity of boots and ladies' underclothing, &c., of which Mrs. Hall, Miss Barber, and Miss lielsby were in charge. The number and quality of articles collected on the stall, under the superintendence of Mrs. Mot 5, Miss Moss, and Miss Jessie Baxter, did the young men who had got them together much credit. In front of the stall was a coloured copy of Millais' " Cherry- ripe," and a little further on was a water-colour drawing of Budworth Church. Conspicuous on the stall itself were portraits of Bright, Carlisle, Gladstone, and Tennyson, and below them capital little sepia drawings by Mr. J. W. Hall, besides photographs of English and American divines. A doll's bed also claimed attention, and dolls attired as a bride and a baby, and a rich wedding cake. There were also for sale a model church, painted plaques, and numerous ornaments, (Sze. The refresh- ment stall, neatly adorned with flowers and evergreens, was set off with a tempting display of confectionery and more substantial fare, well served by Mrs. Bamford, Miss England, Miss Smith (Dutton), and Miss Hall. Additional facilities for enabling visitors to spend their money were provided in tlte shape of a post office in charge of Miss A. Heesom, Miss E. Heesorn, and Mr. Crowder; a fish pond guarded by Miss Clara Bollass and Mi•!. Eva Hall; a mechanical steamer sailing under the direction of Mr. Arthur Woollard, of Liverpool ; a flower stall, presided over by the Misses Crowder, Simpson, and Timms; knitting machinery, ex- hibited by Miss Harrison (Manchester) and Miss Fernley; and a toy stall, superintended by Miss Jeffery and Miss M. A. Jeffery. We should state that the hall had baeu decorated by Messrs. J. Back, Jackson, Lee, and E. J. BM. The bazaar was opened by Mr. W. Long, of Grappenhall, who was supported by the Revs. J. Yonge, J. Warnock, J. Eglinton, J. Agar Beet, W. Mules, W. Pilling (Hill Cliffe), H. Davies (Lynam), W. C. Tavler (St. Helens), J. Morton, and E. Moore- Dr. Smith, and Messrs. Jos. Davies, F. Monks, Z. Armitage, S. Broadbent, and G. Wallington. The Rev. E. Moore made a statement as to the object of the bazaar, after which Alderman DAVIES apologised for the absence of the Mayor, who was engaged in municipal duties, but had yenta sovereign remedy, which he handed to Mr. Moore amid considerable laughter.—Mr. Logo, in addressing the assembly, expressed the pleasure he had in standing upon a platform where all religious denom- inations could come together, and remarked that he thought people were beginning to see that with so many differently constituted minds as there were there would always be different theologies. Still they might all unite when they have a great common enemy, and found in their towns scepticism, infidelity, ignorance, and sin; and he thought it behoved all to lay aside their distinctive theologies, and come together to help forward such movements as that. After speaking in favour of bazaars, Mr. Long declared the bazaar open, and business was at once commenced. In the eveningivn, ansd n selections of vocal and instrumental music were g "art" gallery and " waxwork " exhibition, with Mr. A. Woods as showman, afforded much amusement to the patrons.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A special meeting of the Council was held on Tuesday, at the Town Hall, for the purpose of adopting a resolution or resolutions authorising and directing an application to the Board of Trade, under and in pursuance of the Electric Lighting Act, 1882, and the rules under the same, for a license or provisional order, empowering the mayor, alder- men, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington, to supply electricity for public and private purposes, within an area co-extensive with their limits of gas supply; and of authorising the Town Clerk to take all steps prescribed by law for the promotion of such application. The meeting was presided over by his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and there were also present Aldermen Davies, Chandley, Kean, Webster; Councillors Broadbent, Monks, Crosfield, Wallington, Taylor, 'W oolfall, Brown, Litton, Pierpoint, Mackie, Dixon, Platt, Whittle, Sutton, Milner, Burgess, Wright, Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), and J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk). THE ELECTRIC LIGHT. The MAYOR said the object of the meeting was because the General Purposes Committee thought it desirable that application should be made to the Board of Trade for powers to enable them to get a provisional order to light the town of Warrington with the electric light when they thought proper, and not to allow any other company or body of men to get it before them. The committee had determined to keep the power in their own hapds. He thought they would all understand the subject of the electric light which had been so often before them. Their object was to obtain a provisional order, so he would move "That application be made to the Board of Trade for a pro- visional order to enable this Corporation to supply elec- tricity within the borough, under the Electric Lighting Act, 1882, and the Board of Trade rules, and that the Town Clerk take all necessary steps for the purpose." Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the motion. In reply to a question, the MAYOR remarked that they had had notice of application from seven or eight companies. The Tows CLERK said other Corporations were asking for the same privilege they were now seeking; and Councillor WALLINGTON thought it desirable that they should have it. Councillor AILCICIEI expressed his great plelsure that the subject had been brought forward at that the last meeting of the municipal year. He had been going through the proceedings of the past year, and had been rather surprised at the little they had to show to those who had sent them of positive work. He thought it was well that they should have full assurance either from the Mayor, or Town Clerk, or some responsible gentleman that the proposal to have the electric light was really a bone fide proposal, and that it was not being made with the intent to strangle the electric light or to make it subservient merely to the gasworks. He thought they had as a town an opportunity of really lead- ing the way and pointing an excellent example if they took active steps either directly or by means of any of the com- panies now in the market of bringing the electric light into the town. But if they were merely taking powers in a sort of "dog-in-the-manger spirit," he would strongly protest against it, as he did ia the earlier stages, because so far as he had been able to see, where Corporations had medalled with the subject, and been at the same time connected with gas works, they had done it with an amount of coldness and doubt that it made their action very suspicious indeed. Alderman CHANDLEY, as the seconder of the mo- tion, felt that he should perhaps explain why he seconded it. In doing so he did not feel that the Council was committed to the course suggested by Coun- cillor Mackie. He took it that the motion was to arm the Coencil with power to furnish the borough with electric light at such a time as they might think it expedient to do, and that it did not pledge itself to immediately take steps for the adoption of the electric light for general purposes. He thought they had a number of years before they were compelled to take any steps—perhaps the Town Clerk would kindly tell them how many? The Tows CLERK: Within three Tears. Alderman CHANDLEY (resuming) said he thought the Coun- cil's course would be to judge by circumstances, and if it was thought expedient to adopt the electric light in the interim to do so, but certainly he felt that the resolution did not pledge itself to any immediate action unless the conviction of the Council generally was that it will be advantageous for the borough. Councillor PLATY thought they were taking a wise action in obtaining powers under the present resolution to apply the electric light throughout the borough. (Hear, hear.) It was advisable for the power to be in the hands of the Council, and it was not advisable to allow any other com- pany to obtain a monopoly, which they might have to pur- chase at some future time, perhaps at a heavy premium on the money that had been expended. He did not agree with Dr. Mackie that they were pledged to take any immediate steps in the matter, and he did not think it advisable to do so for this reason. Although perhaps there was no doubt that the electric light is to a large extent the light of the future, still at the present moment it was undeveloped, and there were many ways of applying it, and it was impossible for them to judge at the present time which was the best mode of doing se. (Hear, hear.) It was better to take the special powers they were now seeking, and then wait until it was further developed, and not make any rash experiment. Let other people do that, and they could take advantage from it. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR observed that the question as to whether they should light the borough with electricity was not before them—that would come on later. The question was whether they should apply for a provisional order or allow some other company or body of men to do so. The question of lighting the town by electricity was in the future, and he wanted them to vote whether they should apply for a pro- visional order or not. The motion was then carried unanimously. • This was all the business.

div.head: CONCLUDING MEETING.
div.p: CONCLUDING MEETING.

The last meeting of the Council for the municipal year was afterwards held, under the presidency of the Mayor, and besides the members present at the special meeting, there also attended Aldermen Holmes, Thewlis, and Burgess; Councillors Fairclough, Greening, Collin, Barker, Jeans, and Francomb ; :Mr. Chorley (borough treasurer), and Mr. Longdin (borough surveyor.) THE WITCH cousurrxri : CONSTABLRS IN PLAIN CLOTEEII. The MAYOR proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee, remarking that they would observe that the authorities would allow them six additional polise for the force.

div.head: ' Councillor FAIRCLOUGEI seconded the motion.
div.p: ' Councillor FAIRCLOUGEI seconded the motion.

Alderman Holm's thought it desirable that they should have a number of police officers in plain clothes, by which means it would possibly tend to the detection of crime. This was done at other towns. _ .

The Mayon: It is done so here. Mr. Hunt exercised his discretion, and sent several men in plain clothes in different parts of the town. He did not send the same men over and over again, but changed them. They formerly had a detective officer, but he got so well known in the town that when he made his appearance everybody ran away. The minutes were passed. TRH YINANC4 110MMITTEE.
Alderman HOLME3 moved the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, and coupled with it a vote of thanks to Councillor Woolfall for his services in auditing the accounts.

Councillor MILNER seconded the resolution, and Councillor PAIRCLOUGH bore testimony to the efficient and valuable services Mr. Woolfall had rendered to the com- mittee during the last 12 months. Councillor PLATT wished to call attention to the fact that many large towns, such as Liverpool and Birmingham for instance, were borrowing their money at a much cheaper rate than they were in Warrington. Councillor PAIRCLOCGH : It is a question whether they are or not. We get ours at 31 per cent. now. Councillor PLATT: I understood the rate now was 4 per cent.
Councillor Fainctotrou: We are borrowing money now at 3i per cent.
Alderman DAVIES made a statement to the same effect.

Alderman HOLMES remarked that although nominally they paid 4 per cent. for their money, yet they always got a premium which would adjust it. Very frequently they took up loans at 3i per cent. . Councillor PLATT : I am very glad to hear it. The minutes were then passed. STREET IMPROVEMENT COMArITTEE : A SLIGHT ERROR. In moving the adoption of the Street Improvement Com- mittee's minutes, Councillor BROADBENT observed that there was a slight clerical error, which was very rare, on the printed summons, with regard to the light- ing of the lamps. It stated that the recommendation of the committee was that the large lamps should be turned out at 12 o'clock, midnight, but it should be to turn out all but one—that was two of the three—in order to effect a saving of the gas in the large lamps in which the comumption was very large. Councillor PLATT seconded the passing of the minutes. But Mr. Broadbent had made a slight mistake—(laughter) —with regard to the lamps. The recommendation was to turn out three of the four and not two of the three. There were 18 of those large lamps in the borough, and the recommendation of the committee was that they should be at a reduced power after twelve o'clock midnight. The MAYOR did not think it advisable to turn out the lamp opposite the Police-station. He thought it should be kept on full power. Councillor PLATT said that it would be advisable also to keep on the one opposite Arpley station, as three lamps were taken away when room was being made for it. It took the place of three other lamps, and that, with the one opposite the police station, might form the subject of a special reso- lution at some other time. It was also suggested that a lamp should be placed opposite Froghall-lane, across Bewsey-road. Alderman CHANDLEY remarked that there was a recom- mendation as to the payment of some money for land to Mr. Reynolds. He wished to ask whether the arrangement was that the land should be given for the wall being built. He understood so at the time. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR replied that he thought not. Councillor Duro's said that he understood the lamp in front of the Post Office and Town Hall was put up for an experiment, and he wished to ask if it was satisfactory. From 10 o'clock at night it cast such a shade that it was very dark, and on the Saturday night when the footpath was not wide enough there was a lot of persons knocking against each other. He should be glad if the lamp was brought on the curbstone, or on the other side of the street. The MAYOR thought that Councillor Dixon's speech had better be made when the Gas Committee's minutes were before them. The resolution was as to reducing the lamps. Councillor BROADZEIIT thought that the question raised by Councillor Dixon was a matter for the Gas Committee

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 1882.

rather than the Street Improvement Committee. With re- spect to the land of Mr. Reynolds, the land was purchased. Mr. Reynolds himself built the wall and sold it and the land to the Corporation, on what they then considered, and did yet consider, very fair and reasonable terms. (Hear, hear.) It was a question which course they should take—whether the Corporation should build the wall as an equivalent for the land, or whether Mr. Reynolds should build his own wall and sell the land to the Corporation. The minutes were then passed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE :

THE COUNCIL AND THE RURAL SAKITARY AUTHORITY. Alderman KEAN, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee alluded to a recom- mendation with reference to the Pig dulcet, which would, no doubt, be put in a proper sanitary condition.; and also to a recommendation as to an arrangement with the Rural Sanitary Authority with regard to the -eewers in connection with the new scheme at Latchford. With regard to the sew scheme at Latchford all was going on right. They were waiting for a little machinery, and they had every reason to believe that when the work was completed it would give satisfaction to everybody. It would be one of the best schemes ever submitted to that boroegh or Council. Councillor WOOLEALL seconded the passing of the minutes. Councillor PLATT thought the recommendation with re- gard to the Rural Sanitary Authority was rather premature, and that it would have been better had the Corporation waited to see if the new machinery would do its work thoroughly and well and cope with the existing sewage, which they were bound to do before taking any additional work. He thought it would have been better had they. waited to see whether it was able to do so. Alderman BURGESS thought it would be deeirable, if the. Paving and Sewerage Committee were not in too great a haste, to make arrangements with the Rural Sanitary Authority. The Authority had given that Corporation a good deal of trouble and did not seem to care hew much trouble they caused the Corporation. He was not disposed to acquiesce in any arrangement until he could End there was a greater disposition on• their part to conform to what was absolutely necessary so far as the working of the Cor- poration was concerned. They were an Authority outside of the Council, and did not hesitate to make statements which ought not to have been made, and which the public ought not to have been made aware of. He thought the Paving and Sewerage Committee should be cireful before they came te any such terms. Councillor Sumer asked if the arrangement was to be a permanent or temporary one. The TowN CLERK : It is to be renewed annually. Councillor WALLINGTON said they had not made any agreement at present. The Paving and Sewerage Committee had not come to an agreement. Alderman BURGESS: I hope they won't. Councillor WALLINGTON said the recommendation con- tained the substance of the proposed arrangemen. They went very carefully into the matter, and he thought it was a very fair arrangement. The sanction of the Council was asked. Cpuncillor Mecum asked if, supposing the minutes were passed, could the Rural Sanitary Authority claim against them for breach of contract if they were not able to do what they undertook? The TOWN CLERK: I don't think they would. It Is merely a recommendation asking the approval of the Coun- cil to the terms. Councillor MACKIE said he was assuming that they were approved. Supposing they passed the resolution, were they legally bound to accede to the terms whether or not the machinery accomplished all they hoped it would. The TowN CLERK replied that they could certainly, according to agreement, but it. contained terms as to its termination. Councillor MlCKllesaid he would then conclude with an amendment that the minutes, so far as they referred to that arrangement, be sent back to the committee. He thought it was a most serious thing to undertake anything of that kind until they had proof that their machinery was competent to do their own work. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WRIGHT seconded the amendment. Councillor MoNers said he did not agree with the amend- ment. He did not see why they should hamper the Paving and Sewerage Committee. If they were disposed to make those terms, which appeared to be a fair and equitable arrangement with the Rural Sanitary Authority, he did not see why they they should not. He had sufficient faith in the committee that they would see the Council were not landed in any difficulty such as Dr. Mackie apprehended. He thought It would be a mistake if he did not accept the terms. Councillor PIERPOINT said from his reading of the minutes he found that he should be conscientiously bound to support the amendment, because he thought the question as stated in the minutes was a very vague one. The MAYOR said it would probably ease the minds of the members if he told them that the present scheme for the sewerage of Latchford would take all the water there and of the Rural Sanitary Authority's district for 30 years to come, calculating the population at the present rate of increase, so that he did not think there was any fear of not being able to carry out the arrangements. Councillor Dixoer thought the committee had taken every precaution to ascertain that the machinery was sufficient to do all the work required of it. He had no doubt that the machinery wouli take the sewage both of Latchford and of the Rural Sanitary Authority's aistrict. (Cries of "Prove it first.") Alderman DAVIES pointed out that if the Rural Sanitary Authority accepted the terms set forth in the minute they were as much bound by the agreement as the Corporation. It was contended that the Corporation would betound and the Authority free; but as he had said they would be just as much bound as the Corporation. He had a great deal to do with the contracts that were entered into with regard to taking over the Liverpool-road and Winwick-road dis- tricts, and in those contracts were clauses which protected the interests of the Corporation; but so that the Council should not put themselves in "a false collar," he suggested that the consideration of the minutes should be adjourned so that the Town Clerk could look up the agreement and advise them thereon. This suggestion was agreed to, and at a later stage of the proceedings, Alderman KEAN said he was recommended by the Town Clerk to move that the minutes be passed with the exception of those recommending the terms upon which the Rural Sanitary Authority should be permitted to connect their sewers with those in course of construction in Latchford. It was better the discussion should stand over—(hear, hear)— and he thought that would meet the wishes of the Council. As to there being any doubt in the minds of the members of the Council as to the scheme answering, he thought they must ease their minds on that subject, as the system had been tried in every way and found satisfactory. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the motion, which was carried.

or was interested in any way in the borough, to support the project as much as he could, and endeavour to get the scheme carried through. So many pamphlets, letters, and papers, of one sort and another, had been sent to the inhabi- tants of the town and members of the Council, that it would

be unnecessarily taking up their time for him to enlarge upon the subject. Still he could say that he attended the first meeting of the committee, and although he had no in- terest in the matter except that of the general welfare of the town, he would do his utmost to forward the scheme, and be only hoped the Council vrould be unanimous in supporting the resolution, so as to strengthen the hands of the Provi- _

sional Committee. Councillor MACKIE mked if it would not be better at this stage to make some addition to the resolution so as to secure unanimity. The concluding line in it stated that the Council pledged themselves. 'The giving of the pledge was a serious matter. It was more than a resolution. They

pledged themsertves to support an application to be made to Parliament in the ensuing session for powers to carry out the work. He was afraid they were going to far in that, and thought it would be quite sufficient for them, as a Council, and all that the Manchestgr Company would expect, if they were to pledge themselves to do so, so far as the powers sought by the Manchester Company were consistent with the interests of Warrington. He thought they would be tying themselves hand and foot if they paised the resolution as it stood. Alderman Worms thought these remarks irregular, as there was a proposition before the Council which was not seconded.

Councillor Macron said he would second the resolution with an addition such as he had suggested. Alderman Banonss most cordially seconded the resolu- tion. So far as Warrington was concerned there could be us second opinion, he believed, in that Council, and he did not think there was a second opinion in the town—(hear, hear)—that the carrying out of this gigantic echeme for a waterway to Manchester capable of acconamodating vessels of so large a tonnage as have been represented to them,would be fraught wiLla the greatest consequence to Warrington, and that of the most beneficial character imaginable. So far as the subject of the resolution was concerned, it was a very old question of his. His venerable friend (Alderman Thewlis) would recollect that when he was Mayor, he suggested to him a scheme for the alteration of the river—that was for

straightening it from Howley to Wilderspool. That was looked upon as being to big a thing for Warrington over to dream of carrying out, but tkis ship canal scheme not only preposed to effect that, but to do infinitely more for War- rington than any person in the town ever contempated. For himself he had not the slightest misgiving as to the result, 4f the scheme Were ever carried out. People told them that the ground was already occupied; that they had railways almost innumerable; that they had plateways proposed to be made; and facilities for the removal of merchandise that would meet all their requirements. If any gentleman would take the trouble to look back at the history of the county _ _ _

for the last 50 years, and would compare the population o this county and the adjoining county of Yorkshire 50 years ago with what it was to-day, and would consider, taking the same increase of population as had taken place in the last 50 years, what it would be 50 years hence, that gentle- man, he was persuaded, would arrive at the conclusion that all the facilities proposed to be given for removing the products of these mighty counties would be all insufficient. They might have all their railways, they might have all their plateways, and they might have everything else, but if the population grew in the same ratio as it bad grown in the last 50 years, they might rely upon it, unless they carried out this canal scheme, which would do more good than all the rest put together, they would be as fast as they were to-day, and they were just as fast to-day as they were 50 years ago before railways were introduced. He had no mis- giving whatever as to the correetness of-what was proposed to be done. He believed it was absolutely necessary this scheme should be carried out. There was nothing to his mind that would meet the requirements of this vast district so much. He was persuaded the proposal before the Council now for a navigation which would enable vessels of large tonnage to reach Manchester, was the only thing that was worth considering at the present time; and he should be de- lighted to find the difficulties that attended a gigantic scheme like this were overcome. They might depend upon it if the scheme was not carried out this year, it would be at a very early period. Councillor CROSPIRLD said he did not want to throw cold water on this grand scheme, but he was one of those ecceatric and peculiar individuals who did not believe in it. If any- body would make the canal he for one would be very mach obliged to them. His firm was as much interested in the navigation of the river as anybody perhaps in the town— (hear, hear)—and the better the navigation of the river the better it would be for them individually. But if he were to give his name to a scheme like this he should feel he was doing something which was wrong, because he might lead his friends to invest their money in a scheme which he did not believe could ever pay, or would ever yield a farthing of interest. Therefore he could not conscientiously either join in the scheme himself or advise his friends to join it. There were plenty of people who would put their money in concerns that did not yield interest. That was for the benefit of the people, •and they were local patriots. His friend Alderman Davies did not believe he had got any local patriotism in him—(laughter),--but he had got a little, and if he believed the scheme would yield a return he would not mind jolting it. But he believed it to be a general opinion in this country that nothing could be done if it did not pay, because it came to an end. Of course there might be difficulties to overcome, but engineers in these days, given plenty of money and plenty of time, could do any- thing but fly. He dared say they could make a canal, but his humble opinion was that their friends in Manchester had precious little notion of what they had undertaken, and he did not believe the engineers knew much of toe diffi- culties that they would have to encounter in the estuary of the Mersey. But what the Council had to consider was what they had to do to protect Warrington. His firm used the river for their steamer and so did Messrs. Fairclough and Mr. Litton, and they had not one farthing rate to pay. The river was worth £l,OOO a year to them (Messrs. Crosfield) ; but if the canal were made, and their Manchester friends laid out millions of money in building enormous docks how did they know hut what they would levy a rate upon them for their vessels? which would be a serious cost every year. The Corporation must take care to protect the town against Manchester charging upon Warrington what Manchester it- self ought to pay. He r posed as an amendment that the following words be added to the resolution subject to the application to Parliament being such as will provide for all the advantages to which Warrington is deemed to be en- titled by this Council." (Hear, hear.) He merely wanted to make it clear so that they would not be left in the lurch if the scheme were carried out. Councillor MACKIR seconded the amendment. He said far be it from him to ;take the same despairing tone as Councillor Crosfield, but at the same time he claimed that great minds thought alike in this occasion. (Laughter.) They would remember that he mentioned, when the subject was introduced two months ago, they should take care that Warrington enjoyed all the privileges which it had under the Act of 1720. (Hear, hear.) At that time a clause was passed in which it was secured to War- rigton for all time that no charge should be made upon it for vessels passing between Liverpool and Warrington. He was bound to say the state of circumstances was materially altered by what the new company propose& They proposed to do what the company of 1720 did not propose. The present company proposed to make the river between Liver- pool and Warrington really fit for ocean-going vessels, and therefore he at once saw it would be their duty to submit to a pro rata tax, at any rate, upon all vessels cpming only as far as Warrington. The subject was one of those upon , which their character not only at present, but for a long time to come, might materially depend. The step which they took that night might dishearten, or it might cheer. He had subscribed a small sum towards the preliminary expenses, and he was prepared to do more for the carrying out of the scheme. He believed all the engineer said would be done, and that reasonably within the amount he had mentioned. He impressed upon the Council the fact that if they passed the resolution they would shut themselves oat entirely from any locus standi before the committee of the House of Commons. They pledged themselves to take the whole Bill as the promoters might bring it forward in a lump. Now, what were the dangers to which they were liable? First and foremost, there was the question of rates. If a concern like that of Messrs. Crosfield's was to he fined to the extent of £l,OOO a year, it would be a very dangerous thing for Warrington to go on with such a scheme. There must be tome clause introduced to save these who were protected already. Then there was the question—should they have the river straightened from Liverpool to Warrington and onwards, or was Warrington to shunted? It might be Warrington would get the "go-by," and that Latchford was to be the favoured child. It might be the question of poor rates would become a material question. If they had a large sea-faring population, and men connected with the docks, dx., living within their boandary, for whom they had to provide in the day of their destitution, and the property itself so far removed from them that they could make no claim upon it, that would be a dangerous thing. He suggested that the Borough Sur- veyor should be authorised to take such steps to ascertain whether any of the interests of Warrington would be affected as would enable him to appear before the committee of the House of Commons in due time. If that were done, he had not a doubt Warrington would find a fair share of the money, and he had not the least doubt the Manchester men would look upon them as shrewd, business' aad fair- play men when they read the proposition made that night, / He made it, not with a feeling of opposition, but with the very reverse. Councillor MONKS supported the amendment because he felt the original motion was rather too vague as to the in- terests of Warrington. He did not see that there could be any possible objection to the amendment because they gave the scheme their firm support, and he was quite sure that they would not do it unless they felt their interests were understood and protected. As to what their interests were, that was a question for the Council to consider and deter- mine in conjunction with others in the town who, like Messrs. Crosfield, made use of the river. At the same time he thought their minds were pretty well made up as to what they all conceived to be the best for the town. He thought in any scheme proposed for carrying out the Manchester Ship Canal, Warrington should have free navigation at least equal to that which it enjoyed at the present time. (Hear, hear,) He did not take the same view as Councillor Cros- field in reference to its financial Success. He thought when they considered the vast interests in Yorkshire, Lancashire, and the Midland counties it might prove to be like the Suez Canal, and turn out a success. However, it was a matter for the future to decide, and if they had had to wait

until they saw their way clear to making a profit he was sure a good many of them would have been worse off :ham they were that day. (Hear, bear.) In the success of the Manchester Ship Canal they must exercise the same faith as they did in their own businesses, and hope and work for returns. He happened to know some of the men connected with the scheme, and they were shrewd business men, men of great capacity, who had made their own way in the world, and who did not throw away money foolishly, or put large sums of money where they would be unremunerative. He hoped an opportunity would be given to the public of not only considering the scheme financially but of seeing the plans and sectiens, so that they might see exactly the route of the canal, the depth, and how the proposals of the engineer affected 'Latchford. He was not so much afraid of the poor rate as Councillor Mackie. He thought Warrington could not help but largely benefit by the canal if it came within a mile of the present course of the river. In that event they would get all the accommodation Warrington required in the bend of the river, which they would be able to lock. Ile believed this was an opportunity such as had never before presented itself in the history of War- rington, for giving the town an impetus, and making it one of the most flourishing towns in the country—(hear, hear) —and he thought everything the Council could do should be done with a view to giving their very best support to the scheme. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES said as regarded the advantages that would accrue to Warrington there could be no question. There was not a person but must feel that the scheme as far as Warrington was concerned was one of vital importance. He thought the gentlemen who had made the amendment were quite right in doing so, and he should be very glad to support it. He suggested that the Mayor should allow it to become part ot the original motion, because it would be quite as acceptable to the promoters of the scheme. (Hear, hear.) The promoters were well aware of the present ad- vantages possessed by Warrington, and they were quite pre- pared to take them into consideration, and to provide in the Bill that Warrington should have advantages equal to those now possessed by it of being free up to Bank Quay. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FAIRCLOUGH : What about Mersey/Mills? Alderman DAVIES : Mersey Mills will not be overlooked. He was quite prepared to accept the amendment, and very likely it would enable the :Council to pass the resolution unanimously. He was sorry Councillor Crosfield's patriotism ended at his pocket. (Laughter.) He as much as said so bec tuse he said he could not support the scheme because 1:e thought it would not pay. [Councillor CEOs- FIELD: And a very good reason, too.] A very good reason indeed, as he would now have so much more money to de- vote to other charitable objects in Warrington. (Laughter.) He would be satisfied if the Mayor allowed the amendment to stand part of the resolution; and he would undertake that the promoters would bring plans, sections, dr.c., to put up in that room, or some other public place, for the inspection of the people of Warrington. With the consent of Couneillor Crosfield, the Mayor amended the resolution as he had suggested. Councillor SUTTOIt had no difficulty in supporting either the resolution or the amendment, because if the scheme were carried out it waslbound to be beneficial to Warrington under an circumstances. They had at present a disagree- able river, used by nobody except the people on the route, and if they were deprived of any rights or interests which they enjoyed at present there was no doubt they would be compensated for any loss they might sustain. But at all events they might feel assured when the time came War- rington would look after its own interests. Councillor Pr..arr was glad the resolution had been amended, because he thought the interests of Warrington were very much bound up in the river, and would require very careful watching when the Bill came before Parlia- ment. In regard to the question as to whether the canal would pay, he must confess he bad had some doubts but Councillor Crosfield had removed them that night. He told them the river was worth £l,OOO a year to his firm, and he (Councillor Platt) asked himself how many firms in Manchester and the district were there to whom the river would be worth £I,OOO if the scheme was accomplished; and from the numbers there was a probability that not only would it be to the interest of Manchester and Warrington, but it:would be a paying concern. (Hear, bear.) He was sure there were scores of firms to whom the canal would be worth £l,ooo,and who would be quite willing to pay for any benefits they received, and if the promoters did not look for a heavy rate of interest they might look for some return upon their outlay. Even if they did not expect to get any return for their money it was the duty of every influential man, and those who could afford, to lend the scheme some help in the shape of taking up shares so that the scheme might go on. Councillor BURGESS was glad the resolution had been amended. He did not think there could be any doubt at all in anyone's mind that the carrying out of this scheme must be of immense advantage to Warrington. No one could look at the map and see that Warrington was the only important town between the cities of Liverpool and Manchester with- out seeing at once the great advantage ot the scheme. The question of paying was outside the discussion altogether. What they had to consider was what was the advantage to the town, and he did not think there could be two opinions about that. (Hear, hear.) Of course there were great dif- ficulties to be overcome, but he hoped it would prove, as it had proved many times before, that difficulty only meant to the men of Lancashire a thing to be overcome. If the scheme were carried through the population would he three times what it was 50 years ago, and Warrington would be- come not only a great manufacturing centre but also a com- mercial town. The EX-MAYOR (Councillor Fairclough) supported the amended resolution. He said he had no fear on his part if the canal were made it would be a paying concern. The only difficulties were as to the formation of it, and if these were overcome he had no fear of the result. (Hear, hear.) Councillor CROSFIELD apologised for having said anything about the canal paying or not. He only did it in defence of his personal character and to explain why he did not support the local committee. He did not want to lead any of his friends to support a scheme which would not pay. The MAYOR was glad Councillor Crosfield had thought of the amendment, and he was quite sure the Provisional Com- mittee would be very glad the subject had been brought for- ward. (Hear, hear.)—He was about to put the resolution when Alderman BURGESS said he bad not agreed to any altera- tion as yet. (Laughter.) He,however, seconded the resolution as amended, and said he bad studiously avoided the question as to whether it would pay or not. All he contended was that it would be a grand thing for Warrington if carried out. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was further amended as to read :—" That this Council, having considered the scheme known as the 'Manchester Ship Canal,' for deepening, widening, and otherwise improving the rivers Mersey and Irwell, so as to render them suitable for navigation by ocean-going vessels hp to Manchester, hereby expresss its approval of the pro- ject, and pledges itself to accord every support to the scheme, provided the application to Parliament contained such provisions as will ensure to the borough and its in- habitants all the advantages to which in the opinion of this Council they are Entitled." It was put in this form, and carried unanimously. THANKS TO THE RETIRING MAYOR.

Mr. Alderman HOLMES next rose, and moved the follow- ing resolution :—" That the best thanks of this Council be presented to the Worshipful the Mayor, John Richard Pickmere, Esq., for the able and satisfactory manner in which he has sustained the dignity of the important office of Mayor of this borough during this, his third successive year of office; 'and for the unvarying courtesy, kindness, and impartiality displayed by him when presiding over the deliberations of the Council, and in his intercourse with its members." (Applause.) Alderman Holmes said he had had to propose a similar resolution for several years past, and he began to think it was time some other gentleman moved it, because he would then perhaps introduce language of a different character to that which he had to repeat. The Mayor bad presided over the deliberations of the Council in a manner that was most remarkable. He knew of no previous Mayor who had presided over the Council meetings So well, he knew of no one who had kept the Council in such thorough order, and of na one whom the Council so thoroughly respected. (Applause.) In presiding at the police court, too, his Worship had given his decisions in a manner which had given great satisfaction to the public, and probably also to some persons whom be had had to punish. (Applause.) The great readiness with which he had always come before the public and taken part in all movements intended to further the interests of the borough, and the way in which he had always been ready with his purse to subscribe to all schemes which the public wished to carry out had been worthy of his high office; whilst he had amply and generously recognised the services which the teachers as well as the promoters of elementary educa- tion rendered by the conversaziones given in their honour. (Applause.) He also desired to speak, if he might be allowed to do so, of the Mayor's good lady, Mrs. Pickmere. kApplause.) She had always been most willing to render what assistance she could, and she had been a- grand help- meet to the Mayor. Wherever a lady could go, she had gone, and rendered what help she could, and she had won from the inhabitants of Warrington their esteem, and left behind a pleasing recollection one which would be ' indelible. It must have been a great pleasure and gratifica- tion to the Mayor and Mayoress—as it was to those who witnessed it—to have witnessed the scene in that Hall on Thursday evening last. (Loud applause.) It was one which was unique in the history of Warrington, and many years must pass before any of them would forget such a gathering as that was. (Loud applause.) Mr. Alderman WEBSTER said he had great pleasure in seconding the proposition made by his friend Mr. Alderman Holmes. He found it very difficult indeed to add words which would adequately express his (Alderman Webster's) feelings on that occasion, or, indeed, to add anything to what Mr. Alderman Holmes had so ably expressed. He was certain the whole of the members of the Council, and not only the whole of the members of the Council, but also the whole of the inhabitants of the town, felt towards the Mayor a deep debt of gratitude for the manner in which he had conducted the business of the town, and also for his general conduct in the chair of the Corporation. (Applause.) There were few if any of them who had not participated in his worship's boundless hospitality on various occasions, and all of them had participated in that fairy scene—which could scarcely be equalled—a few evenings ago in that building. (Applause.) He concurred in the observations of , Mr. Alderman Holmes as to the manner in which the Mayoress had supported the Mayor. On all occasions when she had come before the public she had aided him very , much, and he was sure she would leave a very warm and r cordial impression on the memory of all those who had L come in contact with her. (Applause.) He did not know ; that he could say more, except that it vroald be

The minutes of the School Attendance, Cemetery, Town Hall, Park and Baths, Markets, Gas, and Sanitary Com- mittees were passed with little or no comment.
TIER ELECTRIC LIGHT IN LIBRARIES.

Councillor GREENING moved, and Councillor BROADBENT seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Museum Com- mittee, which contained among other things, a report from the Librarian (Mr. Madeley) of the annual meeting of the Library Association which ha had attended. The report contained the following:—" The librarian of the Liverpool Free Libraries on Electric Lighting,' dealt solely with the results from a librarian's point of view, and spoke very strongly of the immense advantages that followed the use of electricity in lighting the Picton Reading Room." Councillor Milner called attention to the valuable remarks of the librarian on the use of the electric light, as proved by its use in the Liverpool Library, and said gas was certainly very deletereous to books, while the electric light did them no harm. _ _

Councillor CROSFIBLD, in confirmation of that statement, said that when he was in London some months ago, he went to the auctioneers' who sold the late Mr. Marsh's library, and they told him his books were in very bad condition owing to the effects of gas. Alderman Wausma said when the electric light became practicable it would be adopted, but in a little place like Warrington at present the expense of its production put it out of question. The minutes were then:adopted. TUB CHARGES OF THE WATERWORKS COMPANY.
The confirmation of the minutes of the General Purposes Committee :having been proposed by the MAYOII, and seconded by Alderman WRBSTBR, - _ -

Councilfor PLAIT said he did not know whether the matter he was about to mention was one for the consideration of the General Purposes Committee, but he thought same action should be taken by the Corporation with a view to opposing the rate• which the Waterworks Company still charged the public. It was a great hardship that this ap- peal should :hang over so long, as the company kept charging the inhabitants at the old rate, which, as decided by two judges, was illegal. But in spite of those decisions the company kept sending in demand notes for the same rates, and people kept paying them, but it was very pro- blematical whether they would receive the money again. He thought the committee should take the matter up. Alderman BURGESS did not see that the Corporation should meddle in the matter. He believed if the people did not choose to pay the demand it remained unpaid, and there were a great number of people who were enjoying an im- munity they never anticipated in regard to the water rate. He thought it was better the matter should remain as it was, as it was hardly wise that the Corporation should meddle and bring about such condition of things that people would have to pay. Councillor PLATT said it put owners of cottages in this dilemma: if they refused to pay they lost a composition of 20 per cent. allowed if the money was paid by a certain date, and that was more than the excess they were charged. The minutes were confirmed. THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

The MAYOR moved the following resolution :—" That this Council, having considered the scheme known as the 'Man- chester Ship'Canal,' for deepening, widening, and otherwise improving the rivers Mersey and Irwell, so as to render them suitable for navigation by ocean-going vessels up to Man- chester, hereby expresses its approval of the project, and pledges itself to accord every support to the application to be made to Parliament in the ensuing session for powers to carry out the work." That was a resolution, said his Worship, which he had very great pleasure in moving, because he thought every inhabitant of the town must wish such a good work to go on in the interests of the borough. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt about it, that if the pro- posed Manchester Ship Canal were made, Warrington would gain immensely by it. He thought it was the duty of every inhabitant of the town, everybody who had land or houses,

difficult to find such another gentleman to follow Mr. Alder- man Pickmere. He was certain when the Mayor retired he would carry with him the best wishes and the best feelings of every member of the Council, and also of the inhabitants of the town. (Applause.) He cordially concurred in con- veying to Mrs. Pickmere the great pleasure which the Council felt in expressing their gratitude to her for the manner in which she had aided and assisted the Mayor dur- ing the several years of his Mayoralty. Mr. Alderman THEWLIS said he cordially endorsed the sentiments expressed by the mover of the resolution, Mr. Alderman Holmes, and the seconder, Mr. Alderman Web- ster. He, and no doubt many other gentlemen, had watched the career of the Mayor whilst in office, and a more inde- pendent and more straightforward gentleman occupying the civic chair he never had met with during his connection with the Council, which extended over a period of 24 or 25 years. All that Mr. Alderman Holmes had said the Mayor richly deserved, and there had not been the slightest fulsome language contributed in any shape •whatever, because all the Mayor's actions had been impar- tial from the beginning to the close of his Mayoral career. (Applause.) He sincerely hoped his successor would take a leaf out of Mr. Alderman Pickmere's book, act as impartially in the deliberations of the Council, and dis- charge the duties of the high office in the same straight- forward and honourable manner that the present Mayor had done. (Loud applause.)

Mr. Alderman -BURGESS said he could not allow the op- portunity to pass without saying how deeply grateful he was for the services the Mayor had rendered the borough. He had known the Mayor now a great many years, he had promoted Mr. Alderman Pickmere's election three years ago when he was called upon a second time to take the office, and the feeling then entertained by all of them that the chair would by Mr. Alderman Pickmere be most worthily filled, had been much more than realised. He quite agreed, therefore, with all that had been said about his worship. He was exceedingly sorry to part with the Mayor, and he wished it could have been otherwise. (Applause.) With reference to the Mayoress all they knew was that she had contributed enormously to the great success which had attented the Mayoralty during the past three years, and he hoped both the Mayor and Mayoress would be long spared to look back upon the time which had been spent, and so well spent, in the interests of the borough. It would be a source of gratification to them t o reflect upon the opportunities they had had of being of service to the inhabitants of Warrington and he hoped they would at the same time realise to the fullest extent how much they were lrald in the esteem and affection of the people of the borough. (Applause.) Mr. Alderman Warms observed that the charm and worth of the resolution consisted in the honest and hearty manner in which the thanks were accorded. (Applause.) In pass- ing the resolution they felt they were only expressing the voice of the people :of Warrington' who were satisfied with the manner in which the Mayor had fulfilled his duties in the chair. He was certain that those outside would be very much disappointed if they did not feel they had a voice in the matter. The resolution contained no idle words, but it was the expression of their deep conviction. Mr. Ceuncillor CROSFIBLD said that amongst all the Mayor's excellent qualities he did not think there was one greater to his (Mr. Crosfield's) mind than that of the Mayor's strict impartiality. He had admired the Mayor at all times for the manner in which he had conducted himself in the chair, and he did not think that anybody could have told whether the Mayor was a Tory or a Radical, a Whig or a Conservative. His politics had never been shown in the least degree; and all had been treated with fairness. (Applause.) Mr. Councillor BROADBENT said he joined heartily in the vote of thanks, for he thought the manner in which Mr. Pickmere had discharged his duties was something most marvellous. It was generally the case that a Mayor ran some risk, in occupying the post a second year, of his popularity diminishing; but be believed that in this case Alderman Pickmere had occupied his position for three years with ever-increasing popularity. (Hear, hear.) His impartiality and his admir- able good temper—which latter had never failed him on one occasion—were the secret of his influence over the council.

(Applause.) He also joined heartily in the sentiments of regard and admiration expressed for Mrs. Pickmere. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Alderman CHANDLEY said the Mayor had faithfully and admirably fulfilled all the duties he was expected to perform; and he thought the Council and the town generally owed the Mayor a deep debt of gratitude for hay- ing devoted so much time to their interests.. He trusted the Mayor and Mayoress would be long spared to enjoy the reflection that they had well earned a crown of laurels; and he was sure nothing would give them greater pleasure than to reflect upon the good they had done and upon what had been said, for every word was well deserved. Mr. Councillor .FAIRCLOUGII (the deputy mayor), in putting the resolution to the meeting, observed that very little remained for him to say, and he would therefore con- tent himself with eudorsing, and he did it very cordially, all that had been said about the . services the Mayor and Mrs. Pickmere had rendered to the borough. The resolution was then put, and carried with acclama- tion.

tt•,The Meson, on rising to respond, was received with loud ' applause. Speaking with considerable emotion, he said he must confess that they had made him very hot and pecu- liar. Ho did not think it was the heat of the room, but rather the effect of hearing so many kind words said of him. He really felt he did not deserve one-half of what had been said. He had been supported very well, he was happy to say, by every member of the Council when he had had the pleasure of meeting them in that Chamber. He did not think he had ever had any annoyance; in fact, he was sure he had not had any annoyante from any member. Every question had been argued fairly, they had agreed to differ with each other, and they had shaken hauds with each other at the end of the debates. He must, therefore, thank them all most sincerely for the mariner in which they had supported him during his chairmanship. He felt it was not his power and ability which had contributed to the success of his Mayoralty so much as the kindness and courtesy of the membeFe of the Council, not only towards himself but towards each other, whichalad led to that good result. (Applause.) He also begged to thank them very heartily for the kind words that had been said of hie dear wife. (Applause.) When he told her she would indeed be very much pleased and gratified. (Renewed applause.) He would not say more because he now occupied one of the most difficult positions a man could be placed in, and that was to hear kind words spoken of one's self. He had

further: to thank the ToN;n Clerk, and all the other officers of the Corporation,—Mr. Chorley, Mr. Longdin:and Mr. Hunt—for all the kindnesses he had received at their hands. They had, he felt, gone out of their way many times to render him services; and really be could not have carried on the work of the Corporation so well but for their assist- ance. He must, however, particularly name the deputy Town Clerk, who had been at his elbow often before be was wanted, and who had been untiring in his exertions. He had reason to be grateful for all the kindnesses he had received from the officials, who, he was glad to say, did their work honestly and well. They might say that they paid the officials well for what they did. They, however, strived to do their utmost and the best they possibly could for the Corporation and the inhabitants of the town. (Applause.) That was the last time he would have the honour of addressing them from that chair except on the 9th November, and again he begged to thank them all for their kindness. (Loud applause.) The Council then adjourned.
LECTURE BY THE REV. PETER McKENZIE AT EARLESTOWN.

The well-known preacher and more popular lecturer, the Rev. P. Mackenzie, visited Earlestown on Wednesday last, and preached and lectured in the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Cross-lane, in aid of the new organ fund. His visit had been looked forward to with considerable interest, and many persons connected with the various religions denomi- nations went to hear the famous speaker. In the afternoon the rev, gentleman preached to an interested and attentive congregation, mid a collection was made in aid of the new organ fund. In the evening the Rev. P. Mackenzie gave a lecture in the chapel, entitled "The Good Samaritan, a noble type of Christian philanthropy." Notwithstanding the un- favourable state of the weather there was a large attendance. After the meeting had been opened with the singing of a hymn, the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn remarked that their good friend Mr. Walker had kindly consented to preside. Mr. B. Walker then took the chair, and in calling upon the Rev. P. McKenzie, said the subject was one which had occupied the attention of our countrymen for many years, namely, charity. The title was the good Samaritan, and he hoped and prayed that they might receive much good as the result of their gathering. The Lecturer was warmly welcomed. He observed that they were all very pleased to take any part in promoting their Master's glory, or to assist in any form to help forward that which was pleasing in His sight, and that which would secure for them His smile and benediction. He had fro- quently lectured on subjects from the Old Testament, but that evening he was to speak of the New Testament—" The good Samaritan, a noble type of Christian philanthropy." He had had some good times with the Old Testament worthies; but leaving those he was sure there was plenty in the good Samaritan. They would first notice his home, his history, his characteristics, and noble example. The home of the good Samaritan, Samaria, was situated in the very centre of Palestine, nestling in one of the richest and most beautiful portions of that country. When Christ came into the world he observed the Jews had no dealings with the Samaritans, so much enmity and strife had sprung up be- tween them. Having briefly pointed out incidents in Christ's journeys through Palestine, the Lecturer proceeded to state that a certain lawyer came to Jesus—he believed not with a bad intention, although to " try " Him—with an enquiry not like that of a man who sought to entangle Christ in his talk, but to ask him "What must I do to inherit eternal life? " It was not an empty or idle question that! It was a sublime and grand one. It was not like those who asked him about a family of brothers having married one woman, and who was to have her at the judgment, or whether she was to be raffled for—(laughter) ; nor like the man who came asking if it was lawful to give tribute to Ctesar, thinking that if Christ said it was, then they would make it hot for him, the poor devil, the miserable blackleg. If he said it was not, then they would institute a charge against him, and put him into Kilmainham. (Loud laugh- ter.) When Christ told him that he must "render unto Cesar the things that are of Cmsar, and unto God the things that are of God," the fellow went away as if he had scalded boiling water upon him, and he never came back in his life. - He got such a scalding that he never got over it. (Laughter.)
