div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS. Dr. Steele presided over the monthly meeting, which was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday. There were also present Messrs. T. Norman, Dobson, W. Fisher, Williams, G. S. Hazlehurst, Timmins, It. Shaw, P. Briscoe, J. J. Speakman, W. H. Linaker (clerk), William Brooks (secre- tary), W. Barker (surveyor). IHE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.—THE lIPIDEMICS.—PROPOSAL TOcescilw that the number Dr.Mornerz,zthemoesdn DAYizaele:fficert reported of deaths registered In Runcorn during the past month amounted to 45, representing a death rate of 36 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths 13 were due to pulmonary complaints' S measles, 7 diseases of the nervous system, 4 abdominal diseases, 2 scarlatina, 4 debility, 2 diarrheea, 2 mara.smus, 2 senile decay. Cancer, diarrhoea and premature birth account for one each. One death took place at Halton- within-Runcorn; one inquest was held: total deaths, 45. Thirty deaths occurred among children of five years old and under, and 23 under one year. The deaths for the corres- ponding month last year were 16. Measles and scarlatina since his last special report had so fluctuated that it was im- possible to give a definite opinion as to abatement.—Mr. Fiseiset wished to know whether the epidemic was increas- ing, and Dr. Moresiez replied that he could net say, because sometimes he tad aunany as 15 cases in a day, while on 'Wig he had only t7se or four.—Mr. FISHER remarked that there was a larger number of children in attendance at school than there was a month ago. This he considered a good sign. He thought the disease was decreasing. The Medical Officer of Health made a special report to the Highway and Sanitary Committee on the 25th October, in which he stated that the death rate of Runcorn is con- siderably augmented since last June, the total number being 165 as compared with 73 for the same period during 1881. Within the present month 5 deaths took place from measles and two from scarlatina. Under the above circumstances he would suggest the temporary closing of all schools, also that an inspector of nuisances be appointed to make house to house inspections. Infantile mortality was something appalling. The epidemics of scarlet fever and measles which had been prevailing in Runcorn since last June was one of the most extraordinary character—measles first, and subsequently scarlet fever. No diseases had more plainly demonAtrated seasonal mortality in Runcorn than the above. October was always considered the month in which occurred the maximum of mortality from zymotic diseases, and he sincerely hoped it would prove so. It was quite obvious that the deaths at the present time bore no fixed proportion to the cases under treatment. In consequence of this report the Committee forwarded letters to the managers of the several public schools inform- ing them of the suggestion made by the medical officer, and asking them to give it their serious consideration. In an- swer to those communications letters were read from the Rev. Canon Barclay and the clerk to the School Board,whicb stated that they considered the step advised by the medical officer unnecessary.—The CHAIRMAN said he was rather glad to hear that the schools were not to be closed. The children when playing about the streets, and going from house to house would spread the infection more than they would if they went to school.—Mr. Fisrama thought the time had gone past for closing the schools. Speaking for Trinity schools he might tell the Board that whereas about a month ago they had an attendance of 120, they now had over 200 —that was in the boys' school alone. That showed that the disease was dying out, and that its extinction was only a question of a week or two.—Mr. Slum showed the serious- ness of closing the schools, and suggested that in case of future epidemics a committee of the Board should co-operate with the School Board and the medical men in the town to stamp out the disease.—Mr. NORMAN related the incident told to the School Board, and reported elsewhere, and said Mr. Rigby thought the Board ought to prosecute a man who acted in that way.—The CHAIRMAN said it was a ques- tion for the law-clerk as to whether the Board had the power to do so.—Mr. NORMAN: Mr. Rigby says we have.—Mr. Demos; said he believed the abatement in the epidemic was attributable to the active exertions of Mr. Barker. (Hear, hear.) He had used disinfectants to a large extent during the last fortnight or so. (Hear, hear.) All back premises had been disinfected, and pitch and tar had been burned in the passages. and wherever this had been done there was a decrease in the number of cases. He believed if the Board left the matter in the hands of Mr. Barker and the school inspector, who rould report any new cases that might come under his notice and the places would be immediately dis- hafected, that the disease would be ultimately stamped out. —The discussion on this matter then ceased. THE LIBRARY QUESTION. A SCENE.—MR. HAZLEHURST RESIGNS. The minutes of the Highway and SanitAry Committee stated that a letter had been received from Mr. H. White complaining of a further nuisance from the Glycerine Works. Resolution, that the letter be acknowledged, a copy sent to Mr. V. Cletus, and that he be asked to state what was being done to abate the nuisance. Mr. Clolus replied, and explained the process which had been adopted to pre- vent the smell, adding that he should be glad if any of the Commissioners would inspect the works. It was resolved that plans of eight houses in Handley-street, and three houses in Egerton-street, proposed to be erected by Mr. W. Farrell, be referred back for amendment. The offers of Mr. Hazlehurst and Mr. Holmes to rent or lease the Commissioners' offices were considered, and it was recommended their further consideration be adjourned until the close of the present financial year, March next. The surveyor was instructed to write to the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company asking them to put their portion of the Old Quay footpath in repair.—Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. FISHER seconded, a proposition that the minutes be con- firmed.—Mr. HAZLIGIURST : lam free to admit, Mr. Chair- man' ' the reasonableness of the minute adjourning my offer of adaily reading-room to the town, until March next, the close of the present financial year. If the Commissioners have not in this year's estimates provided for removal, this hdjournment requires no explanation. I have, however, examined the estimate that shows the cost of removal to Waterloo House, and find that for the sum of £25 the Com- missioners can meet as comfortably there as here. Mr. , Chairman, I now lay my cheque for that fire and twenty pounds on the table, which you can accept as prepayment of rent for these rooms. Let me put the matter in another way. I will engage that the Commissioners shall meet as comfortably at Waterloo House as they meet here, until March next. Now let us review the whole matter. This Board has been shown that a free library in the most frequented part of the town will be more likely to benefit the non-reading classes of the popu- lation than a library placed in a quiet residental position like Waterloo House. More important still, it has been shown that a daily reading-room cannot be established ex- cept by aid of private benefaction. That is offered. Now comes the objection that the Commissioners have not pro- vided for the expenses of removal. That objection is en- tirely met by my cheque lying upon the table. Mr. Chair- man, my position on the Library Committee depends on my holding a seat at this Board. I value my position on that set nmittee more than any public office I hold, but neither that nor any other consideration shall induce me to sit with a Board that can so deliberately betray the welfare of the town by refusing the offer of a daily reading-room for the benefit of the public. I wash my bands clean of the whole affair. I move, as an amendment, that the next meeting of the Board be held in Waterloo House.—Mr. SHAW objected that this was not an amendment.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : I don't like to stand on technical terms. I know the objections are not made from any love of order; they are simply made because you don't wish this thing to be. Mr. SHAW: It either is an !amend- ment or it is not. It is not because—The CLERK ruled the amendment out or order. Mr. SHAW thought Mr. Hazlehurst ought to withdraw the remark he had made. [Mr. NORMAN: Hear, hear.] No gentleman wanted to object on any technical grounds to the Free Library reading-rooon being held in that room. He had had as much to say on this subject as perhaps any member of the Board, and he took it that there was a much larger question than Mr. Hazlehurst put before the Board. The root of that question Mr. Hazlehurst had not touched at all in what he had suggested to do. Mr. Hazlehurst ought to know that the Commissioners could not leave that room and go into Waterloo House with any expense only of £25.— Mr. HAZLEHLRST : I can show the figures.—Mr. &taw : I don't care what figures you show.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : I have met all objections by saying that the Board shall meet as comfortably at Waterloo House as they do hear.—The CHAIRMAN: It is not the case.—Mr. DOBSON suggested that the resolution be referred back to the Highway and Sanitary Committee for further consideration.—The CHAIRMAN: That is the only course to take.—Mr. DOBSON : I don't see that there is any ether course to adopt.—Mr. HAZLESURST : Simply this, that you lose £25 by doing so.—Mr. Donsoet : If we wish to take this into consideration we ought to do so in a proper way that is - by referring it back, and if Mr. Hazlehurst wishes to meet on the case there is an opportunity of doing so.—Mr. HARLEIIIIRST : No, I will not have it put back a single meeting. That cheque lies there only for this time. I have been bothered enough. Mr. Seem : lam sure no gentleman can accept the offer. The Board cannot be forced into a thing like this under a threat.—The CHAIRMAN: It ' has always been my plan through life never to do anything by being driven. Here comes Mr. Hazlehurst with a threat and an attempt to drive the Board. We should be sorry no longer to seem him hers, but I think under the circum- stances that we ought to utterly ignore his offer. However, I leave it to you, gentlemen, to decide. If Mr. Hazlehurst likes to refer the offer back for further consideration.—Mr. BARLEHINIST: NO, I shall only leave the cheque here to-day. —The CEAIRMAN said he Mr. had no zdioeuhbutr sat m greatighdt eahlavmeighhits - be said on both sides. views on the matter' but he had not satisfied the Library Committee how far he was going to meet the expense of keeping the Library open every night. [Mr. Hazlehurst: It will all pass through my hands.] If he (the chairman) were not anxious for the success of the Library, he would ae— say, "Let him (Mr. Hazlehurst) have his own way; tha de, Library will come to grief in a twelvemonth." But he Wee 1 wished the Library success, and he advised Mr. Hazlehurst 12e.SW to pull quietly a little by putting the money towards buying e". books for the Library. Get the Library started first, and stet then open it as a reading-room. If Mr. flazlehurst wished to endow the Library with £2O or £3O a year, do so for the purpose of buying books. Then the Board would be happy to pull with him, but he could fairly say if Mr. Hazlehurst's offer was accepted that in the course of a few years the Library would be in a difficulty.—Mr. HAZLEIIIIRST : It could not be so, when I have given a guarantee that there shall be no financial difficulty.—The CHAIRMAN: A legal guarantee P.—Mr. HAI:LEW:MST : Yes.—Mr. NORMAN said he was sorry, as vbajeman of the Sanitary Committee, that Mr. Geo. Haele-

burst should have cast these reflections upon that commit- tee. He was sure that nothing could be fairer and put in better form than this matter was at the committtee. They had never tried to ignore the thing. At the meeting of the committee he suggested that they should allow that room to be open every night as a reading room until March, on the conditions that the expenses were paid, and he believed the members generally were in favour of that course. It was not required at the present time that there should be a reading room open all the day. As a member of that Board he should be sorry that any man should come forward and offer to pay for the removal of the Commissioners to Water- loo House. It would be a great shame if the Board were to accept a sum of money like £25 from any gentleman, to go forth to the wcrld that they, as representatives of the rate- payers, and acting in their interests, could not afford to re- move themselves. All the committee did was this : that if the Library Committee required that room they should have it every night by paying the expenses up to the 20th March, when the matter would be thoroughly gone into and settled properly.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : That is not on the minutes. —Mr. NORMAN : That is what we discussed.—Mr. Illarx- HURST remarked that that course would not me:A the case, , as three nights a week the room would be wanted for the lending library.—After some further conversation on another subject, the minutes of the Committee were passed.—Mr. liezrEnunsr then rose and said: Mr. Chairman, I beg to tender my resignation; and immediately left the room. COMMITTEES. The minutes of the Canal Boats Committee, which con- tained nothing of public interest, were read and confirmed, on the motion of Mr. FISHER, seconded by Mr. NORMAN.— The minutes of the General Purposes Committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. BRISCOE, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS, contained a recommendation that the market inspector be provided with a new uniform, cost not to exceed £5. In reply to a communication from the Committee, the secretary to the Gas Company wrote stating that the increased price of coal forbade any hope of a speedy reduc- tion in the price charged for supplying as to street lamps. —The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for October amounted to £515 12s. 7d.; and accounts amount- ing to £166 on general account and £llO on loan account were recommended for payment.—The c9llector was in- structed to give notice to owners of property in Ashbridge- street and rercivals-lane requiring payment of their accounts for street making within one month from the date of demand.—The minutes were passed on the proposal of Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN, seconded by Mr. BRISCOE. BILL OF MR. BEASLEY'S COSTS. Mr. LINAKER announced that the taxing master bad fixed Friday, at 11 o'clock, at London, to tax Mr. Beasley's bill of costs. On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. TIMMINS, it was decided that Mr. Linaker should attend on behalf of the Board. This was all the business.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.'
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.'

The monthly meeting Vas held at the Board Offices, Bridgewater-street, on Wednesday. The Rev. Canon Bar- clay presided, and there were also prtseat Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. J. Simpson, T. Norman, R. Lee, J. Prit- chard, P. Briscoe, and Rigby (clerk).

div.head: ASSISTANCIi FOR THEI VISITOR.
div.p: ASSISTANCIi FOR THEI VISITOR.

The CHAIRMAN said the first business was to discuss the application of Mr. Bowyer, the visitor, for an assistant in his duties.—Mr. :Bowvma was called into the room, and said that during the last month there had been 1,200 cases reported. The work had been increasing for the past five months, and he had more cases than he could attend to.— The CLERIC remarked that the routine work was continually increasing under the new code.—Mr. NORMAN moved that a man be appointed to assist the visitor in his indoor and out- door work for five hours each day at a salary of 10a. per week.—Mr. BRISCOE seconded the motion, which was car- ried.—lt was decided to advertise the situation. TUE BOARD AND INFECTIOUS DISEASES: IMPORTANT STATEMENT.

A letter was read from Mr. William Brookes, the secretary to the Commissioners, stating that the medical officer of health had presented a special report to the Sanitary Corn- mittee drawing attention to the large increase in the mor- tality at Runcorn during the past few months; also to the prevailing epidemic of measles and scarlatina, and during the present month (October), up to the 20th inst., five deaths had occurred from these diseases, and under these circumstances suggesting the temporary closing of all schools. The Commissioners respectfully asked that the managers of the several public schools in the towu take the suggestion into their serious consideration.—The Caen:t- wat : Shutting the door when the horse is stolen. If they had given that notice a month ago we should have been delighted.—Mr. SIMPSON: If they had proposed that action a month or six or six weeks ago it would have been reason- able, but the attendance since it reached the lowest point has increased more than one-half. The teachers say that there are comparatively few children ill in cases where our schools are affected.—The CHAIRMAN: That is just the case with ours. I wrote to Mr. Brookes acknow- ledging the:receipt of his letter, and told him so, saying that had it come three weeks or a month ago it would have been acted upon promptly, but as our schools had come to their tnormal average attendance, the managers did not think it necessary to follow their sug- gestion.—Mr. NORMAN: There is no pressure at all by the Commissioners. It is only to clear themselves.—The CLERK said the difficulty was in not checking the spread of the disease. The disease was not altogether spread by reason of the children going to school. Mr. Bowyer had reported a case where a man was living at one end of Runcorn in a house where there were three children suffering .from scar- latina or scarlet fever. One of the children died, was buried, and the other two still had it. Last week the parent removed from one end of Runcorn to the other, taking with him the bed the child had died upon. He was now living there, and in the house next to him there was a case of scarlet fever. There was not one when he went. If the Commissioners had prevented the removal of his chattels, they might have prevented the spread of the disease in that instance.—Mr. NORMAN said that man might have removed his family and furniture had the Board 20 inspectors. The Commissioners did not get a report of the cases of infectious disease from the medical gentlemen in the town, and they did not knew anything about these cases. The man in question might have removed to that house whilst he bad scarlatina in the family, and neither the Commissioners nor the inspector would know anything about it.—The CLERK : But in a town where the Sanitary Authority is singularly ac- tive a man if he were known to remove his chattels from one place to another when he had disease in the house, would be indicted and punished.—Mr. Normals was understood to say there might be that done now.—The CLERK said if in London there was a house known to be inhabited with chil- dren down with scarlet fever, and one died, that house would be put under some kind of inspection or supervision by the sanitary authority; and if the parent was known to remove his chattels to another part of the town he would be ; punished.—Mr. NORMAN remarked there was a case of small- pox which came down from Liverpool to Runcorn in a barge. It was reported to the authorities at the former place, but they refused to take any proceedings.—Mr. SIMPSON said there were instances where chaff beds from houses in which there was scarlet fever had been put upon waste land.—The CLERK asked suppose the case he had mentioned had come under the notice of the authority before the mischief had been done and precautions taken, would not that have been a check upon the epidemic P—Mr. NORMAN: How are you to get it ?—The CLERK: By appointing a sanitary inspector.—Mr. NORMAN: We have one.—Tho Climaxes( asked Father Fennelly how his schools were going on.—Father FENNELLY said he thought he had the poorest population in the district, and he had not had a single death from scarlatina or measles for three months.—The Clearneeees : Is the average attendance so low that you wish the schools to be closed?-Father FENNELLY replied in the negative, adding that he did not see the use of closing the schools.—Mr. NORMAN, answering an observation by Mr. rritchard, said the Commissioners never thought the schools would be closed.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that lie thought the epidemic was travelling from one end of the town to the other, and that was the reason he questioned Father Feenelly.—lt was decided to answer the letter from the Sanitary Committee by saying that for the most part the epedemic had subsided, that the number of children at school was increasing, and that the managers of the schools who were also members of the Board, considered there was no necessity to close the schools. THE SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION.

The CLERK 'read -sa'C'o-ni-nil;i-c;;;irOt; the Education Department, which stated that the recognised accommoda- tion afforded by Runcorn Trinity boys' school was 253, girls 156, infants 222, total 631; National, boys 389, girls 236, infants 290, total 915; Mill Brow 124; making a total accommodation for these schools of 2,713, being an increase of 424. The accommodation last year was 2,289. VISITOR'S REPORT.

The returns for the past four weeks ending October 20th, show a total number on the rolls at the public elementary schools of 1,848, and an average attendance of 1,709.8. The average attendance for the corresponding period of last year was 2,040.9, showing a decrease in the average attendance as compared with last year of 331. Number in attendance at private adventure schools, under 9d. per week, 74. In the retarns for the past four weeks, you will notice that that there is still a decrease in the attendance at the various schools. Measles and scarlatina have somewhat abated, bat they still are very prevalent, and many children are un- avoidably absent from school. During the past month I have taken proceedings against the list of parents ordered to be dealt with for contravention of the bye-laws. In 27 cases convictions have been granted, and the usual fine of ss. imposed. Seven cases have been proceeded with under the Canal Boats' Act, against parents who are in the habit of taking children on board their boats. In each case a fine was imposed, with a caution from the magistrates that in future they would have to see to their children attending regularly`to school. Three parents were apprehended under warrant for not appearing to the magistrates' summons. One Las been committed to prison in default of not paying the fine, and one case is adjourned until Monday, the parent haying absconded. There was no other business for disposal.

The reason why so many are unable to take Cocoa is that the varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plea of rendering them soluble; while really making them thick, heavy, and indigestible. This may be easily detected, for if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. Cadbury's Cocoa Essence is genuine; it is therefore three times the strength of these Cocoas, and a refreshinabeverage like tea or coffee.—,ddvt.

THE EXPENSES OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. CHAMBERS said that Mr. Hartley and he had waited on Mr. Dodson, the President of the Local Government Board, at London, with respect to expenses of Guardians whilst making enquiries into relief cases in the districts. Although their mission was not entirely successful, yet they had been received in a most courteous manner, after being introduced by Sir Richard Cross, and Mr. Dodson had re- quested Mr. Hartley to put their requests into writing, and send it to him, when he would give the matter his most careful consideration. With respect, however,_ to the ex- penses of the Guardians who attended the Poor Law Con- ference, Mr. Dodson said he could do nothing towards allowing them as the law stood at present.—ln answer to the CHAIRMAN, Mr. HARTLEY said he hoped to get the letter to the Local Government Board off that evening.
THE LATE MR. BAXTER. Mr. W. H. LINAKER read the following letter:— ..._

Acton Grange, September 25th 1882—Doer sir,—Allow'me 09 behalf of Mrs. Baxter and family, throu4h you, ts thank the Guardians of the Runcorn Union for their kind letter of con- dolence, which came duly to hand, and to say that it is a groat cAnfort to them, amid their sorrow, to know that he whom they loved so much was also so highly respected by the Board. At the same time please accept our thanks to you personally for your own words of comfort and consolation, for we know that your friendship was greatly esteemed by the late Mr. Baxter as it is by us.—Yours faithfully, FaaNcisi VAIRATTILST.—H. Linaker, Esq.

LECTURE BY THE REV. GEORGE HACK, OF RUNCORN- MEETING LAST NIGHT. Last evening, under the auspices of the Independent Order of Good Templets (Hope of Runcorn Lodge), the Rev. Geo. Hack delivered a lecture on " J. B. Gough: His life and work," in Camden School, Runcorn. Mr. Thomas Norman presided.—Mr. Gough, said the lecturer, was known to some of those present by sight and ear, and to most of them by reputation, as an accomplished teetotal orator, as possessing a magnificent voice, fine elocutionary powers, and as able to quiet a congregation into profound fend prolonged attention 1 while he delineated the terrific evils Of strong drink, and be- seeched the drunkard to abandon it entirely as the only hope of salvation. But that which constituted the chief consti- tuent or element in Mr. Gough's oratorical powers was the intense conviction inspired by experience of that of which he spoke. Having been drunken and enslaved into fearful degradation and misery; endured all the tyranny of an in- I satiable and maddened appetite; endured the appalling tor- ' tures of delirium tremens • and having been rescued through total abstinence, and uplifted into a Christian character and a splendid career of usefulness, they could imagine, there- fore, the force with which he spoke. Nay, his very appearance was a trophy of teetotalism, and afforded the public incontrovertible evidence of the power and value of temperance in rescuing men degraded, besotted; wallowing in habits worse than bestial; and restoring him to the throne of his manhood with his intellect exercising its royal functions, and his soul in restored fellowship with his God. Mighty as were the arguments of his speech, the argument of his presence was more powerful than them all. Notwith- standing that Mr. Gough might be considered an American by reason of his long residence in that country, he was an Englishman by birth, having been born at Sandgate, Kent, 22nd August, 1817. His parents were poor but respectable. His father was an old pensioner in the 40th and famous 52nd regiments, and fought in the Peninsular wars. At the age of 12 young Gough was bound for a certain period to a family who were going to America, on the condition that they should give him a trade and start him in the world. The family neglected this cendition, and his religious and secular education, and at the age of 15, with the consent of his father, he left them and made his way to New York,with only a single half dollar in his pocket. He obtained a situation and so prospered that he sent for his father, mother, and sister. The two latter arrived and lived with him, but in a few months, through depression in trade, they were reduced to extreme poverty. Whilst in these indigent circumstances, his mother died. Young Gough then obtained employment as a bookbinder, and commenced his sad career of dissipation. His habit of attending theatres was certainly a powerful factor in con- I tributing to his career of abject degradation and unutterable misery. There were respectable men and professing Chris- tians who would defend the habit of theatre going, and he (Mr. Hack) believed that by many it was consideced an evi- dence of narrow-mindness to condemn it. Well, approval or no approval from the audience, he unhesitatingly condemned attendance at theatres. There was a proverb "that a man Is known by the company he keeps." Let that be applied to theatres, and they stood condemned. Who attended them? The drunkard and the licentious, the gambler and the harlot, the infidel and the off-sc€:uring of society crowded there by the hundred and the thousand. Let a crowd of vultures swoop down to a place and they might be sure there was that against which all nature stood aghast— carrion. And so when any place was crowded by the immoral, by men to whom religion was a matter of buffoonery; to wham the sanctity of home, the sacredness of married life, and all the nobilities of life were as scorned things, then they might be assured there was spiritual death, and that it was no place for the Christian, the moral, and the youthful. What surrounded them ? Why, public-houses in exceeding number; and any place that was pre-eminently associated with the public-house, and to which the public-house was a necessity, could not be demonstrated to be good. What was the result of theatre attending? Why, appalling ruin—young men becoming dissipated, licentious, and impoverished was the result—young women becoming frivolous, drunken, and insensible to the sacred modesty of their sex, and living a I life of unutterable shame was the consequence. Young people, he warned them. Let but the habit of theatre going enslave them and farewell—farewell to all that was lovely in character, farewell to all that was noble in life, farewell to all that was successful in business. They launched themselves in a boat that would be tossed and dashed, shipwrecked and swallowed in the whirlwind that had crushed in its wrath unnumbered thousands. Dissent in sin was easy and startlingly rapid, and so J. B. Gough found it. Mr. Hack described the life of Mr. Gough whilst a drunkard, and quoted his own narrative of his terrible feelings whilst suffering from dilirium tremens. Describing the circum- stances of Mr. Gough's conversion to the principles of total abstinence, the lecturer said it were better to attempt to climb to the moon on a rope of sand, or to resist the mighty waves of the Atlantic tide by the babes of sand-heaps, than to attempt to cure drunkenness by moderate drinking. Why. the first glass to a drunkard's Eeppetite was like a lighted match to a powder magazine, like paraffin oil poured upon a slumbering fire—the very thing which would arouse the appetite te a craving beyond all mastery •, to a cry " give, give," so determined and importunate that the men must drink, ay, though it be with fearful remorse and terrific forebodings, and unto the tortures of despair. There was only one absolutely certain remedy, and that the total abstinence pledge given in the strength of almighty God. Mr. Hack eloquently contrasted the misery and wretched- ness of J. B. Gough's life when a drunkard and his power and happiness as a temperance orator. Sometimes scores, hundreds, and sometimes thousands had signed the pledge as the result of a week's or fortnight's mission conducted by him in any given place. He himself had a pledge book witd 150,000 names which he had personally taken. In conclusion, Mr. Hack made a passionate appeal to moderate drinkers to become teetotallers, and showed the rapid strides which temperance had made in private and public life dur- ng the past few years. The meeting closed in the customary way.

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. Yesterday the monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, when there were present Mr. W. Derbyshire (in the chair), the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. E. C. E. Cooper, J. Houghton, R. Kilshall, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. H. Gornall (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and G. Rawling (nuisance inspector). THE REMOVAL OF PAILS. The CLERK read the following coyy resolutions which he hail received from the Town Clerk of Warrington :—(1). "That it is net considered necessary to appoint a special inspector under the Alkali, &c., Works Regulation Act, 1881, to act within the borough, experience not having so far shown that the inspection by the general inspector under the Act is insufficient." (2). " That the removal of pails solely in the night time is impracticable at present, and that the request of the Rural Sanitary Authority that this should ,be done cannot be acceded to."—Mr. COOPER said I the second resolution was all nonsense; the pails were removed in the night time in other towns. He asked, sup- posing an order were made upon the Corporation to discon- tinue the nuisance, what would be the effect ?—The CHAIR- MAN thought they would not notice it. He, however, thought it would be practicable for the Corporation to cease the nuisance after nine o'clock in the morning. He asked what the Clerk's opinion was.—The CLERK was afraid the Authority had no control over the Corporation as to the removal of their pails.—The CHAIRMAN Said all the Autho- rity complained of was the passage of the carts through their district in the day time.—Some further discussion ensued, but ultimately the subject was dropped. LOVELY-LANE DRAINAGE. The SURVEYOR, in his report, stated that the inspector having reported the partial filling of this sewer with sedi- ment, he gave notice to the contractors that the Authority would hold him responsible under his guarantee. The con- tractor had been over, and with his (the surveyor's) assistant examined the sewer. In consequence of what was seen, he had given notice to Mr. Swabs to open a connection he had made with the sewer without his permission, for his inspection. He was now waiting a written intimation of when this connection would be open for his inspection, and he should report further to the Authority. Mr. Owen further reported that Mr. Job Swales applied to have a sewer laid in a new street, in the Lovely-lane drainage district, as he was about to build houses' and the sewer would be necessary. The new sewer would be about 200 feet long, and if done at the present time, before the land was filled up, it would be done at a cheaper rate. There was a balance in hand of £B2 15s. sd. from the loan of these sewers. If the Authority enter- tained the application—and there was no doubt about the sewer being required—he should require instructions to proceed with the drawings and specifications, and to procure estimates from the contractors the Authority might see fit to ask for tenders.—The report was adopted, and the requisite Instructions were given to Mr. Owen. BUILDING WITHOUT DEPOSITING PLANS. The SURVEYOR said the inspector having reported to him the following parties as building without having first de- posited plans, he (Mr. Owen) had in each case written to them, and had, where necessary, forwarded copies of the bye-laws :—Mr. Yates, addition to house, Padgate ; Mr. Wallington, new house, Grappenhall ; the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, pumping station at Bank Quay; Mr. Thos. Bennett, new building, adjoining farm, Padget°. LATCHFORD DRAINAGE. Mr. Omni submitted the report from the sub-committee appointed to consider the terms offered by the Corporation on the above subject (which had been previously published ' in The Examiner). The report stated that the sub-committee having considered the conditions, recommended the following , alterations as being necessary. (1.) That inasmuch as no surface drainage of land is to be allowed in the new sewers, the rate of id. in the £ for land be omitted. (2.) That a general reference clause be added to the agreement as to all matters and things. (3.) That otherwise the conditions be , generally acceded to. (4.) That a separate drainage dis- trict, consisting of the three township; of the union in the County of Chester and outside the borough boundary, be formed. (5.) That the surveyor be instructed to prepare the necessary plan of land likely to be built upon in the district, such plan to be approved by the authority and , attached lo the agreement. (6.) That the nature and value , of the machinery and works referred to in clause 2be de- fined to the authority by the Corporation.—The report was I adopted. This was all the business.

div.head: CONTAGIOUS DISEASES.
div.p: CONTAGIOUS DISEASES.

Mr. Brookes, clerk to the Runcorn Commissioners, wrote stating in reply to a communication from the Guardialas, saying that the Commissioners would be glad to co-operate with the Guardians in adopting such measures as might tend to check and stamp out contagious diseases; but the Com- missioners had not been advised of any cases, pauper or otherwise, which they could deal with or treat in the hospi- tal. They had, however, communicated with the medical gentlemen of the town asking them to advise the Board's sanitary officer of any contagious cases that arise, in order that he may apply disinfectants as necessary, and take such flat ther steps as he may deem advisable.

div.head: FINANTI.
div.p: FINANTI.
Rev. J. LOCKWOOD reported that the Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £35 173. ld.—Passed.
THB AUDIT.-A ROOM WINTID.

A. letter was read from the clerk explaining his non- attendance at the Board, and stating that much inconveni- ence and expense was caused to him by the auditor holding his audit at his office. He had therefore given him notice that he would have to find another place on the next occa- sion.—Mr. Dams, the auditor, wrote to say that he would hold his next audit at the Workhouse' with the permission of the Board.—The consideration of the matter was deferred until the next meeting ef the Board. HALTON PAROCHIAL MATTIRL—AN UNFOUNDED REPORT. Mr. LOCKWOOD said he had to bring forward a little matter in connection with his own township. As Guardian ef Halten, he was currently reported at the present mement as having shown great partiality and favour towards people who were members of the Church of England in his own township, and it made hint very unhappy in his mind. As the representative of the people of Halton, it was very un- pleasant that these remarks should be floating about, and he had asked the reason from those who had complained, but no case, except one, could be given. That case he wished to be brought before the Board. A woman came to him two months ago and asked him if he would endeavour to get her some relief, as her husband was ill. He told her to go to the relieving officer, informing her where and at what time he visited Halton, and tell him that he (Mr. Lockwood) had sent her, and he would do what he could to support her case. Next morning when Mr. Wright brought. his book before the Board and the cases were completed, he said to him—perhaps the chairman would remember it—" Have not you another case? Mrs. Moores, applying for her husband." Mr. Wright re- plied "No," and he (Mr. Lockwood) took no further notice about the matter as Mrs. Moores had not made a personal application to Mr. Wright. He thought it was only right that the Guardians should have this statement made pub- licly so that this report, which was so utterly untrue, would be silenced. He thought this was only fair. He should certainly have supported the case as far as possible, and he thought every Guardian ought to do the same in every case known to him, but the application should be made to the relieving officer in the first instance.—The CHAIRMAN: Is the allegation that you are unfair 2—Rev. J. LOCKWOOD : That I don't bring these cases before the Board.—The CHAIRMAN : You oannot de it.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD concurred, and added that he did not like these rumours floating about.—Mr. Nocauct : As a Guardian you are expected to do your duty for every person in the parish irrespective of creed.—The matter Chen dropped.

div.head: STATE OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: STATE OF THE HOUSE.

The MAYII3II reported that there were 192 inmates in the House, as compared with 190 in the corresponding week last year. During the week 29 vagrants had been relieved. There were 32 boys and 31 girls in attendance at school, and 12 boys and 13 girls were receiving industrial training. Oat-door relief Mad been given to 657 persons at a cost of £67 14s. id., as compared with 619 persons relieved at a cost of £6l ss. 10d. for the corresponding period of last year. This concluded the business.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday, when there were present Mr. S. Marsh (chairmln), the Revs. J. Barnacle. T, Chambers and Father Finegan, and Messrs. Lowe. New- some. Tyrer, W. B. Longton, Dobell, Birch&ll, Swift, Jack- son, Hall, Buckley, Saddler, Hulme, Leatherbirrow, Eitock, Griffiths, Kenwright, Fisher. Meadows and P. Longton. TRE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.
The Workhouse Master reported that there were 416 in- mates in the workhouse this week, as against 416 last week, and 471 for the corresponding week of last year. AN UNUSUAL COMMUNICATION.

The CLERIC read a letter from the Local Government I Board stating that Dr. Ricketts was appointed to the Sutton district, although he did not reside in that district, at a time when there was no resident medical practitioner; but the Local Government Board were informed that there was now a medical practitioner resident in the district, and they there- fore intimated that Dr. Ricketts' appointment should ter- minate at Christmas nest.—The CLERK said that was a most unusual communication, and it was evident that some one had been in communication with the Local Govern- ment Board. He (the clerk) had not been aware that there was any resident medical practitioner within that district, and he knew there was not at the time Dr. Ricketts was appointed.—Mr. LEATHERBA.RROW : Suppose we appoint Dr. Ricketts again 2—The CHAIRMAN : No, that would not do the Local Government Board says not.—The matter then dropped

div.head: SCENE.-A LESSON IN CHARITY.
div.p: A SCENE.-A LESSON IN CHARITY.

Mr. MEADOWS said be wanted to say a few words in reply to Mr. Chambers.—Mr. CHAMBERS (interrupting) : I beg to enter my protest against Mr. Meadows making any further reference to the chapel.—Mr. MEADOWS said it was an ex- planation of what he had said at a previous meeting. From the remarks made by Mr. Chambers at the last meeting he was evidently under the impression that he (Mr. Meadows) blamed Father Henry for the expenditure of money he had made for furniture for the worship of the Roman Catholics, but he did nothing of the kind as he considered the Roman Catholics were as worthy—Mr. CHAMBERS (again interrupt- ing) : I again prctest against Mr. Meadows going on, and appeal to the majority of this Board as to whether the sub- jc,ct has not been sufficiently ventilated.—Mr. BARNACLE: Let every man have his say. Mr. CHAMBERS: You have had yours.— Mr. BARNACLE: No, I have not; but I shall have it.—Mr. MEADOWS (resuming) said the same was due to the Roman Catholics as to the Protestants; the Roman Catholic had just as much right to furnish his chapel as the Protestant, but that was not what he meant at all. There was an application made to the Local Govern- aunt Board for permission te build a new chapel, which was to cost £l,OOO, but that amount had been exceeded by over £lOO, and, he said, it was a piece of injustice to expect the ratepayers to pay it. As was shown by Mr. Chambers himself, it was only after considerable difficulty that they could get three Guardians to sign the cheque, and, he repeated, it was a piece of injustice to expect the ratepayers to pay for that extravagance because it was clearly repre- sented that the chapel would only cost £l,OOO. If, as Mr. Chambers had said, he made a "hobby horse," he did not at any rate make a "hobby horse" of extravagance, and that remark of Mr. Chambers was quite tm- necessary.—Both Mr. Barnacle and Mr. CHAMBERS rose at this point, the latter gentleman eaying that he begged to assure Mr. Meadows that any jocular remark about his hob- by horse econotny was made as such, and he had not the slightest intention to wound his feelings, but if he had done so he heartily apologised.—Mr. BARNACLE said he had not made any speech in reply to Mr. Chambers' remarks.—Mr. CHAMBERS said he did, and he asked the chairman to put his foot down on the whole thing.—Mr. BARNACLE: I did not refer to you in the shameful manner you did to me; I have got a letter in ray pocket in which you had to retract what you said regarding me, and if you are the gentleman I always took you to be you will retract again before we separate. I wish the ratepayers to understand.—Mr. NEW- swim (interrupting): I beg to propose that the legitimate business for which we are assembled here be proceeded with. —Mr. Lown : I second that. Mr. BARNACLE: Am I to be gagged. There are certain assertions brought against me, and I think I should have a fair hearing. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN said he agreed with Mr. Barnacle, if it was an explanation of something that had been said there.—Mr. BARNACLE: It is.—The Cuernmerr then ruled that Mr. Barnacle was entitled to give his explanatien.— Mr. BARNACLE then said he wished to explain what had given but what ought not to have given, foundation to Mr. Chambers' remarks. Some weeks ago he attended a meeting of the Finance Committee, as a duty which devolved upon him as a Guardian, and on that day the particular account referred to, which he had not seen before, came before him, and it struck not only him, but also the rest of the Guar- dians present, as being an unusual one. Afterwpds, doing what he thought was his duty as representative ol Rainford, and without any feeling against either Father Henry or Mr. Chambers, he gave notice to the Board that he would at the next meeting propose that some explanation should be given of the matter. That was all he did, and he con- sidered that was his duty as a Guardian. But what took place? Mr. Chambers, of course, read it in the pa pers and then attacked him, and he asked anyone if it was just, as he

div.head: REPRESENTLTION OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE REPRESENTLTION OF WIDNES.

The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of his letter of the 23rd Oct., expressing the regret of the Guardians that the Board had not thought it expedient to authorise the election of two Guardians for the township of Widnes' and requesting the Board to re-consider their decision. The letter stated that the Local Government Board had given the further re- presentations of the Guardians their best consideration; hut they saw no sufficient reason to justify them in altering the decision contained in their letter of the 18th Oct. The Board would, however, in deference :to the wishes of the Gnardians issue an order authorising the immediate election of the Guardian for Widnes.—Mr. SADLER asked if there would have to be a special election for the one Guardian before next April.—The CLERK: Yes.

div.head: STAINED-GLASS WINDOWS FOR THE CHAPEL.
div.p: THE STAINED-GLASS WINDOWS FOR THE CHAPEL.

Mr. CHAMBERS said that since the last Board meeting be had had a communication from Mr. Garner, a St. Helens artist of some note, who told him that he had placed stained- glass windows into several churches. He (Mr. Chambers) did not think it was necessary to go to London for the glass if they could get it at St. Helens, and therefore if this gentleman could bring forward sketches which would show that he could do the work, he (Mr. Chambers) would be very glad to withdraw his motion with regard to getting the glass from Mr. Morris. (Hear, bear.)—The Board then adjourned.

THE REV. S. MEES, OF RUNCORN, ON SCRIPTURE AND SCIENCES On Wednesday evening the Rev. S. Mees, Wesleyan minister, Halton, delivered a lecture on "Scripture and Science" to the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Class, Runcorn. In the course of his remarks, Mr. Mees said it was one of the commonest and falsest statements heard in modern times that religion and science were hostile the one to the other. Undoubtedly there bad been con- tradiction of the flattest kind between the Bible and much that had passed current under the name of science, as well as between clearly ascertained facts in nature and much that had pessed under the name of Scripture. Still, he ventured to assert that between true science and Scrip- ture rightly read there would be found to exist the most beautiful and complete harmony. Nor should they con- found an hypothesis which might appear probable, but was by no means demonstrated, with facts which were so clearly proved that no intelligent person would ques- tion them. On the other hand, let them not confound their own or any interpretation of Scripture with Scrip- ture itself, or imagine that the grand old Book was in danger because their view of any portion of its teachings is shown to be untenable. Many apparent discrepancies r had been cleared up as knowledge had advanced. Might they not rest assured that in respect of certain difficulties not yet cleared up, the solution would by-and:bye be forthcoming and the harmony between revelation and nature be once more triumphantly vindicated ? Surely he would be a presumptuous man who should affirm that nature had no more secrets to disclose ; that all the scien- tific dogmas ef the day are infallibly ad i unchangeably true; and that none of them would ever be shown to be erroneous. None but a bigoted and ignorant person would dream that all was known of Scripture that was to be known—(applause)--or that many of their ideas of Holy Writ will not need to be revised under the additional light of advancing scholar- ship and of increasing scientific knowledge. The lecturer gave one or two examples of revision and cor- rection, which were furnished by the history of theological and philosophical thought. first referring to the constitu- tion of the solar system. He touched upon the Ptolemaic theory and the discoveries of Galileo, remarking,if the former agreed with the Book of Joshua did not the Copernician system disagree with it. If astronomers proved that the earth revolved, and not the sun, did not this show that the author of the Book of Joshua was ignorant of the facts of the case; that he stated what was disproved by science, and that consequently the Bible was mistaken, and therefore not inspired? It was not enough to answer that the Bible was not a book of science. If the Bible affirmed that which was disproved by an established fact of science, the Bible must be wrong, and their faith in its truth, inspiration and authority must be fatally shaken. Just as one theory a the solar system, when exploded, gave place to another, so the evidently false interpretation of the Ajalon episode had to be superseded by another equally feasible and more conson- ant with the proved facts of astronomy. Of course, the literal rendering was on all sides abandoned,and no one now thought that the sun and the moon were arrested in their flight through the heavens. Nor were they bound even to suppose that the motion of the earth was suspended. A miracle of some liind, by s hich daylight was prolonged, they must, of course, admit; but what the miracle was they were not bound by the terms used to explain. Did they net speak analogously in their every-day speech when they said that the min rises," knowing all the while he did not rise at all ? Moreover, as a recent writer had shown, the whole passage was intensely poetical, and to apply to it rigid and literal rules of interpretation would be unreasonable. At all events, they might safely sly that there was not neces- sarily a contradiction between the narrative in Joshua fairly read, and the universally admitted facts of astronomy, and that was all they needed. Take the question of the creation of the earth and the heavenly bodies. It was but a com- paratively short time ago that there was no such science as geology; and so long as that state of things continued there seemed to be no difficulty in accepting the "six days" of the first chapter of Genesis as natural days of twenty-four hours. But in process of time geologists proved incontes- tibly,first, that the earth must have existed many millions of years, instead of the 6,000 allowed by theologians. And next, that the creative processes described in the first of Genesis must have occupied not six literal days, but thou- sands of ages. Of course the religious world was alarmed, for did not these startling conclusions clash disastrously with the teaching of Moses? There were loud outcries against the wickedness of infidel science. But time and patience brought new light, and then it was seen that Moses might be as correct on the theory of millions of years as on that of thousands, on the theory of vast creational epochs as on that of six literal days. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." There was nothing in astronomy or geology which threw any doubt upon that, nor anything that Moses said to the contrary, that" beginning " may have been billions of centuries ago. Nor did he pretend to tell them how long the state of chaos lasted ; how wide was the gap between the beginning and the first divine attempt to create life and order. (Applause.) Another point of which a great deal had been made was that Moses represented light as having existed before the creation of the sun. This was . once thought to be a fatal impeachment of this accuracy; but now science itself had demonstrated not only that such a thing was possible, but there must have been light before the sun was condensed into its present form. Regarding the order in which the various forms of life appeared on the earth, the records of Moses were now believed to be in perfect accord with latest science. The lecturer referred to the speculation of recent years calculated to account for all existence on purely materialistic principles, and without the hypothesis of a Creator at all. It had been held that Moses taught a succession of separate acts of creation, whereas many scientists held that the study of the various forms of life, past and present, showed that the method was that of evolution or development. But a writer in a recent number of the Quarterly Review, whom he believed to be the Rev. W. H. Dallinger, one of their own ministers, declared, first, that separate creations were not necessarily affirmed by Moses; and next, if they were, the doctrine of evolution which -disproved them was itself not absolutely proved. (Applause.) He had but touched upon the fringe of an almost boundless question. Do not let them as Christians be jealous of science or afraid of new light from any quarter. Truth would survive all tests. Let not the man of science confund speculation with facts, and let not the man of faith fear that any fact of science would ever militate against the Word of eternal truth. (Applause.)—A discussion ensued, and remarks were offered by Messrs. Craig, Ohew, Glover, Frederick J. Norman, A. Harrison, 0. Leak, and T. Simister (the president).

'rim Comm.—Early risers in this district on Sun- day morning last had a view of this much talked of heavenly visitor. About half-past four it presented a somewhat dull hazy aspect, no doubt owing to the light shed abroad from an almost full moon. From five o'clock to half-past five, when the moon was obscured by clouds the appearance of the comet was extremely brilliant, and its long tail of a closed fan-like form deeply impressed the beholder. It is stated that the comet is the most magnificent and important cne within recollection, and it is even added by some writers that none for hundreds of years past have been equal to it.

ECARLET FEVER.—Throughout England scarlet fever is hay- ing its usual autumnal ravage. Preventive measures are desir- able in every house and imperative where there are young chil- dren. Put WRIGHT'S COAL TAR SOAP into bedroom, bathroom. and nursery, and take away all other soaps, no matter how agreeable they may be. Buy only the genuine, which is branded " Bap° Carbonis Detergens, Wright's."—AanT.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Japanese Government intends to order two ironclads to be constructed in England. At the Dublin Commission, yesterday, Judge Berry fined 109 jurors £5 each for non-attendance. At Leicester Assizes, yesterday, John Winzar, a solicitor's clerk was sentenced to 14 years' penal servitude for raising mortgages to the amount of about £2,000 by means of for- ged deeds. Their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales with suite arrived at Kings Lynn by special train from London yesterday evening, and afterwards drove to Sandringham. A dismounted detachment of the Second Life Guards, un- der Lieutenant Anstruther Thompson, arrived at Windsor yesterday evening from Egypt, having travelled via Ports- moath. The men met with a cordial reception from their comrades.
Yesterday morning P.C. Edworthy, of . the Darwen police

force, received a me—dal and clasp from the Royal litimane Society,London, for having rescued a married woman named Bury, a would-be suicide,.from drowning in a lodge at Dar- wen. The constable saved the woman at considerable risk to his own life, he having his clothes and heavy boots on at the time.

Dr. Harrison, the medical officer, has reported to the Local Government Board and to the Local Authority a serious outbreak of scarlet fever at Haslingden. There have already been five deaths, and in the doctor's opinion there are a large number of fever cases in the town. Dr. Harrison recommends the closing of the schools for a month, and his suggestion will come before the School Attendance Com- mittee.

div.head: EDINBURGH ELECTION.
div.p: EDINBURGH ELECTION.

The city of Edinburgh election resulted yesterday as follows :—Waddy, 8,455; and Renton, 7,718. This shows a majority for Waddy of 737. Both candidates were Liberals, and the vacancy was by Mr. Cowan (Liberal) re- tiring in consequence of ill-health. THE CHESHIRE HUNT.

The members are celebrating the opening week at Tar- porley, the headquarters being at the Swan Hotel. Among the members of the hunt at present staying there are Lords Combermere, Chesham, Cole,and Grosvener ; Maiors Little- dale and Dixon; and Mr. Corbett, master. The Duke of Westminster, who is a member of the hunt, has sent a pre- sent of a wild boar to grace the festive board. The sport every day has been good, but the weather is wretched.

DISASTROUS COLLISION: TWO STEAMERS SUNK. It appears from private information just received that a collision has occurred in the river Niger, on the West Coast of Africa, the injury sustained by the vessels being so serious that both of them foundered soon afterwards. The colliding vessels are stated to be the steamers White Rose and Iduna' the former belonging to Liverpool, and the 'dune to a French firm. No particulars of the disaster have been received, so that it is unknown whether any lives have been lost through the accident, or if the vessel had any cargo on board at the time. MAZEPPA SENT TO PRISON. Atithe County Sessions at Liverpool, yesterday, Zal Gay- ton, a circus artiste, who had appeared with great success at Sanger's and other circuses as " Mazeppa," and William Marshall, a theatrical business manager, were charged with stealing a quantity of wearing apparel from their lodgings in Bootle. The prisoners were found living together in Glasgow with the goods in their possession. The male prisoner was discharged, and the female, who said the goods were lent her, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment. SHOCKING AFFAIR IN THE UNITED STATES.

SIX PERSONS KILLED AND THIRTY WOUNDED.I A telegram from the Daily Naos New York correspondent states that a shocking loss of life occurred on Thursday in Kentucky, owing to the attempt by a mob to lynch two murderers who were in custody of the State Militia. A boy having discharged a piste', the Militia fired, wounding three persons, and afterwards killed six others who were mere spectators, besiles wounding about thirty more. DEPUTATION TO THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.

Yesterday a deputation from several West of England counties, waited upon Mr. Hibbert, at the Local Govern- ment Board, for the purpose of asking the government to make uniform the Berkshire system of administering relief to vagrants. The system is worked by the tickets which distinguish regular from casual tramps.—Mr. Hibbert, in replying, admitted the good working of the system, but said he did not think the Board would be able to recommend its adoption throughout the country. Such a system required the assistance of the magistrates to carry out, and the Local Government Board had no power over the magistrates of various counties. EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF CATTLE STEALING. The Broxton (Cheshire) magistrates were occupied until a late hour on Thursday evening investigating an extraor- dinary charge of cattle stealing, preferred against William Roberts, cattle dealer, Shocklack, Cheshire, and Samuel Lewis, butcher, Marchwiel, Denbighshire. It was alleged that the prisoners stole two heifers belonging to Mr. Joseph Hough, farmer, Shocklack, drove them to Messrs. Pickering and Nightingale's Auctiou Mart, at Chester, and sold them for £37 12s 6d. The cattle were entered in the name of Turner. Helsby and two witnesses identifizd the prisoners as the men who left them. Mr. Nightingale, who paid a cheque for the amount at which the beasts were sold in the name of Turner, could not identify either of the prisoners. For the defence four or five witnesses were called to prove an alibi, declaring that the prisoners were driving 15 miles from Chester at the time they were said to be in possession of the cattle at Chester. The prisoners were committed for trial.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE HOLY CARPET.—Mr. CHILDERS, replying to Mr. R. Fowler, said he had considered the subject of the British troops attending the departure of the IF)ly Carpet for Mecca, and justified the attendance to ensure order being preserved. Sir Garnet had furnished him with a memorandum on the sub- ject, which he would produce if required. LORD DUFFERIN'S MISSION.—Sir C. DILKE, replying to Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, said no representations had been made by any of the great powers with reference to Lord Dufferin's mission to Egypt. Represen- tations had been made by the Porte, but satisfactory expla- nations—stating no change in the diplomatic relations was intended—had been given. THE CLOSURE.—The adjourned debate on Mr. Gladstone's first resolution on procedure was resumed.—Mr. HARCOURT, who moved an amendment to provide that there should be a majority of five-eighths to put the Closure into operation. Simply, his amendment was, that in a House of eighty the assent of fifty members would be necessary.—Mr. GLAD- STONE objected to the proposal, and a discussien ensued.— Mr. CHAPLIN supported the amendment, and justified the Conservative party resorting to every technical right they possessed to defeat the measure, which they believed destructive to the 'rights of the House of Com- mons.—Mr. NEWDEGITE also expressed a similar opinion. —Mr. J. FOWLER supported the amendment, and justified many of the amendments now on the paper, notwithstanding the decision the House came to last night, on the ground that some of them might prove acceptable to independent members on the Government side of the House.—Mr. MAC- FARLANE opposed the amendment, and Mr. ASHMEA.D.. BARTLETT thought the extraordinary remedies proposed by the Government were not required, and that they were only proposed in order that some legislative measures might be thrust down the throat of Parliament.—Mr. DALY insisted the Conservative party were now wilfully wasteing the time of the House, and abusing the privileges of Par- liament by mere sham amendments.—Sir W. BARTELorr denied that the Conservatives, in the coarse they had adopted, had any desire of muzzling the Irish members.— On a division, there voted for amendment 70, against 146. The two next amendments, one standing in the name of Mr. McFarlane, and the other in that of Mr. A. Mike, were withdrawn, after a short discussion.—Mr. SALT moved an amendment to the resolution in order to increase the majority necessary to put the closure into force from two to three hundred.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the acceptance of the amendment would practically be sweeping away, nearly in its entirety, the fabric they were engaged in setting up.

TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAB FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Bell, Let out on Hire, or Parchase, Lease, GAS COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be s3lected from the best makers for economy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, will lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.
